speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will address the important Budget announcements related to Singapore's long-term future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thereafter, I will make some broad comments about the Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And finally, I will speak on Singapore's fiscal situation and the Government's Budget marksmanship.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, the big picture and our physical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The development of Tuas Port and Singapore's record highs in vessel arrival, tonnage, container throughput and bunker sales have, in the words of the Finance Minister, reinforced Singapore's role as a leading maritime hub.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are no mean feats and Singaporeans are proud of the achievements of all who made this happen.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The future is exciting and we will herald more changes and transformation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The advent of nuclear power and the signing of the "123 Agreement" on civil nuclear cooperation with the United States (US) portends a future in Singapore that comes out of science fiction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even the import of electricity from neighbouring countries may be difficult to fathom for some Singaporeans more used to scenarios from not too long ago, where acrimony surrounded the purchase of critical resources, such as water.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is not out of place for the public to ask important and far-reaching questions on nuclear safety and resource resilience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Equally legitimate, are queries on the cost implications for Singaporean households.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What will be the impact on the bills for clean power, compared to those for electricity generated by fossil fuels?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As these and other new vistas open, from artificial intelligence (AI) and sustainability to climate change, Singaporeans must be well-prepared by our education and retraining systems, to be the ones best placed to take on the jobs in these areas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Finance Minister has sought to assure the public of the Government's intentions in this regard, and there is significant public interest in seeing Singaporeans compete and succeed in securing jobs, created or transformed by these developments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Coming on the cusp of General Elections, that Budget 2025 would be an "Election Budget" was not a surprise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister and Finance Minister, and Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong had set the stage by providing numerous assurances that cost of living concerns would be addressed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The concerns on the ground about cost of living are known to all in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We started the first Budget of this Government's term in 2021, with the disbursement of Community Development Council (CDC) Vouchers worth $100.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Cost increases have hurt people from across all segments of society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Beyond the $800 CDC Vouchers and $800 SG60 vouchers, more than a few political watchers noticed the People's Action Party (PAP) Members of Parliament (MPs) thumping their armrests in unison when the Finance Minister announced that Climate Vouchers worth $400 were being extended to private household dwellers too – a relatively small and, generally, more well-off segment comprising of about 15% of our population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Reflecting on the cost of living crisis, this enthusiastic gesture was both telling and ironic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But for many, the lived reality of Singaporeans over the last 12-odd months does not correspond with the bright summary revealed by these figures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Life is very tough for the Singapore that is in the heartland.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Concerns over jobs, prices, housing costs and opportunities continue for many Singaporeans and their households.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The numerous vouchers will give us help for a little while, but not for long.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After all, no Goods and Services Tax (GST) Offset Package lasts forever.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the first time ever, our total population crossed six million.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The 2019/2020 Housing and Development Board (HDB) annual report stated that the projected ultimate number of dwelling units in Singapore would be slightly above 1.55 million.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: According to the latest HDB report for 2023/2024, this number has gone up by 53,000 dwelling units even as the earlier number of 1.55 million was not intended to be a target to be reached, according to the answer to a Parliamentary Question (PQ) given to Sengkang Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Member of Parliament Mr Louis Chua in 2021.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the ultimate dwelling units number is not a target, on what basis is it moving upwards?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For some, these realities make the Singapore of tomorrow a difficult one to imagine and for others, a difficult one to find affinity with.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With finite land, other Singaporeans question, in the interest of their children, how many more does the Government seek to squeeze in?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And what cans are we kicking down the road for future generations of Singaporeans, who will live in a far-denser city than today?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2017, it was announced that auxiliary police officers (APOs) would be hired from Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Last month, the Ministry of Home Affairs confirmed that it was looking at hiring APOs from China, India, the Philippines and Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few days ago, it was announced that the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) would be looking to hire foreigners as paramedics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With a growing population and a manpower shortage in many areas, it is inevitable that more of such basic manpower needs of our country will go down a similar path.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Alongside these recruitments are fears that Singaporeans may face competition from foreigners who apply for some of these jobs, which were traditionally filled by Singaporean men and women.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Integration and a sense of rootedness will continue to be a major issue in Singapore in the years to come and no amount of vouchers can make people feel rooted to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government is aware of this and it is no surprise to hear Government leaders extolling the importance of unity and integration of foreigners into Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This issue continues to be a soft underbelly of our society with fault lines that can be easily exploited.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Government policy leaves much to be desired, for example, with democratically elected opposition MPs being kept away from new citizens during their citizenship ceremonies by design – ostensibly for political expediency and advantage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Creating a sense of unity in Singapore is a work-in-progress that is made tougher by the PAP itself, when it hamstrings integration efforts with such small-minded and short-sighted policies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While there are even more newcomers to the scene, a CNA report earlier this month identified the entry of cash-rich foreign players, prepared to pay higher rents and salaries as a reality of the local F&B scene.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In business circles, the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone, while on the whole received positively, has also raised concerns about the hollowing out of businesses in Singapore, particularly, those that serve the Singaporean middle class.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Arising from the cost-of-living crisis, the increase of the costs of basic goods in Singapore leads many Singaporeans to make regular trips across the border, to extract a good 30% or more in savings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Services are cheaper in Johor Bahru too, from seeing a dentist to getting a thorough health check-up at a reputable private medical facility.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the Johor Bahru–Singapore Rapid Transit System Link starting operations in 2026, many businesses will have to seriously review how far they can expect Singaporeans or other local customers to continue patronising them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also remains to be seen how long bookstores and cinemas will be able to continue surviving in Singapore, and whether the Government is prepared to offer such businesses a helping hand with grants or by requiring building owners to reserve a portion of their built-up areas for such businesses, to ensure that Singaporeans have localised, high quality, holistic and affordable options within our borders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In May last year, I asked a PQ on JTC and whether it was empowered to lease industrial properties to local small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) at a discount to the market rate, and whether the Ministry had plans to expand schemes that reduce business costs for local SMEs by way of lower rentals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister for Trade and Industry shared that his Ministry and the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) had formed an Alliance for Action (AfA) on business competitiveness to deep dive into how businesses can remain competitive amid global uncertainties and structurally higher business costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the AfA's business competitiveness report released last November covered a range of business related issues, in the main, they addressed matters specific to bigger enterprises.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the Government the largest landowner in Singapore and a not insignificant player in the in the industrial space, land costs and rentals are something that need to be looked into more acutely to appreciate the challenges to business and entrepreneurship in the immediate term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On a separate note and to assist more SMEs, some measures announced at the Budget should be reviewed immediately.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, the Government should free the second portion of the SG60 Vouchers for use anywhere beyond just participating supermarkets, to include all small businesses and shops located in shopping malls too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Apart from helping SMEs, this will enlarge choice for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) spoke on the cost-of-living crisis in a Motion this House debated about 18 months ago, where we looked beyond voucher relief towards structural changes to address the cost of living, looking at utilities and healthcare among others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, and among other subjects, I will revisit the subject of land costs for Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats in the Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Apart from the goodies that were expected in this Budget, it was the fiscal position at the end of the term which raised many eyebrows.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government's exceedingly healthy fiscal position has led many Singaporeans to question why the GST had to be raised in 2023 and 2024.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And if one casts their memory back earlier in this term, it was estimated by the Government that 2021 and 2022 would see deficits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, these turned out to be surpluses instead.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some years ago, I spoke of how the chill felt by some multinational enterprises (MNEs) in Hong Kong could result in an advantage for Singapore, as these businesses relocated to other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The increase in corporate income tax collection, overtaking even the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) has been attributed to a change in the investment decisions of MNEs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With another $3 billion devoted to the National Productivity Fund, in addition to the $2 billion last year, all things being equal, it is hard to see how Singapore would suddenly turn unattractive, despite the US withdrawal from BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fiscal situation appears healthy, notwithstanding the absence of financial medium-term projections, which other jurisdictions publish.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This naturally has led many to question the necessity of raising the GST.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP raised this matter on numerous occasions in this House, even participating actively to consider alternative levers of revenue in the Budget debate of 2023.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even as imported inflation contributes to price rises locally, there was no need for the PAP Government to add fuel to the fire and fan the flames of inflation further with the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if a decision was made to raise it in 2023, there was ample policy space to delay the second increase in 2024 when the country was in the thick of inflation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Why the PAP went headlong and headstrong into raising GST, and thereby turbocharging inflation further, is something only the PAP itself can answer to Singaporeans for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As every Singaporean knows, a 1% rise in GST does not lead to a 1% rise in the cost of a cup of coffee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Increases are incremental, as we have experienced in how purchases from the local shop or weekly supermarket trip have cost a good 30% to 40% for Singaporeans since the GST was hiked in an inflationary environment never seen before in decades.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The decision to go ahead with the GST hike, with inflation raging, was poor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have seen Assurance Packages and CDC Vouchers dished out to cushion the GST blow for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But when these handouts stop, as they eventually will, the 9% GST will remain, until any subsequent increase the PAP Government sees fit to impose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would not be out of place to ask then, how many Singaporeans would believe the accuracy of a PAP Government's projections about the need or the immediate need for future expenditures?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government has shown poor fiscal marksmanship in trying to match Singapore's expenditure needs with revenue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fairness, at last year's Budget, I recounted the reflection of economists quoted by The Straits Times, who commented that it was getting very hard to project Government revenue because budgeting accuracy in specific tax collections could vary between 17% and 27%, and that gone were the days when Budget marksmanship of 2% was the norm.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans would not be out of place to ask: why is there a need to collect so much money when the Government's fiscal projections are so unpredictable, but somehow always so healthy when elections have to be called?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I am sure the fiscal headroom is politically attractive and even desired by the PAP at the end of the term, notwithstanding its constitutional obligations, it should not underestimate the correlation between this poor marksmanship and potential public cynicism in future when taxes must be increased for legitimate reasons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I anticipate the Finance Minister to reply that all these increases were either down to one-off abnormalities or upsides that could not be anticipated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if we accept this, the Government's poor fiscal marksmanship raises and strengthens a different argument – and that is, that the money set aside for spending can certainly be accounted for in a more institutionalised fashion with greater public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP brought up the idea of an independent Parliamentary Budget Office at the beginning of the term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was roundly rejected by the former Finance Minister and with the Leader of the House positing that it would only benefit the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues and I beg to differ; and perhaps in light of unpredictable projections, such an institution would also benefit the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Compared to 10 years ago, total public expenditure has close to doubled in nominal terms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The age-old question of greater fiscal accountability and the introduction of institutions that track and account for public expenditure in a dedicated manner are ideas whose time has come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, and in the throes of COVID-19, the Government committed $25 billion to fund its Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 (RIE2025) plans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the name of fiscal prudence, is it out of place to ask how well these monies have been spent?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Have the plans proved to be value for money?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The public has a right to know because while expenditures can be tracked, tracking returns is a different matter altogether.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the same vein, it would be important for the Government to issue a report card on initiatives that have come to an end.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, when the Capability Transfer Programme was first mooted at Budget 2017, the aim of the programme was to improve local foreigner workforce complementarity by facilitating transfer of capabilities from foreigners to locals, with the goal of ensuring that there is a sufficient supply of Singaporeans with the requisite job skills.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A number of Members, including myself, have spoken or asked questions about the programme during this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope to see the Ministry of Finance's occasional papers reporting on the outcomes of such initiatives, complete with an impact assessment on jobs and opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Only then can better alternatives be promulgated and advanced, not just by the Opposition, but by ordinary Singaporeans who care about their country and the direction it is headed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As I have said so previously, the new social compact between citizen and state, as flagged by Forward Singapore (Forward SG), demands it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our social compact would be strengthened by such accountability for public expenditure and programmes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This scrutiny would represent a different approach to governance, but it is one that the WP would opine is the expectation of a participatory society and of the Singapore that is imagined by the Forward SG report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They stand to change Singapore for the better.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, there is a bigger picture whose focus has changed even more sharply since the inauguration of the Trump Administration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Much international media attention was focused on the phrase "landlord seeking rent".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, I found the question put to his audience at the end of the speech more significant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The question was, "who, if anyone, any one country or region or bloc, can step in if the US declines to protect the global commons, and how effective and against what resistance".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is even as the 2024 Asian Barometer Survey believe that China far outstrips the US in influence over Asia and this gap will only widen going forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is the perspective of Singaporeans who were surveyed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, Sir, and in my last Budget speech, I devoted a final section on a call to strengthen our national unity – a multiracial national unity – in an uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The security these agencies provide is an important source of strength for Singapore and all Singaporeans must give our men and women in uniform our full support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At its core, we adhere to two key main thrusts, to achieve long-term fiscal sustainability: firstly, consistent prudent financial management; and secondly, growing the economy to generate sustainable streams of revenue.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It has served us well all these years and has, time and again, enabled us to make available substantial fiscal resources in each Budget to deal with both the immediate and longer-term challenges, as well as still have the financial means to invest into the future, whether it is to enhance our economy or to improve our social well-being.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We see that manifest again in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The immediate task, of course, on hand, remains to help Singaporeans tackle cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Support schemes have been upsized, such as the CDC Vouchers and the U-Save Rebates, and more broad-based schemes added, such as the Child LifeSG Credits and expanded Climate Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are over and above the Enhanced Assurance Package and other earlier announced support packages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is also more support for families and the seniors, such as the Large Families Scheme, the Matched MediSave Scheme, the enhanced support for long-term care costs and the enhanced Home Caregiving Grant, to mention a few.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These assistances are spread across most calendar months, till January 2026.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Taken together, these support packages amounted to substantial assistances for each family.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the Budget Statement speech, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also signposted the potential future deployment of nuclear power in Singapore, given the promising developments of safer operational small modular reactors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This could be a game changer in our efforts to build energy resilience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme that supports mid-career Singaporeans to reboot their skills has been enhanced to include part-timers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A new SkillsFuture Workforce Development Grant and the redesigned SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit have been introduced to provide funding support to companies for job redesign activities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are again, over and above the comprehensive set of schemes introduced to support workers in earlier Budgets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In each of our Budgets, we make sure that we always have the fiscal capacity to carry out the key priorities of the Government, many of which are multi-year commitments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The ability to always have significant stable funding to tackle short- to longer-term challenges and yet able to invest for a better future and, of course, still have savings for rainy days is what makes Singapore's budgets unique and distinctive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many governments in the world would find achieving this an uphill task or an almost impossible task to achieve.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, let us look at a jurisdiction quite similar to us: Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A city economy and a financial centre like Singapore, Hong Kong has been running persistent large deficits in the last three years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In fact, in the last five years, they have run into four deficits.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the current fiscal year, it is estimated that Hong Kong will, again, run into deficit to the tune of around HK$100 billion or S$17.1 billion.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is more than what they have forecast at the start of the year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Recently, the Hong Kong Financial Secretary has assured the Hong Kong public that its government aims to balance the book in the next two to three years, "primarily through reducing expenditures, complemented by generating revenue".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What that could mean is that the Hong Kong government would likely have to either raise taxes and fees, or to significantly cut expenditures, or to do both to reduce the large deficits.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Otherwise, the Hong Kong international ratings may be at risk of being reviewed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the case of Hong Kong, revenue from land sales form a major source of the government's revenue unlike Singapore and it has seen significant decline due to weaker property market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Based on reports, they have also dipped into their fiscal reserves and which has seen shrinkage to the tune of about 40% from the high.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Today happens to be Hong Kong's budget day and their Financial Secretary has started his speech, so we will wait for more details from there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But Sir, I want to say that I do not wish to critique on Hong Kong's fiscal management, but there are valuable learning points for Singapore here.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What happened to Hong Kong, in terms of running multi-year budget deficits, can happen to Singapore as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Especially in our case, where we have other big-ticket spending items, like defence and foreign affairs as well as strategic areas that we need to invest and commit capital expenditure, such as water and energy security.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Unlike Hong Kong, we also do not have the hinterland of China to help us underpin or backstop the economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, for Singapore, it goes back to the twin mantra that I mentioned at the start; prudent fiscal management and growing the economy to generate top-line revenue; which are critically important to achieve long-term fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Being prudent has never failed us in our history.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It strengthens our financial position for the longer term and provide insurance against our inherent vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the years, the Government has stepped up spending in more areas, in particular, healthcare and social support spending.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They have all increased significantly and would continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are commitments that the Government made to our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It gives Singaporean a peace of mind that the Government have their backs and the people take our assurance that the Government will have the sustainable funding to continue providing the subsidies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Just imagine, if we mismanage our finances and are no longer able to fulfil these commitments, it would immediately add anxieties to Singaporeans and, of course, to impact the quality-of-care that they would receive later.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the report, it mentioned Singapore as having an international reputation for fiscal discipline in budgeting and policies and that has helped ensure Singapore's long-term fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It credited the Government of Singapore as having "a well-defined budget framework with clear fiscal objectives".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It said the fiscal rules, such as the Constitutional requirement to maintain a balanced budget over each term of Government, instill responsible budgeting.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The report also mentioned that these tax changes has made our tax system more progressive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It reflects the value system of this Government and is the foundational bedrock that will ensure Singapore's long-term survivability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the Budget speech, the Prime Minister shared that we are now in a fragmented and troubled world, with the situation likely to worsen in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore, once again, has to find ways to navigate a turbulent and troubling external environment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Like Hong Kong, Singapore is also exposed to the escalating trade tensions, including the potential knock-on effects of a slowing global economy as a result of the trade war.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given this backdrop of greater global uncertainty and downside risks, the last thing we want is to face this turbulent landscape in a position of weakness.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We neither have the domestic scale, the size nor the hinterland to help us to buffer the external shocks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, Singapore must brace the future unknowns and uncertainties that will surely come in a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our strong financial position is the best defence and insurance to protect Singaporeans from effects of external shocks, some of which could devastating or prolonged.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, let us not give away that security cover and as a result, fully expose Singaporeans to the ill-effects of any crisis that comes our way.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In Mandarin):   First, I want to highlight a unique aspect of our Budgets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Prudent fiscal management has enabled us to have substantial financial resources in each Budget to address the challenges before us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For instance, in this Budget, we continue to strengthen our efforts to help Singaporeans cope with the current high costs of living.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Furthermore, we ensure sufficient fiscal resources to tackle our medium- and long-term challenges.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These include building more healthcare facilities to meet the demands of future demographic changes, developing long-term stable energy supplies, rejuvenating our towns sustainably, strengthening our national security and defence, and caring for vulnerable groups in our society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Few countries' budgets can match Singapore's fiscal strength – not only can we address immediate needs, but also pave the way for future development, ensuring steady progress and giving Singaporeans peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the saying goes, "Caution enables a boat to sail for thousands of years." Since Independence, we have upheld the philosophy of prudent fiscal management.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This has allowed us to accumulate valuable resources and prepare for future challenges, greatly enhancing our ability to respond to various international crises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is indeed our best strategy to enable Singapore to develop and prosper with stability and resilience. : Sir, in this Budget and the one before, many of our wish lists were answered.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am pleased that a number of my suggestions to the Prime Minister, have also found its way into the Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Indeed, many ideas and suggestions from Singaporeans were taken on board, especially those from the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Although it should be noted that the Assurance Packages in earlier Budgets would have delayed the effect of the GST rates increase by at least five years for the majority of Singapore households.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And with this Budget on, it could be delayed further.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In Budget 2024, the corporate income tax was initially estimated as $28.03 billion and later revised to $28.38 billion.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I can understand that with a stronger than expected economic growth in 2024, the corporate income tax revenue is expected to rise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Conversely, if the economy slows, or enter into a recession, there could be downside to corporate income tax.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These large capitalisation numbers get added into the overall fiscal position and contributed to the larger overall surplus numbers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to seek clarification from the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister, as to why are these capitalisation values being added to the overall computation of the fiscal surplus?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Is this capitalisation an accounting item or is it a cash item that can be used to fund current expenditures?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I applaud the Government for introducing the Large Families Scheme to support families with three or more children.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having more kids would also mean higher household expenditures for families.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, any additional assistance and support would be welcomed by families.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask if the Government can extend this rationale of support to housing as well?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is understandable that families with three or more children would also need more spaces in their home.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I hope HDB can look into helping these larger families and consider giving them priorities when they apply for bigger flats, like the 5-room flats.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, this year, I would like to put up a similar request for the Government to consider another once-off subsidy should the Public Transport Council again recommend to increase the public transport fare.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It would go a long way to help relieve public transport costs for commuters and, hopefully, help nudge more to move towards a car-lite society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Budget measures help to ease their financial burdens and ensure that they can continue living with dignity and security in their homes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, I would like to centre my speech on three areas: one, evolving our housing and national development policies to further support social mobility and community development; two, developing a holistic model to enable seniors in private estates to age in place; and three, ensuring that Singapore fully harnesses the potential of AI by building a national AI system that is anchored in our values.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These are critical issues that will shape our society and economy for the future, and I believe that we must act decisively to ensure our policies remain inclusive, forward-looking and resilient.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Singapore's property market has remained strong, despite multiple rounds of cooling measures introduced in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This underscores the resilience of our housing market, but it also raises questions about affordability and accessibility for some young families and first-time buyers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, the global economic uncertainty – rising interest rates, inflationary pressures and external shocks – not to mention the looming trade war, adds to the complexity of ensuring that our housing policies remain sustainable and equitable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In this context, it is critical that we continue to strengthen access to homeownership without destabilising the long-term value of our housing market.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And this is why some of the proposals put forward in this House over the last few years merit serious scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This will put downward pressure on resale values, affecting homeowners who have spent decades building their housing equity in their flats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Meanwhile, the Millennial Apartments Scheme, which expands the state-controlled rental housing, could dampen demand for both resale HDB flats and private estate rentals, reducing rental yields and making it harder for homeowners to monetise their flats in their later years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am raising this issue because for many in Kebun Baru – my constituency – their HDB flat represents not just a home, but a key pillar of their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A sudden depreciation in housing prices or rental values would mean less financial security for seniors looking to right-size or lease out their flats to support their retirement.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must not take housing price stability for granted.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In China, housing values were seen as rock-solid – until they were not – and now millions of homeowners face uncertainty and financial distress.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sweden, Germany, South Korea and New Zealand have seen meaningful drops in their property market value in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Singapore's housing market is built on trust, careful planning and a fair balance between affordability and asset appreciation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If we introduce policies that artificially suppress resale values and weaken the rental market, we risk shaking that foundation, eroding confidence and hurting homeowners who have worked hard to invest in their future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: While we should always strive to make housing affordable for young families and first-time buyers, we must do so without destabilising the savings and retirement planning of existing homeowners.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our push should be one of careful balance, not drastic experiments with uncertain outcomes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The recent Plus/Prime/Standard model is a powerful way for us to ensure that many Singaporeans, even those with less income, have a chance to stay at central locations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Specifically, we can look at the income ceiling and supply of or executive condominiums.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This allows them to own their own quality homes at reasonable prices, rather than being placed into the much higher price points of private condominiums.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And now that the supply and demand is more in balance for the BTOs, I believe it is a timely period to consider this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, increasing the supply of executive condominiums – our hybrid housing model – will provide not just aspirational yet attainable housing ownership for Singaporeans, ensuring that we preserve the well-structured housing ladder that has been a key driver for our social mobility.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By strengthening rather than disrupting the existing system, we can make housing ownership more accessible for the next generation while ensuring that the housing market remains stable and resilient.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Singapore's public housing market has been one of the most successful in the world, precisely because it balances affordability with long-term value retention.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Instead of drastic experiments that risk destabilising housing values and retirement adequacy, we should enhance our current framework to help young Singaporeans own homes without compromising the financial well-being of existing homeowners.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is how we can continue to preserve the ladder of social mobility, ensuring that capable and hardworking Singaporeans can progress in life without extreme financial stress or strain or undue reliance on family wealth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond ensuring housing affordability and stability, the Ministry of National Development (MND) can also play a greater role as an enabler of evolving social needs, making our neighbourhoods more vibrant and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One way of doing so is by working with National Parks Board (NParks), volunteers and grassroots organisations to fully activate our community parks, particularly in private estates, where community engagements may be more limited.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of these green spaces remain underutilised when they could be more active social hubs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, I recommend that NParks could facilitate the development of community-driven amenities, such as public tennis courts similar to what you see in Luxembourg Gardens and Paris, or designate, let us say, pickleball courts, creating accessible space for sports and recreation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Additionally, investing in infrastructure to support Sunday markets – such as power and water access for pop-up stalls – could transform these parks, including the upcoming beautiful Hillrock Park within Kebun Baru, into vibrant weekend markets, gathering sports, sparking stronger community bonds and giving local entrepreneurs a platform.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These are very important steps to ensure that our senior Singaporeans, regardless of where they stay, can continue to age in place safely and with dignity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of these seniors, especially those in our private estates, face unique challenges when it comes to home accessibility and care support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Government's efforts to extend accessibility and upgrade and retrofitting private homes with elderly-friendly features are truly commendable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, I believe that more can be done to help frail seniors, especially those in private estates, to remain independent and well-supported in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One important way is to build Active Ageing Centres within large parks within private estates, such as the Kalidasa Estate, which is part of the Teachers Estate in Kebun Baru, which is also going to be benefitting from the upcoming Estate Upgrading Programme for Silver Estate soon.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We can go beyond physical infrastructure to rethink how Active Ageing Centres can operate within these private estates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This will allow frail seniors to benefit from structured engagement within their parks near their homes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A trusted digital platform could help caregivers, whether it is children, grandchildren or domestic helpers, to track services, billing and medical needs in real-time, reducing the stress of care coordination.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond structured care, technology can also empower caregivers and improve emergency response.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One simple but powerful step is to extend the Singpass app and our seniors for local activities, while caregivers can authorise key decisions remotely.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With proper safeguards in place, this could significantly reduce response times in life-threatening situations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To truly build an ecosystem of care, we must bring together the private sector, residents and Government agencies to design a comprehensive framework that ensures that every senior, whether in HDB or private estates, receives the support they need.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In Kebun Baru, we have one of the largest numbers of seniors living in private estates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If there is anything I can do as a Member of Parliament to push this agenda forward, I will be happy to step up to work with the Government, industry and community to make these ideas a reality.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Ageing in place should not be a privilege; it should be a right, supported by the best that our society can offer.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Lastly, I like to touch about how Singapore can fully harness the potential of AI by building a national AI system that is anchored on our values.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: AI is advancing at an unprecedented pace and we are rapidly approaching a future where AI will surpass human capabilities in certain domains.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sam Altman, chief executive officer of OpenAI, has observed that AI programmers could soon be among the best in the world within the next few months.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Meanwhile, Google DeepMind's AlphaFold 2.0 has effectively solved the complex challenge of protein folding, opening up revolutionary possibilities in biological and pharmaceutical research.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These breakthroughs demonstrate that AI will fundamentally reshape industries, scientific discovery, and global competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is not an issue of whether AI will transform economies; it is a question of whether Singapore will lead or follow in this transformation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In the 1990s, Singapore was ahead of the curve in embracing digitalisation and computerisation, even before its full potential was clear.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our early investments paid off, enabling us to build a highly efficient and technology-driven public sector that continues to serve us well today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must apply that same foresight to AI.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We have a unique opportunity to leverage AI to enhance governance, streamline public service, reduce regulatory complexity for businesses, and empower our research institutions to push the frontiers of science and technology.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By embracing AI early, we not only improve governance but also strengthen Singapore as a trusted global hub for AI innovation, ethics, and responsible deployment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, deploying an AI at a national scale is far more complicated than simply subscribing our civil servants to existing AI tools.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Large enterprises and our Government cannot simply embrace and adopt generic AI models off the shelf.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Doing so would pose risks to security, regulatory compliance and adherence to our national values.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Even cutting-edge AI systems, such as Palantir, which integrates truth-seeking AI models like Grok, may not always align with Singapore’s approach to governance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Such models may optimise for efficiency and raw intelligence, but they may not fully account for humanistic considerations, such as social harmony, security and ethical decision-making.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must ensure that our AI systems are both powerful and aligned with our national priorities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But this does not require us to reinvent the wheel.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Instead, we could consider collaborating with AI service providers that prioritise ethical AI alignment, such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Rather than building costly AI infrastructure from scratch, we can finetune existing models to align with Singapore's governance framework and cultural values.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is especially since we may face increased restriction on AI-compute power from America's likely AI-deficient loop.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Once finetuned, the national AI model can then be deployed within Singapore, using both locally controlled AI data centres for inference and integration with sensitive national datasets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This hybrid approach balances cost-effectiveness with security, ensuring that Singapore has full control over critical AI decision-making or minimising infrastructure investment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Building a national AI system, finetuned for Singapore's values, is not just an option.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: AI-driven governance and business processes will increasingly shape regulatory frameworks, public sector efficiency, and economic development.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Moreover, as we integrate AI-enabled e-businesses from global providers, our national AI can also act as a check and balance, ensuring that externally sourced AI solutions do not introduce misaligned incentives or governance risks.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond our national interests, developing expertise in AI alignment will also enable and allow Singapore to influence global AI governance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: AI will eventually be embedded into international decision-making processes, from global trade regulations to maritime and air traffic systems.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By establishing a strong foundation in AI alignment, Singapore can contribute to the development of ethical AI standards globally, shaping the rules that govern AI at the international level.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Additionally, this expertise will enhance Singapore's attractiveness as a hub for AI research and development, regulatory alignment services and business continuity planning (BCP) for global AI firms, such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our policies must strike the right balance between preserving what works, improving what is necessary and embracing what is possible.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In housing, we must ensure that affordability for young families do not come at the expense of existing homeowners' financial security.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The choices we make today will define whether Singapore remains a beacon of stability, innovation and inclusiveness in the decades ahead.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in support of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These vouchers and credits are ad hoc benefits given out by the Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are dependent on the availability of surplus collection of tax revenues and at the discretion of the government of the day.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Older Singaporeans may remember the $2.6 billion Progress Package in 2006 and the $3.2 billion Grow and Share Package in 2011, before the General Elections in those years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have gone from Growth Dividends every few years to CDC Vouchers seemingly every year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be unhealthy if Singaporeans become increasingly reliant on these ad hoc gifts to manage rising costs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In contrast, PSP has proposed a package of systemic measures to reduce cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our policies are structural and not ad hoc.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are intended to empower Singaporeans and allow Singaporeans to achieve as much financial independence as possible on their own, without being dependent on ad hoc handouts from the Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP's policy proposals are also based on a better balance of social and economic considerations, unlike PAP's current policies, which are too heavy on economic considerations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PAP's current policy of transferring the full market cost of land used for HDB flats into the reserves is based on economic considerations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this places a heavy burden on Singaporeans because the land cost must be recovered from Singaporeans through the cost of flats or additional taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Flat buyers only need to pay the land cost upon selling it in the resale market.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This places a greater emphasis on social considerations of keeping housing more affordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By doing this, we are also empowering Singaporeans to have the financial resources to achieve their dreams, instead of chaining them to 30-year mortgages that are increasingly unaffordable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, Mr Leong Mun Wai, will speak more on housing later.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Earlier, Mr Henry Kwek has said that PSP's Affordable Homes Scheme has the potential to destabilise the resale market.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps, he does not understand our proposal well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have already explained repeatedly that under our scheme, when the flats are resold, the owners will have to repay the land cost with interest.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it is not going to crush the resale market.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And in any case, since resale prices have increased by 50% since the last General Elections, far outpacing general inflation or wage increases despite the cooling measures that have been implemented, does the Member not think that the resale market needs some dampening?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's policy of setting rent based on the highest bid is purely based on economic considerations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This places more weight on social considerations of keeping food prices lower for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our proposal is a structural change to lower cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In contrast, Budget 2025 provided a one-time rental support of $600.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has proposed a new system that incorporates needs factors with bidding, so that those who have greater needs for a car will have a better chance of obtaining one and can do so at a lower cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This, again, better balances social and economic considerations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another contributor to higher cost of living is the raising of GST from 7% to 9% in 2023 and 2024, at a time when Singaporeans were hit with high inflation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that any additional revenue required for higher social expenditures can be raised from reforming the corporate income tax.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have stated before, in my Budget speech in 2023, that under our current corporate income tax regime, companies with the highest profits actually pay the lowest percentage of their profits in corporate income tax.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The global agreement on a minimum effective tax rate for large multinational enterprises has compelled us to adjust the taxes on the largest companies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope that it will not be affected by the US President’s Executive Order that has no force and effect in the US.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even under this agreement, many companies are not covered, because it applies only to very large companies with a group revenue of at least €750 million annually.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Adjustments will still need to be made to make our corporate tax regime to make it more progressive and equitable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Corporate income tax reform would allow us to reduce GST, which is a regressive tax, even though the Government says that the GST Voucher scheme makes it not regressive.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has said on many occasions that the tax revenue from different sources all go into the same Consolidated Fund, from which all expenditures are then paid for.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not designate specific revenue streams for specific purposes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, there is nothing linking the GST to the GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The vouchers can still be paid for even if we raise the additional revenue for it by increasing corporate income tax on the most profitable companies, instead of by raising GST.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will make our tax system even more progressive.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has said that this scheme is not intended to incentivise more couples to have three or more children, and, drawing from past experience when large baby bonuses have failed to raise the TFR, PSP also believes that it will not.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we need are structural changes to incentivise employers to be more family-friendly and to create better work-life balance so that Singaporeans have more time to find life partners and to raise families.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we need is to move the needle for those who want children but do not currently feel ready or that they have sufficient resources to have children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has previously urged the Government to introduce incentives to family-friendly employers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will pursue this further during the COS debates.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, we would like to make two new proposals to improve Singaporeans' work-life balance, by increasing the number of public holidays and enacting the right of workers to disconnect.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The number of public holidays in Singapore has remained unchanged since 1968, when the Government reduced the number of public holidays from 16 to 11 to improve Singapore's competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since then, Singaporeans have worked hard and our nation has prospered.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, we face new problems, such as a lack of work-life balance and overwork that are impacting family formation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The exact holidays should be determined in consultation with each community, but we can consider the possibilities of observing Chinese New Year's Eve, the second day of Hari Raya Puasa and Thaipusam as public holidays.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the increased 14 days of public holidays, it will still be in line with the norms in the region and globally.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, PSP would like to lend its support for "right to disconnect" legislation to be progressively implemented in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These would allow employers and employees to adjust to these new workplace norms.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can also do more to create work environments that are friendly to parents, especially single parents, and improve childcare arrangements.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai will speak more on this during his speech.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These changes also need to be coupled with changes to the education system to reduce the stress and competition for students and parents.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will speak more on this during the COS debates.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, this year's Budget continues to use vouchers to help Singaporeans cope with rising costs of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While these vouchers can provide short-term relief, they cannot offer long-term assistance nor address structural cost issues.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Singaporeans become increasingly dependent on these temporary benefits, it would not be a healthy trend.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister said that the Budget would help Singaporeans cope with living costs, but the result has fallen short of people’s raised expectations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In contrast, the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) has proposed a series of structural measures to reduce cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our policies consider not just economic factors but also carefully weighed social factors.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These policies aim to enable Singaporeans to achieve economic independence rather than creating dependency on temporary Government subsidies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Compared to PAP's policies, we are more concerned about whether Singaporeans can afford their HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Affordable Homes Scheme would also give Singaporeans more financial resources to pursue their dreams rather than letting a 30-year mortgage become a lifelong burden.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has also proposed reducing hawker stalls' rentals to lower food prices at hawker centres, reducing GST to 7% and having the Government pay for healthcare insurance to reduce the burden of medical expenses on citizens.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are long-term measures based on social considerations, not one-off solutions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also need more structural changes to create a more family-friendly environment for citizens.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To help Singaporeans better balance life and work, PSP proposes legislating the Right to Disconnect, giving citizens the right not to respond to work-related messages and emails.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP also proposes increasing public holidays from 11 to 14 days.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the Government can discuss with various ethnic groups which specific holidays to add, PSP suggests considering Chinese New Year's eve, the day after Hari Raya Puasa and Thaipusam. : Mr Speaker Sir, PSP believes that our cost of living issues should be addressed through structural policy changes, of which we have proposed several, rather than the band-aid approach of ad hoc gifts and handouts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my speech on last year’s Budget, I had appealed for more support for the sandwich generation, whom I referred to as the group that is providing for the care and expenses of children and elderly parents, while having to plan and prepare for their own retirement needs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am heartened to note that in the year since then, and in this year’s Budget, we have seen additional support for large families, and subsidies and grants for the caring of our elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We celebrate the amount of support given, but we must recognise that some of our families continue to be under significant financial strain as they navigate higher costs of living and a challenging job market globally.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While assistance has been provided, much more remains to be done and I hope that our Government can continue to focus on addressing this issue in this current term and successive terms of Government.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, I would like to propose several specific and actionable recommendations that have yet to be fully implemented to ease the financial and non-financial burdens on the sandwiched group.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also see that we have increased subsidies for residential long-term care services as well as home and community long-term care services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, there are instances where the elderly are not staying with their children and grandchildren, and yet the working children are still providing for their elderly parents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since we have a staggered approach for subsidies by per capita household income, can we also continue to provide some level of support for those earning per capita household income above $4,800?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Otherwise, can we ensure that parents or grandparents who are dependents but have a different residential address be included in the computation of per capita household income for such subsidies?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The MediSave top-ups for large families are very much welcome.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Government can also consider additional MediSave top-ups for large families not simply because they have more children, but also if they have elderly dependents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since October last year, MediSave funds could already be used for home medical and nursing providers supported by the Ministry of Health (MOH).

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I look forward to the early extension of MediSave funds to cover a greater variety of caregiving-related costs such as private home and nursing care providers, respite care and other home care costs like adult diapers and other related items.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Medisave top-ups for large families are very much welcomed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that we can also consider additional Medisave top-ups for large families, not simply because they have more children, but also if they have elderly dependents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since October last year, Medisave funds could already be used for home medical and nursing providers supported by MOH.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I look forward to the early extension of Medisave funds to cover a greater variety of caregiving-related costs, such as private home and nursing care providers, respite care and other home care costs, like adult diapers and other related items. : Second, the transportation needs of middle-income families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The cost of private transportation in Singapore is relatively high and families with young children are worried about the safety of their kids on public transportation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While there are already subsidies for low-income groups, middle-income families face challenges in covering daily transport costs in a safe and sustainable manner.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have also seen how school bus fares have increased the past few years, and school bus operators continue to struggle with manpower and cost pressures as well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would therefore like to propose a targeted transportation subsidy scheme for middle-income families, especially to partly subsidise school bus fares.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the years, there have been steps taken to improve the support given to residents living in private estates.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we must also recognise that the property tax hikes have also affected some of these residents, especially the retirees who are living in their own homes and did not rent them out.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While this is very encouraging, there are private estates in my Henderson Dawson Division that will also require works to be done as the population in our estates continue to age rapidly as well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I hope that the Government can consider extending senior-friendly works to all private estates around Singapore as well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For HDB estates, I would also like to shine the spotlight on HDB flats nearing or above 40 years, which would require more extensive estate upgrading or maintenance works.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since last week, after the Prime Minister delivered the Budget Speech, I have heard and seen many Singaporeans comment that it is "more of the same" – distributing more vouchers, investing in research and development (R&D) and upskilling our workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think Member Liang Eng Hwa has laid out in detail earlier, measures and efforts, which are extensive in this current Budget and not to forget past Budgets which are still ongoing, in helping our residents and helping Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But "more of the same" is not a bad thing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It means our Government is not going to take short-term and populist stances just for special events happening this year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More importantly, it means our approach is working and achieving its aims.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But one thing that is clear is that the global environment is different and fast-changing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Trump 2.0 has just kicked off and many asset managers and funds are already predicting more volatility and turbulence ahead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first area, Mr Speaker, I would like to speak on is attracting investments and good jobs to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is key to a small and resource-lite country that we are.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even as we debated our unexpectedly high corporate income tax collections on several occasions last year, and I am sure this year, some Members will raise this, there is little disagreement that we cannot take it for granted that corporates will always choose to stay in Singapore and not move somewhere else.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As global supply chains shift in the wake of the pandemic and geopolitical tensions, we are also seeing de-globalisation as countries seek to secure their resources and protect domestic jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With that backdrop, countries are competing more aggressively to attract investments and multinational companies (MNCs) to set up operations and bases.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the evolving changes in the global economic, business and political environment, the question I have is whether we have performed an in-depth study of the impact of specific factors on a company's decision to reduce or completely remove its presence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This falls back to the volatility of corporate tax revenue going forward as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the general points are well-known and often repeated – that Singapore cannot afford to compete on cost, that we need to focus on value-add and that our attractiveness lies in our political stability and the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But from industry-to-industry or company-to-company, do we have the mechanisms to study the particular factors that are causing a company to "offshore" its functions from Singapore to another country?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Think of it as an "exit interview" for a departing employee.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should take the chance to learn what did not go well, what we can do better and whether there will be further opportunities to collaborate again in the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, besides doing reflections after the fact, we should also think forward and rationalise our existing investment attraction toolkit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I had raised this when we debated the Economic Expansion Incentives (Relief from Income Tax) (Amendment) Bill in November 2024.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister of State Mr Alvin Tan responded that both the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and MOF have been continuously refreshing our incentive toolkits to ensure relevance and competitiveness, and updating legislation under their purview as required.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On top of incrementally adding, tweaking and removing specific incentive schemes, is it time for a holistic rethink of our investment attraction toolkit and how they fit together to achieve our strategic objectives and which Ministry should take the lead in such an effort?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is all the more the case when we have recently passed relevant measures that are based on OECD's BEPS 2.0 rules.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In light of President Donald Trump's Executive Order on 20 January 2025 withdrawing the US from the BEPS 2.0 consensus, how will Singapore respond?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If not, I would have thought that corporates in Singapore should be conditioned to accept and understand that large corporate tax breaks are a thing of the past.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, I was hoping to see plans to accelerate novel growth pillars in Budget 2025, such as cybersecurity or AI, and possibly, these might be discussed during the COS debate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I use these examples because I believe they are horizontals which have the potential to shake up different industries with their development and deployment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What concrete programmes or schemes are we going to push out to further the 15 Actions and 10 Enablers in our National AI Strategy 2.0?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the Government's assessment of our businesses' uptake of AI presently, especially our SMEs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
