text: And whether the Government play a greater role in facilitating our Singaporean businesses' AI transformation, as I believe it would be a massive gamechanger in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure the Prime Minister cannot mention all of that in his Budget Statement and I look forward to the COS debate from the different Ministries on this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fourth, the continued emphasis on worker upskilling and reskilling will certainly boost our attractiveness as a hub to do business.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are some concerns in this House whether the OECD's Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) flagged a significant decline in literacy after the age of 35, from the Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents who were surveyed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a good idea to redesign the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit to operate like an online wallet, so that companies can use the credits to immediately offset staff training costs rather than do so on a reimbursement basis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While not exactly similar, I think of this like the LifeSG credits, which can now be used through PayNow to shops and vendors directly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there scope to do something similar to make it even easier for individual Singaporeans to utilise their SkillsFuture credits?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Have any surveys been done to study why Singaporeans are not utilising these training benefits which the Government has given to them?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I would like to thank the Prime Minister and MOF for the Budget measures to help families in general.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But in particular, families, middle-income families with dependents, such as elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Families are the building blocks of our society as well as an individual's closest support net.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This does not include "other" household living arrangements, such as a divorcee living with elderly parents only.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When I was preparing this speech, it was also difficult to find the number of households with other dependents, such a person with special needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Based on the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore's (IRAS') data on dependent reliefs claimed, how many resident households have dependents, such as elderly parents, minor children and persons with special needs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are important, as if there are a significant number of families with these dependents, the increasing need for financial help to them might be important.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As they do their best to support their family members, it is only right that we provide them with whatever support that we can.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At a Budget dialogue I attended last year, interestingly, there were a number of questions and feedback requesting for help for working adult children taking care of their elderly parents and whether more help can be done to help them – the sandwich class, middle-class, who are also living with their parents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My three children are way older than six years old now, but even without enjoying the Large Families Scheme benefits, the joy and fulfilment brought by my kids to my life have been immeasurable and irreplaceable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I have also heard from some parents with young kids who have expressed some disappointment because they were expecting more help.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I would explain that the Government cannot cover all child-raising expenses, and that there are more affordable children's programmes compared to others, I do see their point in the message that we are sending across.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do we risk looking out of touch for thinking that amounts newly offered would be sufficient to move the needle or are we interested in getting only the married couples who would like, but cannot afford, to have a third child to do so?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, as this House has heard in a Motion filed by my fellow PAP colleagues, Ms Hany Soh and Mr Zhulkarnain, promoting parenthood is a multifaceted endeavour.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As our Baby Boomers age and health issues emerge, working children and caregivers would need more family care leave to send their elderly parents for medical visits, health checkups and emergency health needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I understand that policies for additional parental leave to care for children who are not newly-born can vary greatly from company to company, but such parental leave will not only allow for working parents to bring their children to the doctors when they are sick, but it can also provide time for working parents to attend at preschool events and celebrations, or just to spend meaningful time with their children or parents during official school holidays and for emergency needs, for example.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the next step for us to strengthen the regime and set some standards on flexi-time, flexi-load or flexi-place arrangements that employers must offer?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is the third consecutive Budget debate in which I focus on this issue, given the extraordinary inflationary environment in recent years, which has diluted Singapore's nest eggs and I have been hearing concerns.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, Mr Speaker, I will do this in Malay and not English.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We try to achieve this aim through the CPF system, which is recognised as one of the top pension systems in the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In recent years, there has been increasing concerns over whether our retirement savings will be enough.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The pandemic and other global issues are causing our daily costs to keep rising.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A mee soto that cost $2.50 just five years ago, costs $4.00 today.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, we must protect ourselves against more inflationary pressures ahead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last year’s Budget contained several measures to boost our seniors’ CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We enhanced the Matched Retirement Savings Scheme (MRSS) for Singaporeans aged 55 and above.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government also provided bonuses through the Majulah Package.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How effective have these measures been in ensuring that our seniors’ long-term needs are taken care of?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What criteria was used to assess the state of retirement adequacy of each senior, and of our society as a whole?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, it may be useful to find out if the MRSS’ utilisation rate has improved and whether more families are taking advantage of such dollar-for-dollar Government support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In contrast, Budget 2025 does not seem to announce any specific measure to boost the CPF or retirement funds of seniors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I am also looking forward to the discussions during COS debates, for instance, for MOM.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, we must continue encouraging and facilitating seniors to stay employed longer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead of looking forward to retiring at 55 years old, Singaporeans will need to see the value of staying active and be a contributing member of society, amid increased life expectancies of 80.7 years old for men and 85.2 years old for women.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Senior Employment Credit and the increased senior worker CPF contribution rates will help.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as I had suggested during the debate of the Workplace Fairness Bill last month, we must go beyond anti-age discrimination to provide positive reasons for employers to employ seniors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is being done on this front in engaging employers or otherwise?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When will the workgroup be expected to come back with their recommendations and when will public consultations be held?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there general time periods where we can expect such progress? : So, I mentioned earlier about the retirement adequacy in Malay, but I think it is a very important topic for Singaporeans at large going forward, especially with the rising cost and also the longer age that we might achieve because of health improvements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A final point I just want to highlight is to address social equity and social mobility and on the cost-of-living support in Budget 2025.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have received feedback asking why this is being given to all Singaporeans and not just the less well-to-do, like in previous Budgets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Members in the first few earlier speeches, including the Leader of the Opposition, mentioned this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The suggestion seems to be that we are taking a step backward in making Singapore a more equal society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we must not forget that costs are rising for everyone, not just lower-income groups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not true that every dollar that we take from upper- or middle-income households will, otherwise, have automatically gone to a lower-income household.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also should not ignore all other programmes that are aimed at helping lower-income groups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just in Budget 2025 alone, there is the tiered U-Save utility support as well as the Progressive Wage Credit scheme that we are enhancing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also ComCare, for which I thank the Prime Minister for raising the financial assistance amounts from April 2025.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For ex-offenders, another area that the Prime Minister mentioned in his speech, who are another group of Singaporeans that Budget 2025 seeks to uplift, the extension of the uplifting employment credit to end-2028 is a welcome announcement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides tracking the number of ex-offenders who have benefited from the uplifting employment credit, do we also track how long each individual manages to stay in employment?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In assessing the success of the scheme, we should also consider how many of these individuals managed to progress in their employment, securing higher roles and even better jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What else can we do to help ex-offenders secure good and suitable jobs beyond the Yellow Ribbon Project's employment assistance?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And since I am on the topic of leaving no one behind, there is one other group which is not mentioned as often, that is, Singaporeans working and living abroad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are Singaporeans as much as you and me and, this year, being election year, essentially, many of them will travel distances and even across states to exercise their Citizens' right to vote.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whereas many of us here would just need to cross the road from our home to a nearby school or HDB block to do so, but because they might not have an address in Singapore, they may not be able to get many of the vouchers, rebates and other benefits that are given to Singaporeans in Budget 2025.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will provide them with the protection we think Singaporeans deserve in the event of overseas layoffs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My final point, Mr Speaker, before I end, is on the point of inflation and the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I have highlighted this in same part as social equity and being equitable across all groups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The cost of living is a major concern —

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: — but inflation being impacted by GST, been turbocharged, may not be a fair point in general.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Because inflation went up in Singapore, like all other countries, due to other things, like war and supply chain disruptions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Inflation at its peak was not as high in Singapore as compared to many other countries in the region or even globally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, I just want to highlight that point in general about the impact of GST on inflation, but there are other factors beyond GST and GST impact is quite slight.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the last 12 months, right-wing and ultra conservative movements have made significant in-roads worldwide, with Europe bearing the brunt of the surge in such right-wing politics.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Parliaments of several European countries are now held together by shaky coalitions that could fragment at any moment due to the fundamental differences that the coalition partners have with each other.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Societies are also fraying, often due to tensions between immigrants and locals over access to economic opportunities and differing ways of life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Countries that could not transform their economies and workforces are struggling with persistently high structural and non-structural unemployment, with unemployment and underemployment among youths being particularly worrisome.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Topping all this off is a capricious and less-dependent USA with mercurial policies that could sometimes leave the rest of the world scrambling for a response.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If left unchecked, each of these issues could easily derail a country from its trajectory, potentially plunging it into an irrevocable slippery slope.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I started off this speech with reference to the global landscape because, in today's increasingly fragmented world, only good policies and good politics will ensure that we continue to thrive.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore's economy and social compositions are more complex today than 60 years ago.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, cost of living is a significant and righting concern for many Singaporeans, as with many aspects of our lives, like job security, raising a family, living a dignified life, retirement adequacy, inclusivity and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While many of these are "wicked" problems that do not have easy solutions, this year's Budget, I am heartened to say, has, to a significant extent, tried to tackle these challenges, especially the cost of living and helping our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Budget has been lauded by many as a generous one that not only provides relief to alleviate immediate cost of living concerns of Singaporeans, but also one that aims to transform Singapore's economy in the longer run by nudging businesses to innovate and individuals to continue to embrace lifelong learning and upskilling.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this era where technological breakthroughs are occurring at an unprecedented pace and countries are trying to outdo each other to incubate the next tech unicorn or to develop the next global company, we need to continue to motivate Singaporeans to strive to be the best versions of ourselves and to inspire Singaporeans to chase their dreams both locally and on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I laud the Government's effort to support our local companies to innovate, as well as the range of schemes that have been put in place to support our workforce, especially lower-skilled workers and workers whose jobs are facing disruptions, to upgrade and upskill themselves.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Amid implementing these schemes, I hope that the Government can consolidate our efforts to nurture Singaporeans to not just be the best versions of themselves as workers but also to be global leaders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that Singapore's future success depends on a bifurcate workforce strategy, comprising renewing the skills of our local workforce so that we are the most competitive, the most educated, well-skilled and productive workforce in the region.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, we do not want Singaporeans to known only as good workers, but also good global leaders as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And the dividend of the bifurcation strategy will take years to realise, I understand that.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But it will certainly pay off in the longer run when we have an ambidextrous workforce that is not only hungry, capable and competitive, but also excels in leadership and leading.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has been a decade since SkillsFuture was introduced.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do these courses translate into tangible employment benefits like job growth, career transitions and wage growth?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SkillsFuture was introduced with the noble intent to support workforce transformation and was designed to encourage Singaporeans to embrace lifelong learning and acquire new skills so that they can continue to be relevant in emerging industries.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The intent of the programme must and should rightly remain so.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The programme must therefore never be reduced to a numbers game where the focus is on introducing as many courses as possible so that Singaporeans have a wide range of courses when it comes to upskilling.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But neither should it be seen as an avenue for some to turn a quick profit by cashing in on the Government's funding.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I thus end my speech in firm support of the Budget, Sir.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When our nation was young, our priorities were clear and urgent: grow the economy, create jobs and ensure every Singaporean had a chance to thrive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: And 60 years ago, in 1965, unemployment rate stood at a staggering 10%.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is a testament to our collective resilience and determination.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Yet, as we celebrate these achievements, we must also recognise that not everyone has benefited equally.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While the majority of Singaporeans have seen their lives improve, there are still those at risk of being left behind.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is why I am heartened to see our Gini coefficient, a measure of income inequality, reach a new low after Government transfers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is a healthy sign, but it is not enough.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We must do more, especially for those who need our help the most: people with special needs (PSN).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Some may refer to this group as people with disabilities, but I prefer the term "people with special needs" because it reflects their unique challenges and extraordinary potential.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Over a decade ago, I had the privilege of being involved in the Enabling Master Plan 2 and 3, initiatives aimed at improving the lives of PSN from cradle to grave.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Special Education (SPED) schools, for instance, are no longer run as charities but are now well-funded by the Ministry of Education (MOE).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This means these schools can focus on what truly matters: providing quality education and improving outcomes for PSN.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Today, the focus has shifted to employment outcomes for PSN.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I am proud to share that my son, who has special needs, has been able to work part-time in a factory – thanks to the School-to-Work Transition Programme run by the Enabling Village.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But while we celebrate these milestones, we must not forget the unsung heroes in this journey: the caregivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As a parent of a child with special needs, I know first-hand that caring for a PSN is a lifelong mission.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When a PSN behaves differently in public, bystanders often rush to judge, blaming the parents for a lack of discipline, unaware of the immense challenges that they face.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is why it is crucial to provide caregivers with the support they need, whether it is connecting them to resources, offering emotional support or providing respite care.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In Nanyang, we have taken a step in this direction with Project Purple Heart, inspired by the Purple Parade.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This initiative brings together caregivers of family members with special needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Our early sessions were emotional as caregivers candidly shared their struggles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But as we connected them to resources and to one another, a strong support network emerged.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Today, we have about 60 caregivers in our network and we have renamed the initiative “Family of Purple Heart” to reflect our long-term commitment to their well-being.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: These caregivers meet monthly and stay connected through a WhatsApp group, offering each other tips, encouragement and emotional support.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Just last night, I received a message from one of the caregivers stating her concern on how her son with special needs can claim the SG60 vouchers as he would not be able to use it, the $600 vouchers, on his own.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I hope MSF can look into this concern.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: One of the members of the Purple Heart, Mdm Sim, joined us recently.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At 58, she cares for her 25-year-old daughter, who has Angelman Syndrome.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Both Mdm Sim and her husband work as delivery personnel with low wages and they also have to support two younger daughters who are still studying.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Life is tough for Mdm Sim, but through the Family of Purple Heart, she has found solace and strength in the company of others who understand her struggles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While this amount may seem modest, it would serve as a meaningful gesture of recognition and help ease the financial burden that many caregivers face.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: About 30 years ago, when HDB built these segmented blocks, residents appreciated the privacy they offered.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Back then, climbing stairs was not a problem.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But today, as these residents age, mobility has become a significant challenge.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: What was once a prized feature has now become a source of frustration and hardship.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Last month, I met Mr and Mrs Chew.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Mrs Chew, who has mobility issues, struggles to navigate steps, especially when going down.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: They have tried multiple times to apply for a BTO flat but have been unsuccessful due to their status as second-time applicants.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When Mrs Chew shared her story with me, she was on the verge of tears.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I promised her then, as I have done year after year since becoming the MP for Nanyang, that I would raise this issue in Parliament once again.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In Nanyang alone, there are 224 such units in 14 blocks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I urge HDB to explore the latest technology to install lifts in segmented blocks to relieve the pain of residents staying in these units.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If technical or cost constraints prevent the construction of additional lifts, I propose the following solutions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With over a million HDB flats in Singapore, almost all of which have direct lift access, it is only fair that we find a permanent solution for the residents still staying in these 2,000 segmented units.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Let us make a bold decision to end their hardship and ensure that every Singaporean can age with dignity and ease.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong conveyed a clear message in the SG60 Budget.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We will not forget any group, including persons with special needs (PSN).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With this in mind, we established the Project Purple Hearts in Nanyang to provide support for residents who care for family members with special needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The hardships of caregivers are often difficult for outsiders to understand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We could call this the “Caregiver Support Scheme” to express society's care and support for them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Next, I would like to focus on the segmented HDB units, flats where residents cannot access the lift on the same floor.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Taking Mdm Er for example, she has a seven-year-old child with special needs who has mobility difficulties, requiring her to carry him up and down the stairs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As the child grows and gains weight, Mdm Er is finding it increasingly difficult to manage.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: She thought of applying for a BTO flat but she knows it is not easy as she is not a first-time buyer, and she faces the pressure of paying the resale levy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Residents living in segmented units face similar challenges.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Therefore, I urge HDB to utilise advance technologies wherever possible to install lifts which will allow residents to access them on the same floor.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If this is not feasible due to technical limitations or high costs, I hope MND could consider the following: (i) first, allow segmented unit owners to sell their units back to the Government at market price, ensuring they are not financially disadvantaged; (ii) second, grant these owners priority for BTO applications and waive the resale levy to reduce their financial burden; (iii) third, provide grants for owners who want to purchase new flats, with enhanced grants for families with members with mobility issues; and (iv) fourth, units bought back by the Government should not be resold to Singaporean or Permanent Residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Instead, the Government can work with JTC to rent these units out to young foreign workers, preventing the problem from recurring.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I urge HDB to take bold steps to resolve this issue once and for all, so these residents no longer have to struggle with daily stair climbing. : Mr Speaker, Sir, in closing, I urge this House to remember that progress is not just about numbers and statistics.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is about people, real people with real struggles, hopes and dreams.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Let us continue to build a Singapore that leaves no one behind, a Singapore that is not only prosperous but also compassionate and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On our latest NDC, I would like to ask how much our plan is currently aligned with the Paris Agreement's 1.5 degrees warming target.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If it is not aligned, how much warming is our plan consistent with, that is, is it a two-degree warming world, three-degree warming world, or so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Second, can the Government clarify what is stopping us from bringing forward our transition even further?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is it possible to accelerate negotiations on renewable imports with our neighbours?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On transport, which I often speak on in this House, I hope the Government can incentivise a faster shift towards vehicle electrification for private vehicles, as well as to expedite the electrification of our public fleets, given that it has more direct control over it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A Straits Times article on 12 November 2024 reported that a number of public buses currently running on batteries have risen to 420, which is 7% of the current overall public bus fleet.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope these incentives will help push the needle on heavy vehicle conversion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I look forward to Ministry of Transport's elaboration of these features and other clarifications during the COS.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would like the Government to explain how each disbursement is accelerating our energy transition as well as to give more details on the nature of projects that have been funded.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Thirdly, the NDC does not explain the proportion to which novel tools, such as carbon captured utilisation and storage and carbon credits, will contribute to the downward trend in emissions after 2028.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To what extent will Singapore be relying on them?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is the Government's view that such tools will be as predictable as incentivising efficiency and emission reductions through higher carbon taxes from 2028 onwards?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On carbon capture, utilisation and storage, the responses to the public consultation on the NDC included concerns on the use of carbon capture and storage, which may not be fully proven and difficult to scale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Government explain how it took into account feedback on the NDC from the public who are key stakeholders in this climate crisis?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Fifth, my understanding is that emissions from international aviation and shipping are not covered under our climate targets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is there a timeline for when our targets will eventually cover these two sectors?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While Singaporeans may all look forward to our air hub expanding, the 50% increase in capacity will, if it goes according to plan, mean a staggering increase in flights and, consequently, aviation emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What are our Government's plans of cutting aviation emissions per plane seat so that we will not inadvertently be accelerating climate change with the increase in airport capacity and flights?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will our sustainable air hub blueprint be stepped up in the next few years to mitigate the increase in aviation emissions after T5 opens?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our linkages in the brown economy are still deep for now, even as we see in 2024 a significant sale by Shell of their assets in Pulau Bukom and Jurong Island.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Are there any shifts toward green transition following the sale, which the Government is able to provide some updates?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask about the manpower transition efforts for our workers in this industry, whether following Shell's sale or generally, what are being done to transition our workers as the industry undergoes green transition?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have asked about this previously and I hope we will get some assuring answers from MOM this time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Although global geopolitics has changed dramatically over the past year, climate change is still the number one existential risk to the world and to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To be clear, the Workers' Party supports ambitious climate action, we have and will continue to back the Government on good, effective climate policy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my Budget debate speech last year, I have said that, as a society, there is a lot more that we can and should do for adults with disabilities among us.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In particular, adults with serious special needs as well as their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For persons with disabilities, the range of disabilities do vary a lot.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the other hand, knowledge and appreciation of the importance of reasonable accommodations to persons of disabilities can be instilled from young in school in both children and youth with or without disabilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This can be specifically included in the character and citizenship education syllabus, where we have been told that the current curriculum aims to develop students to be empathetic, sensitive and respectful to all, including those with special educational needs or disabilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the MOE clarify or consider whether the concept of reasonable accommodations or at least the key aspects of it are currently being taught to both children and youth, with and without disabilities, to better prepare them to foster any inclusive work environment for all when they enter working age?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, transiting persons with disabilities and getting employers to be PwD-ready is one thing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A suitable working environment for disabled persons will also require good understanding, empathy and support from their colleagues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And, indeed, when we talk about disability, there is a wide range.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Provisions can range simply from rent for wheelchair access for the physically handicapped persons to providing assistive technology for those with sight problems and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For those with special needs, for example, mild autism, depending on the individuals, it may involve suitable calibration in lighting or noise or providing for task management assistance or specific communication modes at work and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How many of us can say we know with some details, of the workplace needs of different categories of disabled persons?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I recently had conversation with some Singaporeans who are high-functioning autistic working adults, including a resident.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They shared with me their life journey of struggling with their autism at their workplace, both before and after discovering, belatedly, their autism after they became adults.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A person shared with me her fear of group projects causing her to do badly in school, right through to university and even at work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Another successful, highly educated and intellectual individual shared with me that he will often struggle if his superior did not provide clear instructions or guidance or understandable guidelines for certain administrative tasks, or when he had to conduct seminars or workshops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A sticking issue is the lack of understanding from colleagues of their condition and their needs at work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There is even fear of discrimination of affecting promotion or job security, preventing one from sharing about one's own condition or challenges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that SG Enable can consider how to continue to enhance public education and understanding of the disabled persons at work, so that employers, colleagues at the workplace and, indeed, all Singaporeans will have better knowledge, understanding and empathy for their colleagues with disabilities or special needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While Active Ageing Centres are expected to reach out to many seniors in the cluster they are assigned to, given the number of seniors, there may inevitably be a shortage of resources in terms of spaces for centre activity, time as well as staff or volunteers attending the residents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may create a situation in centres that residents may not get to participate in as many organised activities as they wish or to use the centre space as often as they would like to.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am only concerned that this will lead to loss of interest for some residents, which will be a great waste after centre staff have tried so hard to bring them to the centre.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Earlier that year, the hon Member for Aljunied GRC Mr Gerald Giam, had also urged the same in a PQ.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: WP continues to believe that the annual value should be removed as a means testing criterion for healthcare subsidies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They are determined outside of one's control as they are influenced mainly by the rental prices of neighbouring units.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Imagine a retiree couple who have lived in their low value walk-up apartment for decades.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As a result of gentrification of their estate and perhaps the work from home habits of younger people, the area is sought after.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The annual value of their flat goes above $21,000 and, just like that, they lose the entirety of the healthcare subsidies they had enjoyed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The rise of rents since COVID-19 makes this scenario more common than we know or admit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By extension, at any one time they occupy less than 600 beds in the residential long term care sector, based on bed numbers as at end-2023.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Thirdly, as I have spoken in my cost-of-living Motion speech, there may be a variety of reasons why individual owners are unable to monetise their property, and they are not the only people who are affected by the annual value.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are also family members living together who are caught by the rule.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They are sharing a high annual value property to help care for each other, but they may not be able to get their relatives in the same household to pay for their unsubsidised medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, the cost of dental care in Singapore has become a concern, anecdotally, we have heard of Singaporeans crossing the border to Johor Bahru to seek cheaper treatment, a subject of the PQ in November 2024 by my colleague, MP for Sengkang, Ms He Ting Ru.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It may be a case of paying for more expensive treatment locally or ignoring the problem that will worsen with neglect.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Much more can be done to overcome the accessibility and affordability of local dental services by addressing the overlooked role of dental health in our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A few experts have weighed in over the last few months.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Second, increase the capacity of the current public dental system, which is currently overburdened.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By shortening the waiting times, we may encourage regular visits and turn more patients that need urgent attention away from having to seek more expensive private dental clinics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Last but not least, in my speech during the 2022 Motion debate on Building a Healthier Singapore, I have asked for oral health to be covered in the Healthier SG programme.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With encouragement on prioritising prevention over corrective treatments, I hope MOH will consider this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From babies to seniors, from families to enterprises, this Budget addresses immediate needs and prepares for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They symbolise the economic progress we have achieved since nation building.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our forefathers sowed the seeds of resilience and foresight, coupled with the careful stewardship by our leaders and, today, we reap those benefits.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Two days after the Budget Statement, I did my house visits, went around to visit my residents and shared with them what would be encompassed in the Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many of them have expressed joy and excitement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Seniors, themselves, were also especially heartened to know of the enhanced measures, such as the enhanced CDC Vouchers, the long-term care support and, of course, the SG60 vouchers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They were excited that they now have more support to help them cope with the daily cost of living.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Economic growth is not just about statistics or gross domestic product (GDP) percentages.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is about the lives that we touch.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It means better standards of living, meaningful employment opportunities and the resources to fund public goods and services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But as history has shown, past success is no guarantee of future prosperity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We are operating in a world rife with geopolitical contestations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The intensifying US-China rivalry tests countries around the world in many ways.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is reshaping global supply chains, technology ecosystems and economic partnerships.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore, as an open economy, feels these ripple effects.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The most recent example is that of DeepSeek.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: DeepSeek's emergence prompted multifaceted response from the US, ranging from government scrutiny, industry reactions and strategic reassessments.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Countries, such as Australia, Canada, Italy, the Netherlands, Taiwan and South Korea, also indicated that they would ban the AI app, citing privacy and security concerns.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Then, Singapore came under the spotlight and pressure as the US alleged that DeepSeek got Nvidia chips through Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This issue was clarified in the media and thoroughly discussed in this House last Tuesday, so I will not belabour these points.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But what is clear is that Singapore can get caught when major powers contest.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If the geopolitical contestation continues to escalate to a point where even breathing the same air becomes offensive to the other party – obviously, I am exaggerating a little bit here – how shall Singapore manage these sensitivities going forward and ensure that our own national survival and interests are served?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Then, domestically, we are also not without challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In MacPherson, we are a mature estate with a higher than national average proportion of seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the past many years, I have met with senior residents who are struggling with old age, with having little or no family support as well as the pressures, the worries from having to cope with daily living needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Just very recently during the Chinese New Year period, I went with my team to visit one of our rental blocks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And at the very last part of my visit, I met an uncle who was living alone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Just about a month or two before that he had a fall, fractured his leg and found it very difficult to move around.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He used to be very active, but because of his fracture, his ability of mobility becoming affected, he has been coping up at home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, even though at the beginning when I knocked on his door, he was still generally positive and joyful and cracked a few jokes with me.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But towards the end of that visit, towards the end of our conversation, he broke down in tears.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He felt that his sense of ability, that self-esteem has been debilitating, has been regressing and that fear gripped him.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, when we suddenly came to visit him, even though we have been seeing each other before that, but when we were there at his doorstep, he realised that he has not been forgotten, that there is still someone caring about him.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, obviously, we mobilise community resources to support him, to help him, to make sure that he is connected.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We also found Befrienders through our community partners to continue to engage him, but this is one of those manifestations of how Singapore could be like with an ageing population, with dwindling family support and, if we do not manage this carefully, we are going to have a lot more seniors who will feel very lonely, isolated and then, the whole psychosocial state of them will be affected.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But more than the financial support that we can give them, it is also us, people within the community, across the nation, through our partners, what can we do to help them to give them that moral support, that human touch that cannot be replaced.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, we need to do our best to keep them healthy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to help them recover after they become unwell.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I know that the hospitals are working with our community partners to follow-up with them on that, but we also need to socially engage with them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And this, beyond our usual grassroots, I think this needs all of us to come in to support them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, this is just one of the challenges that I can see from my ward, my constituency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And we ourselves are also doing our best to support them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Not only are we mobilising our own fellow neighbours and volunteers, but we also raise funds to put in place schemes to also give them the extra support, like the MacPherson Care Fund, helping them, to give them that assurance that, apart from what the Government is able to offer them, we help them with their medical needs, including dental needs, as well as other areas that they find important to them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With challenges looming large, whether if it is outside of Singapore and inside, opportunities are still abound.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, with these opportunities, we must continue to remain vigilant.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Against a dynamic world and widespread digitalisation, Singaporeans today worry about job security, skills obsolescence and whether the Government can continue to have their backs in times of crisis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These concerns, if unaddressed, can fray social cohesion and erode trust in institutions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, not only must we continue to ensure we have the right policies, infrastructure and resources for economic success, we must also continue to build up our people so that they can continue to ride waves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this budget, we have many measures that address immediate pain points and needs of Singaporeans, mitigating cost of living and costs associated with caring for the old and growing families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These measures are so notable that several commentators wondered if the Government has given a bit too much, but at the same time, together with Budgets over the past many years, we can clearly observe the long-term provisions and strategies that our Government has in place and this is heartening.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I am in favour of the many measures targeted at building up our nation's capabilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These include continued investment into infrastructures, R&D, specific enterprise support, such as the Enterprise Compute Initiative, aiming to help businesses harness the power of game-changing technologies as well as enhanced SkillsFuture schemes and employment credits to empower our workforce to stay employed and keep pace with the latest market demands.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Building capabilities and resilience in our people and enterprises is far-sighted and the best way in inoculating ourselves against the possible challenges of our future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That being said, to keep Singapore resilient, I still have a few points to raise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This need not be done at one go, but in tranches over the next few years, whenever we can, will be assuring.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This pot of gold accumulated by our forefathers served us well during the crisis of our generation and we owe it to the next generation to restore it whenever we can, if not in full, at least, in part, for the benefit of future generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As geopolitical competition continues to intensify, there will be impact on our economic structure, supply chains and even how we deploy technologies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I hope the Government will continue to build redundancy into our supply chains, foster local tech ecosystems and reduce reliance on external shocks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a related point, competition between major powers is expected to still escalate in the realm of technology, which, in turn, rely on energy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It will thus not be surprising that the competition overspills into the energy space.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a small country, how do we secure sustainable sources of energy while maintaining low carbon emissions?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As such, the exploration of nuclear options, hydrogen fuel and regional electricity imports must accelerate to buffer against future geopolitical shocks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is important that we continue to share the fruits of our collective labour with Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This helps to keep our social compact strong.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This gives meaning to why we are pursuing economic growth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is definitely demonstrated in the many social policies and schemes that our Government introduced or enhanced over the past years and, most definitely, this year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the new year began with a generous Budget.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is a Budget that benefits all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The SG60 vouchers are not just a one-off gesture; they symbolise our economic achievements since Independence.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The fruits we enjoy today come from our pioneers' vision and perseverance, the careful stewardship of our successive leaders and the full cooperation of our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Economic growth is not merely about statistics, nor is it a report card to boast about.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A vibrant economy with opportunities means higher living standards, more meaningful employment opportunities and more fiscal revenue to fund public services and infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In short, economic growth is not just a country’ s heartbeat; it is the continuation of hope for families and people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Globally, we are in an era of intense geopolitical competition.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The intensifying US-China rivalry is reshaping global supply chains, technological ecosystems and economic cooperation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore, as a highly open economy, cannot remain unaffected.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Any trade restrictions or technology decoupling will directly impact us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the saying goes, when elephants fight, the grass gets trampled.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, Singapore must be like bamboo, flexible yet firm, and needs to maintain a manoeuvring space and capability in this complex environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: An ageing population, low birth rates, high costs of living and workforce transformation amid AI and automation waves are all pressing concerns.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, our leadership and Government must not only address immediate concerns like costs of living but also continue to invest for the future, strengthen foundations and pursue new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe this year's Budget addresses these various aspects comprehensively.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This treasure trove, which is passed down through generations, played a crucial role during the crisis in our generation, and we have a responsibility to preserve this important national asset for future generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Social cohesion depends on fair wealth distribution and, with economic growth, we naturally hope to share these achievements with all citizens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): In conclusion, in these uncertain times, we must do all we can to build for the future, while giving assurance to Singaporeans, present and future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With this Budget, it is clear that opportunities will remain, that safety nets exist and that the Singapore story will continue to be one of success and solidarity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, come what may, I believe we will forge ahead together as one Singapore, for a better tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It has been generous and there is something for almost everyone.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: That is why Prime Minister and the Finance Minister had said that it is a Budget for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But the Budget Statement is more than an announcement of the goodies dished out to the citizens.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is also a statement setting out the Government's plans to address the current concerns of citizens, to rally Singaporeans together and it is a roadmap to chart the future direction for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It makes budgeting a lot more uncertain, especially with a new US government with uncertain government policies and quick to impose tariffs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Social expenditure will go up and corporate and tax revenue may be uncertain.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, in an uncertain global economy, I urge Members of this House not to take tax revenue for granted.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The first is equitable treatment for all citizens, regardless of housing type.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For the past many years, I had advocated for Budget surpluses to be distributed in a manner that does not consider a citizen's housing type.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In previous years, the Finance Minister had always given GST Vouchers, U-save rebates, and service and conservancy charges rebates to residents living in HDB flats only.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Residents who live in private estates are left out.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In July last year, several Members and I had asked the Government why it did not provide Climate Vouchers to private estate residents because energy efficiency should be practised by every resident.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of my residents who are retired or are in the lower- middle-income will certainly appreciate the Government sharing the growth of the Singapore economy with them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of my residents who live in private estates and may be better off, they do not need such vouchers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, I think it is important that the Government signals that it acknowledges the efforts of all Singaporeans who have worked hard, paid taxes and contributed to the growth of the country.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, my hope is that Budget 2025 will mark a slight shift in the Government's financial policy to recognise the efforts and contributions of all Singaporeans who have built up Singapore, regardless of their house type.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, Sir, if I can touch on cost of living.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In a recent survey by Blackbox Research's SensingSG, a large number of citizens have expressed concern about rising costs of living and inflation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Whenever I speak to my residents, they, too, complain at the rising costs of consumer products each time they go to the market, supermarket or hawker centre.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And this is despite the fact that over the past few years, the Government has been giving CDC Vouchers and outright cash payouts through the Assurance Package to the residents.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The payouts from the Assurance Package did not seem to alleviate the concerns of Singaporeans about the increased costs of living.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For residents in the middle-income squeeze, they simply have to tighten their belts as they get much lesser help from the Government schemes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In a recent CNA article, former newspaper editor, Mr Han Fook Kwang, said, "The problem is that handouts are at most band aids that do not address the issue itself which is, the rising prices of things that people need.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They will hence never be sufficient, especially if prices keep going up." Sir, I think the Government must review this concern, which is valid.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How can the Government do its part to manage costs of living?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When I speak to businesses, they invariably raised two concerns of running a business: manpower costs and rental.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I think it is time to consider whether we should review the need to allow more foreign workers in areas where Singaporeans clearly do not want to work in.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I urge the Government to consider adjusting the foreign worker ratio for industries like cleaning, shipping, construction and the service line.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: A cleaning contractor told me that he is forced to look for 60- or 70-year-old Singaporean senior citizens to work as cleaners.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is to allow his company the ratio to employ more foreigners.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope that these issues are not sacred cows that cannot be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: While I am happy for the banks and happy for the shareholders, I do urge MAS to review whether borrowing costs for businesses can be reduced.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Excessive profits for banks may simply mean that some organisations down the chain may be paying a higher price for these financial products.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I truly appreciate what the Government is intending to do by providing more financial support to couples with more children.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Catholic Pope Francis has also urged couples to raise children and build families, and not just keep pets.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Or is it because many couples do not want their children to be stressed due to the education system?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We need to reset our definition of what is success in life.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of us work long hours, with reduced family time.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When I visit Australia or the European countries, I see many people out there enjoying the weather and parks from 5.00 pm onwards.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, thank you for acknowledging the hard work of our Parliamentary staff.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Budget 2025 is a testament to this vision: a Budget that is both generous in addressing immediate needs and disciplined in preparing for a brighter future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Prime Minister and Finance Minister has unveiled a landmark Budget to tackle cost-of-living pressures, support the development of workers and businesses and commemorate SG60.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: At the same time, it invests in Singapore's long-term needs, including climate resilience and energy security.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This unexpected surplus is primarily attributed to strong corporate income tax revenue.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With 20/20 hindsight, there have been questions about whether we could have delayed the GST increase or been even more generous with the handouts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With geopolitical tensions and trade frictions intensifying, Singapore, one of the most trade-dependent economies, faces heightened risks from geoeconomic fragmentation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In this volatile landscape, it is absolutely prudent to maintain some fiscal dry powder to respond swiftly to unexpected economic shocks that may come our way.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Moreover, this fiscal strength will give us the agility to seize opportunities as they arise in this rapidly changing world order.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we must recognise that Budget 2025 already provides substantial support across key areas.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: From FY2019 to FY2024, overall expenditure surged by over 50%.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Other critical areas, including sustainability, trade and industry and social development, will see spending growth of around 20% and more.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, by any measure, this year's Budget is not just generous, but a demonstration of fiscal resilience, reflecting a financial strength that few economies can rival.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This has been made possible through years of strategic and disciplined adjustments to our tax system, ensuring a resilient and diversified revenue base.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Its over-reliance on land sales and property market cycles has led to ballooning deficits whenever the market turns, forcing the government to make painful fiscal adjustments.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: At its peak, Hong Kong's land sales revenue contributed 27% of total government revenue in FY2017.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But in the last three years, it has declined to an average of less than 7%.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, as a result, it has recorded annual fiscal deficits exceeding the equivalent of US$20 billion in three of the past four years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, Hong Kong just announced its Budget today and it is now taking painful steps to address deficits by cutting expenditure by 7%.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Had we followed this path, Singapore could be facing the same fiscal vulnerabilities as Hong Kong today.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Instead, we chose a more stable and forward-looking approach.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We manage land sales revenue prudently, investing the proceeds as part of our Reserves and spending only the investment returns through the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC).

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This has provided Singapore with fiscal stability, allowing us to support economic growth and social development without being at the mercy of market fluctuations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, while certain measures may not be explicitly labelled as SME-specific, I think many initiatives in Budget 2025 will directly benefit them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, providing CDC Vouchers instead of cash for SG60 Vouchers will strongly channel and boost footfall to local enterprises, ensuring that our SMEs benefit from increased consumer spending.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Increase in co-funding levels for the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme and extension of Senior Employment Credit and Central Provident Fund (CPF) Transition Offset will help SMEs manage wage costs, easing pressures on their operations while ensuring fair wages for workers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These initiatives send a clear and confident signal that Singapore is serious about attracting world-class entrepreneurs, anchoring high-impact innovations and deepening our financial ecosystem to remain a leading global hub.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, for these initiatives to truly deliver on their promise, their design and execution must align with market realities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While I agree that mobilising capital from family offices add vibrancy to Singapore's equities market, the implementation details require careful consideration.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Moreover, the historical performance of Singapore equities relative to the global benchmarks presents an implicit opportunity cost for investors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Additionally, the current investment options tend to cater to selected objectives, such as dividend stocks or yield plays.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Unlike the US and China or Hong Kong markets, which offer a broader mix of tech, healthcare and high-growth innovation-driven firms, Singapore has relatively fewer such listings.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As a result, any new capital inflows into the local market will likely benefit only a small subset of Singapore-listed stocks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Beyond these concerns, there are also questions regarding investment timeline, lock-in period and the consequences of non-compliance over time.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, any adjustments to the rules must be carefully calibrated, timed and aligned with strategic asset allocation principles, ensuring that they do not impact Singapore's competitive position relative to other global family office hubs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, as AI adoption intensifies in the workplace, it is critical that we also address its impact on the workforce, particularly on less experienced workers who are most vulnerable to automation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As AI models continue to rapidly advance, they will not only boost productivity but also commoditise skills and automate tasks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is often junior inexperienced staff or those involved in routine tasks who face the greatest risk of displacement.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How do we prepare new workforce entrants for a future where traditional entry-level roles shrink or disappear?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How will they gain the necessary experience to progress in their careers if they struggle to secure their first job?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: AI adoption must go hand in hand with comprehensive strategies to manage job displacement, retraining, career redefinition and industry transformation, ensuring that workers are equipped to adapt and thrive in an AI-driven economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For institutes of higher learning, exposure to industry AI tools must be integrated into all curricula.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Climate change is real, accelerating and unforgiving – nature waits for no one.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Staying the course is not just about mitigating risks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The green economy represents one of the biggest growth frontiers in the coming decades.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By investing early and also decisively, we strengthen our position as a global hub for green innovation, attracting investment, creating jobs and securing long-term economic competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Over six decades, we have built a Singapore brand defined by trust, stability, unity and good governance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These values are what make Singapore stand out globally and they will be even more critical in the years ahead.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It has even transformed what it means to be Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: On my overseas travels, I have had bizarre experience of encountering "fake Singaporeans", including professionals, business owners, even tourists who claim to be "Singaporeans", even when they are of some other nationality.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They do this so as to appear more trustworthy, more capable or more professional.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, the Singapore brand has become so exceptional that it is well worth faking, much like a Rolex watch or a Louis Vuitton handbag.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And, like these global brands, you know you have made it when imitation becomes the greatest form of flattery.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In an increasingly uncertain and fragmented world, the Singapore brand will be more valuable than ever.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As businesses and investors seek stability amid volatility, our reputation for transparency, consistency and long-term planning will be our trump card.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is what justifies our premium cost position.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Let us never take this hard-earned advantage for granted, but instead, build upon it to secure our place in an ever-changing world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 2.39 pm until 3.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, Budget 2025 is not just a financial plan, but a significant milestone that underscores the Government's unwavering commitment to economic resilience, worker reskilling and fostering a stronger business ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As we celebrate 60 years of Independence, Budget 2025 holds a special significance for all of us.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It is a testament to our resilience, unity and unwavering commitment to progress.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget is not just a financial plan, but an opportunity to reflect on our achievements, acknowledge the challenges ahead and reaffirm our collective vision for a prosperous and inclusive nation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The SG60 Package is a targeted and timely initiative that not only eases cost-of-living pressures but also reinforces our long-standing commitment to shared prosperity.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This expansion has been driven by increased productivity, workforce upskilling and strategic investments in innovation and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Such economic resilience underlines our ability to navigate global uncertainties and presents an opportunity to strengthen social mobility and economic inclusion, ensuring that every Singaporean benefits from our nation's progress.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This is further complemented by a cash grant to help enterprises mitigate financial pressures and focus on growth.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Partnerships for Capability Transformation initiative has played a crucial role in fostering MNC-SME collaborations, thereby fostering a more dynamic business ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the Government can provide an update on the number of SMEs that have benefited from Partnerships for Capability Transformation over the past year and explore increasing funding support or tax incentives to encourage deeper and longer-term SME-MNC partnerships, driving greater industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Even as we provide direct support to Singaporeans, we must continue strengthening our economic fundamentals to remain resilient and competitive in an increasingly uncertain global landscape.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As we navigate the global landscape, the expansion of the National Productivity Fund is not just an investment, but a strategic move that enables targeted investments in high-growth industries.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These investments will drive innovation, boost productivity and create employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This investment is key to securing Singapore's position as a global economic leader and in instilling confidence in our financial future.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As we plan towards Singapore's next stage of economic growth, strengthening our position as a global hub for startups and innovation is crucial.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
