text: I look forward to the Government sharing its plans for attracting and supporting high-performing, innovative companies and growing our research and innovation ecosystem, particularly in semiconductors and biomedical sciences.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: First, our SMEs need broader support to navigate complexities of M&A successfully.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Government could possibly partner trade associations and chambers to establish dedicated advisory units that provide end-to-end support for SMEs pursuing mergers, acquisitions and joint ventures.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we must leverage existing foreign demand for cross-border M&As, especially in the energy and technology sectors.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I suggest introducing a legal framework facilitating cross-border corporate amalgamation, like the European Union, United Kingdom and Delaware frameworks.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This should include establishing reciprocal agreements with key jurisdictions – particularly with our ASEAN trading partners as well as developed financial hubs – to enable smoother deal execution.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, to address the evolving financing needs of enterprises, particularly startups and high-growth firms, additional flexible financing mechanisms tailored to businesses at different stages of growth are needed.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: One such improvement could be introducing alternative financing options, such as revenue-based financing, where repayments are tied to business performance.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This would reduce the burden on companies facing temporary cash flow constraints.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, streamlining the application process and improving loan approval transparency will help SMEs access funding more efficiently, ensuring that financing remains accessible to a broader range of businesses, especially those that may not fit traditional credit assessment models.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We must also strengthen our intellectual property framework to complement these financing initiatives.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While the IP Grow initiative has made commendable progress in educating businesses, we must take further steps to help SMEs commercialise their IP and integrate it into their M&A growth strategies.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I propose extending incentives for SMEs to acquire and license strategic IP for business expansion, possibly integrating these into existing M&A grant schemes.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure accessibility, I suggest that the Government explore subsidised access to computational resources for SMEs and provide structured training programmes so that local enterprises can maximise their use of advanced digital technologies.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's position as a financial hub will be further solidified with the new listing tax incentives designed to encourage more businesses to list on the Singapore Stock Exchange.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The move will enhance our capital markets, attract investors and offer companies more opportunities to raise funds locally.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome the Government's focus on strengthening our equity markets.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The recent initiatives announced by the equity markets review group chaired by Minister Chee Hong Tat align well with this objective, with significant measures for improving liquidity, enhancing research coverage, introducing incentives for institutional investors as well as simplifying the regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These reforms are essential in boosting investor confidence and fostering a more vibrant capital market.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2025 takes a significant step in uplifting low-wage workers and enhancing social security.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, while wage increases are essential, they must be accompanied by broader efforts to enhance job quality, provide workplace protection and facilitate long-term career development.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Government to ensure that training and upskilling programmes for these workers remain industry-relevant and accessible, helping them transition into higher-paying, sustainable careers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I suggest to the Prime Minister and Finance Minister that the Government may want to leverage this surplus to address emerging challenges with even greater allocations to help businesses to adapt quickly to a digital economy and to the changes brought about by AI.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like this surplus to help our citizens over 60 who have paid their dues, to be able to retire with dignity and maintain the quality of life they were used to during their working lives.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Let us move forward with confidence and determination, embracing the opportunities that lie ahead while staying true to the Singapore spirit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For many Singaporeans, this Budget addresses some of the key concerns that they have in an increasingly uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, it provides broad-based assistance with the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While inflation seems to be lower in the last quarter, people are still adjusting to higher prices of the last few years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The CDC Vouchers also encourage spending with our local merchants and small business owners in the heartlands whose businesses have been impacted over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, we are living in an age where jobs and work are facing disruption like never before.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many companies, including major tech companies and banks, have announced job cuts and restructuring over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Related to this, there is extensive Government spending as well as tax breaks in a range of sectors, including heavy investments in transport, education and health infrastructure as well as tax breaks for qualifying tech startups.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would suggest that it will be important to tie and track these investments against local job creation as far as possible so that the economic opportunities being created by these investments will translate into jobs and opportunities for our people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, the Budget provides comprehensive support for families to gently encourage people to have families and children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is heartening to note that the Government is catching up on the supply bottlenecks for construction of new HDB flats that occurred as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic and that it has plans to continue with construction of significant projects in the coming year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The delays and shortages in BTOs had been a concern over the last few years, especially for young couples hoping to start families, and I am glad that we are now crossing this hill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One point I would ask for though is for the Government to consider bringing back larger HDB flat formats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will be important if we want families to have more children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Currently, the largest flat formats in BTOs are 5-room flats, and these generally have three bedrooms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we are considering multi-generation families or families with more children, three bedrooms may not be enough for them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many have given feedback that as children get older, they prefer to have their own rooms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, large families may need domestic help, and domestic helpers will also need their own bedrooms under the law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand that the reason for holding back on development of larger flat types in recent years has been that there did not seem to be much demand for them among first-time buyers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think it is also important for us to consider not just first-time buyers, such as young couples, but also older, middle-aged couples who have higher incomes but are also likely to have larger families and extended families to care for.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many of the older large HDB flats, such as jumbo flats, are popular and fetch high prices in the resale market, which suggest that it would be good to have a pipeline of new supply of them as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had also argued for the socialisation of early childcare costs from my early days in this House, even before I was married or had a child of my own.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My view was that, given that having more children is a national priority that benefits the country, more of the costs should be socialised rather than privately borne by the parents in the early years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Costs for older children, from primary school onwards are generally well covered, but the earlier costs, when couples have lower incomes, may have been a concern.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am glad that this Budget continues with the Government's plans of the years of subsidising a greater part of these costs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The cost of early childcare will now be comparable to the costs at the primary school level of education.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, there is significant financial support for families with three or more children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These measures will hopefully make it easier for couples who decide to have children, to have bigger families as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Tamil Language Learning and Promotion Committee, which I chair, is a committee under MOE that supports the learning of the Tamil language outside the classroom and has several signature programmes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This committee also supports community organisations in their efforts to organise activities for schoolgoing children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Separately, the Tamil Language Council, of which I am an advisor, a committee under the National Heritage Board (NHB), promotes the use of Tamil in Singapore and organises the Tamil Language Festival each year, which sees more than 40 events organised by different community organisations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These initiatives help keep the Tamil language vibrant in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Indian arts community in Singapore is a thriving one.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we mark Singapore’s 60 years of Independence this year, the well-thought-through Budget not only sets a path for the survival of Singapore in a more uncertain and dangerous world, but more importantly, a lamp to light the way for Singaporeans to seize opportunities at every stage of life to continue to thrive individually, as a family, and as a nation together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These economic figures, working together, will hopefully alleviate the cost-of-living pressures that have been hanging in the minds of both Singaporean households and businesses this past year.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last year, I spoke on support for three key groups during my Budget 2024 debate speech.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are: one, supporting working adults; two, caring for seniors; and three supporting young families and couples.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These three groups form most of my residents in Jalan Kayu constituency living in both HDB and private estates.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened to know that Budget 2025 continues to address their needs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, I will again focus on the Budget support for these three groups.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am encouraged by the key measures in Budget 2025 to empower Singaporeans at every career stage, while promoting a more inclusive and resilient workforce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I welcome the enhanced tier of support under the Workfare Skills Support Scheme, which allows lower-wage workers to upskill earlier with financial assistance for longer-form courses.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have three blocks of rental flats in Jalan Kayu, mostly comprising families with young children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One or both of their parents, my residents, may have been struggling with drugs, incarceration or divorce problems which render them many difficulties in coping with life and work.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government will continue to support Workfare Skills Support Scheme training courses aligned with industry needs so that these residents can have the best chance of keeping and progressing in better jobs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask the Government what the job placement support for participants who completed Workfare Skills Support Scheme courses are and those who are still struggling with just being able to continue with lower wage tough jobs like food delivery even if they aspire for better jobs through Workfare Skills Support Scheme training.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, I am pleased that the Senior Employment Credit has been extended to 2026.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This can continue to encourage employers to hire and retain older and experienced employees and recognise their contributions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the upcoming enactment of Workplace Fairness Act 2025, I believe that there will be more protection against discriminatory employers’ behaviours due to age of employees or would-be employees.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my Jalan Kayu constituency, our Ang Mo Kio Town Council’s contracted cleaning vendors actively employ our residents who want to work as our cleaners.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Among about 70 cleaning supervisors and cleaners in Jalan Kayu, about 10 of them are our residents or those living in nearby constituencies.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All of them are aged above 60 years, with the oldest almost 80 years old.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are a jovial group who shared with me during my Chinese New Year luncheon and ang pow distribution with them that cleaning keeps them active and happy.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She said: “They are responsible, punctual, seldom take MC and keep active by working.” I hope that the Government will continue the good efforts to help our senior employees and that everyone in Singapore take responsibilities to render them with respect, care and consideration as they work.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2021, I spoke in this House about the importance of balancing legislative amendments with tripartite consensus, ensuring that employers and employees both benefit from flexible and sustainable re-employment strategies.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we extend the Senior Employment Credit, can the Government also track and evaluate whether companies which have received the offsets have effectively supported their older workers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also urge the Government to create more platforms for good companies with exemplary age-inclusive human capital practices to share with more companies so that we can create a conducive workplace and culture that allow Singaporeans who want to work as long as they can, a good environment to do so.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, promoting inclusive employment is essential in building a fair workplace.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am encouraged that the Enabling Employment Credit has been extended to 2028 to support employers who hire PwDs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Employment not only provides financial independence but also builds dignity and fosters social inclusion for PwDs and ex-offenders.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This should include persons with mental illnesses as this unseen disability and illness have been increasingly afflicting Singaporeans from all ages and walks of life.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a most recent report by CNA on 24 February, the Joint Autonomous Universities Graduate Employment Survey 2024 showed that fewer graduates found jobs six months after graduation compared to 2023, although the median gross salary for fresh graduates in full-time permanent employment increased 4.3% to S$4,500 in 2024.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I await to see the results of our ITE graduates’ employment rate in 2024.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my 2023 Budget debate speech two years ago, I already raised my concern then that while I celebrate the 87.5% of fresh university grads for landing in full-time permanent jobs with higher pay than the year before, the 6.3% in freelance or part-time or temporary jobs and 3.6% who remained unemployed and still looking for a job need some attention.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The continued downward trend since 2023, according to results of the annual surveys for our university and polytechnic grads warrant deeper analysis by the Government to understand the trends are due to expectation-reality gaps, educational-career interest gaps or some emerging phenomenon leading to unemployment or underemployment of our young people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is to ensure that our young people do not fall behind the career start line without understanding the implications of such delays.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, let me move on to the seniors in Jalan Kayu, whom I care dearly for as most of them are at the age of my own parents and parents-in-law, and the younger seniors are my age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened to read the enhancements in healthcare affordability, retirement support, senior mobility support, long-term care, caregiving and community care options are all key priorities in Budget 2025.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Healthcare costs has been inevitably increasing as our population ages, like all developed ageing societies are confronting.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I welcome the introduction of the Matched MediSave Scheme to alleviate some of the financial pressures faced by seniors and their families.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To support seniors in their desire to age in place, we need to ensure they have access to quality long-term and end-of-life care that respects their preferences.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Building on my previous call in this House through my Adjournment Motion titled “Enhancing End of Life with Choices and Dignity” in May 2023, I urge the Government to create greater awareness and accessibility for long-term care and palliative care to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened to know that the Government will increase subsidies for home and community care to alleviate long-term care costs for seniors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the same note, I propose reviewing the daily MediSave withdrawal limits of $250 for general palliative care and $350 for specialised care to ensure they remain aligned with the rising healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This initiative reflects the Government's commitment to supporting seniors across different housing types.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government will not be too quick to take away this extension after 2028, even if take-up rate may not be high in the first three years as outreach to private estates are usually more onerous even for MPs like me who are committed to conducting regular evening house visits to have the best chance of meeting residents in my residents in the four private estates in Jalan Kayu.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have also previously advocated for senior-care facilities under Age Well SG to be cited in both HDB and private housing estates.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to see more such facilities in the public spaces of HDB and private estates alike, with a higher proportion of seniors, to promote social engagement, intergeneration interaction and community inclusion for our seniors in their familiar neighbourhood.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An Active Ageing Centre cited in the heart of larger private estates, like Seletar Hill and Luxus Hills in Jalan Kayu, will be another public policy and implementation breakthrough that I keenly hope for.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also recommend that the Government consider expanding the Enhancement for Active Seniors programme in both HDB flats and private houses to include technological features, such as installing Smart Home devices, for seniors with mobility challenges or cognitive impairments.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, supporting seniors to age well requires many hands-on board approaches with also caregivers being well supported.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Building on my previous inquiry regarding the adequacy of Home Caregiving Grant in covering caregiving expenses, I hope that the Government will also, over time, tier support for caregivers of seniors based on the required intensity and duration of care they need to sustain.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, caregivers supporting seniors requiring assistance with all six activities of daily living could receive a higher subsidy to offset the costs associated with more complex care needs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To the final group of Jalan Kayu residents, the young couples and families, whom I feel strongly for, having experienced the ups and downs of settling into a marriage, having a child and constantly juggling with work-life balances throughout the past two decades myself.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Strong and resilient families are essential for Singapore's long-term social and economic well-being.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As young couples and families in Jalan Kayu navigate the complexities of starting and building a family, I am happy that Budget 2025 offers several good supports in critical areas of: one, childcare affordability; two, assistance for large families; and three, enhancing social support networks.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Access to affordable and quality childcare is vital for working parents balancing their careers and family responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my speech just last month in this House regarding the Motion on Supporting Singaporeans in Starting and Raising Families, I opened with the sharing of the large extended family that I was blessed to grow up in and concluded with stories of Jalan Kayu residents and Singaporean friends I know who have three or more children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am so grateful to Prime Minister Lawrence Wong that I can convey the good news of the big "ang pow" that he and his hardworking team in Prime Minister's Office (PMO) have prepared for some more of my residents and friends who are expecting to deliver their third child this year in SG60 and, I hope more, for many more years to come.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we bring children to this world, we must take care of the vulnerability that some will face due to family circumstances that are not of the children's doing.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Initiatives like ComLink+ to offer personalised coaching and mentorship to lower-income families, assisting them in overcoming challenges and achieving greater social mobility, are thus important to be continued in earnest.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that my inquiries previously about family coach-to-family ratio and family coach's qualification and experience will be continually reviewed to ensure that vulnerable families receive the guidance they need to enhance their lives.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Budget 2025 demonstrates the Government's commitment to building a resilient, inclusive and future-ready Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Amid a complex and changing global environment, this Budget not only addresses Singaporeans' practical needs but also charts a blueprint for Singapore's future development.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This year, I will focus on three key areas that are supported by the Budget: (i) first, supporting working residents; (ii) second, caring for the elderly; and (iii) third, helping young couples raise family.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Government can promote more training courses aligned with industry needs and provide clearer career development pathways.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I suggest strengthening job matching services for employees participating in the Workfare Skills Support scheme to ensure training leads to actual employment opportunities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To encourage companies to hire senior workers, I suggest increasing the wage subsidy ratio of the Senior Employment Credit for employers offering full-time, part-time or long-term positions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will benefit seniors who wish to continue to work.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Regarding elderly care, I suggest further integrating elderly-friendly public facilities in both HDB and private estates alike, with a high proportion of seniors. to promote active and healthy living in their neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, as more seniors choose to spend their golden years in familiar surroundings, I hope the Government can expand the Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) programme to include smart home technologies, helping seniors with social mobility or cognitive impairment challenges to age safely and comfortably at home.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Excuse me, Ms Ng Ling Ling, could I ask you to wrap up as you are approaching your 20-minute mark?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: I spoke in my maiden Parliamentary speech in this House in 2020 about happiness, which is one of the aspirations for our people in the Singapore pledge.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: The grandma asked, "Tell me the truth, when old people talk of suffering, isn't it tiresome?" The grandson answered, "Isn't that the point?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: To burden us." I felt the profound depth of wisdom and love of both the grandma and the grandson for each other.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: As an advocate for healthy living, intergenerational bonding and sustainability in my Jalan Kayu constituency, my sincere hope is that our residents and all Singaporeans can make the full use of the benefits provided in Budget 2024 to chase after your true happiness that can be passed down from generation to generation.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Dennis Tan, do you have a clarification for Ms Ng Ling Ling?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I have a clarification regarding a point that I made earlier, just correcting the figures for my previous speech this morning.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, you want to make accurate your previous speech?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Is there anything else you wish to add, Mr Dennis Tan?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Over the course of the past year, inflation has tamed substantially.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is amply clear to all Singaporeans, however, that while the speed by which prices increase have slowed substantially, price levels remain painfully high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We need not go again into comparisons of just how much kopi-o or mee rebus or biryani now command, compared to a few years ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But suffice to say that, especially for those reliant on fixed incomes, the cost of living has become ever harder to bear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, even those who are still currently working for a living feel the pinch of how costly things are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if we look at the data, it should not be much a surprise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Annual real basic wages, that is, take home pay, after adjusting for sticker prices, has failed to keep pace with rising costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While, as Prime Minister Wong shared in the Budget, this has rebounded last year, real wage growth over the past half-decade has lagged overall.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This was, perhaps most distressingly, against a backdrop where labour productivity actually increased, especially in 2021 and 2022, and remains at a level substantially higher today as compared to the pre-pandemic period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By a similar token, the employment rate has consistently improved, hitting highs for all age groups, with the exception of youths, aged 15 to 24 years, in 2024.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In other words, it was not for want of productivity improvements or a soft labour market that wages have been suppressed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government routinely trots out numbers for how measured real median household incomes are high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 2024, it clocked in at $11,297, higher than most comparable advanced economies and have steadily progressed, with median earnings growing at an average annual rate of 3.8% over the past five years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Annual earnings per employee have also moved gradually upward, from around $5,500 per month in 2019 to $6,500 in 2023.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But these impressive figures mask some important truths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For starters, the large headline number applies to a typical resident household where both husband and wife work, in contrast to other countries where it is possible to survive on a single breadwinner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, the dual-income household is not always the result of how both father and mother would like to work, but because they feel that they must, if they hope to make ends meet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, once we correct for inflation, wage growth over the most recent five-year period is actually much lower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And as every worker will attest, this high gross wage quickly dissipates once standard deductions are made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After subtracting CPF contributions and taxes, disposable incomes have to be made to stretch further and further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps most troubling in terms of actual progress among local households is that this median may actually be capturing a moving target.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Recall, the numbers trotted out apply to residents, which include permanent residents (PRs) and new citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This resident population has, of course, been creeping up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But since the criteria for those granted PR or citizenship explicitly require economic contributions, it should be unsurprising if the new additions tend to be higher income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The data support this: wage growth was three times higher in the top decile relative to the middle ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The upshot of all this is that, whether one relies on mean or median wages, we are faced with a moving benchmark, one that is steadily drifting upward, even if the standing of our homegrown workforce may be changing much more slowly, if at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is why claims like rising standards of living – like what Prime Minister Wong articulated in his Budget speech – sometimes ring hollow to many low- and middle-class families here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, what I am stating is not meant to foster discord between native-born Singaporeans and new arrivals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Like the Government, I agree that immigrants that come here – and make Singapore their home – enrich the economy and society of our Little Red Dot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we must not deny how many local households feel – that despite impressive statistics, they do not feel like they have enjoyed much of the vaunted progress that the Government crows on about, since the growth of their median earnings do not reflect their own absence of economic progress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we accept this state of affairs, then the relevant question is what policymakers can do about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government’s approach – which, to be clear, I had supported, and even called a moral imperative, has been to rebate much of the higher nominal tax take to workers, as illustrated by the giveaways in last week’s Budget speech which I support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But such handouts, while welcome, are also perceived by many Singaporeans as palliative measures and insufficient to meet the structural changes required in escalation in costs of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For the remainder of my speech, I will offer some suggestions on how we can better realign the seemingly stagnant incomes of working Singaporean families with the harsh realities of a seemingly inexorable rise in the cost of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The bottom line is actually remarkably simple: nominal wages will need to rise and more decisively than they have in the post-pandemic era.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the short run, this may add some near-term pressure in terms of wages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the medium to longer run, however, so long as the increases are in line with overall productivity trends, we should see a rebasing of wages in a manner that reflects the overall higher sticker prices that have emerged over the past half-decade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will restore the purchasing power of our workers to what had prevailed prior to the post-COVID-19 outbreak of inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The reason is simple: doing so will have a salutary effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It not only sends the message that the Government is taking leadership in setting expectations for how economy-wide wages should evolve in light of higher prices but also ensures that our hardworking agents in the public sector are not shortchanged in their service to the nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And how has wage growth been for this class of workers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, the Government does not make public granular data on civil service salaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, we can make some inferences, indirectly, using the expenditure on manpower line item in fiscal budgets from years past.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In what follows, I will use data from MOE.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If MOE is representative of how the rest of the bureaucracy is paid, civil servants are, at least, not falling behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But if we believe in the signal value of Government action in nudging the private sector, then we must surely feel that this relatively slow rate of wage progression, in the face of high inflation rates, falls short.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, the Government has not entirely abdicated its strategic role in the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The National Wages Council (NWC) has consistently offered advice on the direction that wages should trend, and in its most recent guidelines, it stressed that, and I quote, “employers who have done well… should reward their employees with   built-in wage increases   variable payments”.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This push is welcome and helps redress the still-yawning gap in income inequality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And NWC direction on this front has not been for naught: last year, this group saw their real incomes expand at a rate that was more than 1% faster than that of the median.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, the council held back from analogous recommendations for the workforce as a whole.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Admittedly, it is harder to dictate similar increases across the diverse economic conditions faced by different sectors and industries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we need to remember that much like lower-wage earners, the middle class has seen their purchasing power erode in recent years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The inflation tax is borne by everyone, regardless of income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just as important, wage increases premised on addressing rising costs of living should not be made conditional on upskilling and productivity improvements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is not to say just let real wages rise indiscriminately over time, in blatant disregard of efficiency improvements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather adjustments to nominal income that neutralise the effects of past inflation is the very least that employers owe to their workers, especially with so many companies also posting record profits, due to higher sticker prices alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding the difficulties of prescribing generalised increases, NWC guidelines I believe should at least recommend that all workers in profitable firms, not just those at the lower end of the distribution, be inflation-proofed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To help expedite adoption, the Ministry could also monitor adherence to these guidelines across companies, not least how the civil service has fared.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While NWC recommendations should not be mandatory, an economy-wide stocktaking – especially for firms reporting sales turnovers in excess of $10 million – will nevertheless impress on businesses that the Government does indeed care about the extent to which corporations take guidelines seriously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my classes in macroeconomics, I teach my students about the benefits of stabilisation policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Typically, I talk about either monetary policy, via the interest rate, or fiscal policy, via taxes and government spending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But interventionist policies also include those affecting the exchange rate and, crucially, wages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Wage policy is tricky, however; in most economies, workers, that is, voters would often be up in arms if the government were to recommend wage cuts, even if it could, in principle, shore up the aggregate economy during downturns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When asked for an example, I use our CPF system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The employer’s share does not generally factor into household day-to-day expenses – families make ends meet with their take-home salaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, Singapore has historically used this tool to promote economic recovery, with temporary cuts of the employer’s CPF contribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is grumbling and discontent, but the implicit understanding is that there would be compensation, after the storm has passed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When the scheme was in its infancy, forced saving amounted to a mere 10% of wages, with 5% each from employer and employee.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In these early decades, the employer share was even occasionally higher than that of the employee's.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Through it all, the shares borne by workers and their companies were roughly equal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In response to the Asian Crisis, the employer share was slashed in half, to 10%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this was then incrementally increased to 16% at the turn of the millennium, it was cut again in 2003.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This rate then crept up to the present 17% by 2015, but we never again saw a restoration of an equal employer share.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This move, as Prime Minister Wong shared at the time, allows CPF contributions to better keep pace with rising salaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the policy is only material to those who earn above the ceiling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, raising the employer share will help all workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that, ultimately, employers look at an employee’s overall cost in making hiring decisions and that any call for restoring the employer’s contribution to a higher rate amounts to an increase in the company’s overall wage bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Regardless, the imbalance in employer and employee shares should be redressed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 2014, the Labor Movement asked that employers’ contributions be increased to more than those of employees’.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In other instances, NTUC has also called for a delay to employer contribution cuts or an accelerated restoration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But momentum behind this has stalled and our workers have endured an extended wage cut for the better part of two decades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With costs of living so high, there is no better time than now to make workers’ gross incomes made whole again.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For lower-income earners, we can do more, notwithstanding the gains that the group has managed to eke out over the past year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, the time is right for us to formalise our minimum wage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Following revisions to the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) framework in 2022, which expanded the scheme to all companies hiring foreign employees, rather than just those bound by a foreign worker quota, there is now an effective minimum wage for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, the LQS salary, which used to be around $1,000, has been revised upward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is in line with the WP's advocacy of a $1,300 take-home minimum wage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the beneficial effect of a higher minimum wage is not limited to low-income earners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Research has consistently identified spillovers of a higher minimum wage for those further up the wage distribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, elevating the minimum wage is not just good for just those on low salaries; they benefit all workers, by shaping everyone’s earnings expectations and improving their bargaining positions in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While it is true that some companies have suggested that they will pass on some of these costs to their customers, many others have been able to adjust with productivity improvements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A small price rise is to be expected and was a possibility I had alluded to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is more, there have been no clear detrimental unemployment effects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The unemployment rate – including that for youths, the group that is most likely to be negatively affected by a minimum wage – has steadily tapered downward since 2022.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The natural concern with pursuing increases in wages is that it could have negative implications for inflation, employment or productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On inflation, some have cautioned against pushing for wage increases, under the premise that this could revive inflationary pressure and in the extreme, set off a negative feedback loop of higher wages prompting price hikes, and vice versa.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But neither theory nor data lend much support that such a “wage-price spiral” will emerge in response to a one-off wage hike.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One may also worry that rising wages could lead to companies shedding workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the relationship between wage inflation and unemployment has, in recent decades, been very weak.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And as I have shared with this House before, the majority of minimum wage studies point to little or no job loss effects, especially when the increases are modest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With our labour market unprecedentedly tight, it is difficult to envision mass redundancies triggered by a one-off increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet as I have argued earlier, productivity has risen, while wages have not caught up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are even many reasons why slightly higher wages may improve efficiency, by reducing shirking, improving morale, lowering turnover and making hiring easier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is high time for our salaries to rise and there is more the Government can do to expedite this adjustment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This includes ensuring that NWC guidelines are more widely adopted, equalising the employer share of CPF and instituting a statutory universal minimum wage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Restoring the real purchasing power of wages is a sure-fire way to help working Singaporeans cope with sky-high costs of living.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Speaker sir, the Budget is one of the most generous and inclusive, with something for everyone, and has been widely welcomed by our people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With relevant and in-demand skillsets, they will be empowered to get better and higher paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, for some of them, due to family and work demands, committing time and energy for training is indeed challenging.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their priority is to earn as much money as possible to meet their families’ immediate needs, so some take on more jobs or shifts to supplement their incomes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their working hours may be long and if they do manual work, physically tiring.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their children may be young and they may need to look after elderly, sick or disabled family members.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For workers living hand to mouth, more cash in hand would alleviate the daily financial stresses they face.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are some senior citizens who need to work due to challenging circumstances.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They may have no one to support them or they need to support children in trouble and even grandchildren, despite their advanced age.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For elderly workers in the low-income groups, additional WIS would be helpful.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would allow a bigger group of workers to qualify for wage offsets for their employers and boost their employability.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I would like to express my appreciation for the new measures to support large families.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of these large families are also part of the sandwich class, having to provide for more children and to take care of their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our endeavour to push for a higher fertility rate, we must continue to incentivise, reward and support them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those willing to have more children, let us do more to support and assist them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us commit to long-term subsidies, with more for every additional child they have.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In additional to financial support, I urge the Government to consider providing them with reserved allocations, higher priority and even grants for bigger HDB flats, with the quantum correlated to the number of children they have.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry of Manpower consider exempting large families from maid levies?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To the Ministry of Transport, I would like to request that it considers providing large families perhaps with COE rebates for family-friendly cars.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For working mothers, would the Ministry of Finance consider removing or increasing the cap of $80,000 on personal income tax reliefs so that their families get benefit from the Working Mother's Child Relief?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us give these mothers as much support as we can.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, the number of working mothers earning higher incomes who also have more children are not many, hence the loss of tax revenue to the IRAS should be insignificant.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As for couples intending to have children or who are already expecting, MOH should work with doctors to conduct more public education outreach to encourage couples to take up the free genetic screening programme, PaREnthood genetic Disease Carrier Test (PREDICT), at the KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help them make informed decisions about family planning.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also urge MOH to consider allowing couples planning to get married to qualify for this free assessment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would MOH also consider the building of public subsidised confinement and infant care centres to help mothers recover after delivery?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I have some concerns regarding our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to expedite the building of additional healthcare facilities as soon as possible to meet the increasing demand for nursing homes and day care for senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would HDB also build more smaller single room rental flats for needy singles, so that they can stay by themselves in each unit without having to share these flats with strangers and having disputes often?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I personally receive quite a number of such requests at my Meet the Peoples Sessions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Presently, international trade barriers are rising, which may have an impact on investments and the economic environment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would we need to reserve more surpluses to help the people cope with the unfavourable economic environment that may appear in the next few years and, at the same time, cope with the challenges of an ageing society and help the people to provide for their old age?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the average number of family members decreases, young couples may have to support two sets of parents and raise children at the same time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Reducing the burden on young people and couples is also a top priority, requiring us to think out of the box.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government take advantage of the surplus to increase funding and increase childcare subsidies significantly, so that all infants and young children receive the same subsidies?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Make all Government-subsidised childcare services uniformed, which can reduce the family pressure of young couples, thereby encouraging them to have children and consider having more children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This may also reduce psychological pressures and promote fertility.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Psychological pressure is one of the factors causing infertility.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Government will carefully consider the above opinions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: These communities also often have a high quality of life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Enter the “Blue Zone", a term coined by explorer, author and longevity researcher Dan Buettner in 2004, as part of a study that examined longevity hotspots around the world.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Among these pioneering Blue Zones were: Okinawa, Japan; Sardinia, Italy; Loma Linda, California; Nicoya, Costa Rica and Ikaria, Greece.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: These regions share common lifestyle habits such as plant-based diets, frequent low-intensity physical activity, strong community ties and a sense of purpose.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This was an accolade significant for reasons beyond the longevity marker that Blue Zones represents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Unlike first generation Blue Zones like Okinawa, Singapore does not boast of a deep-rooted tradition of healthy living.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our pace of life is fast and often hectic, and not getting enough good quality sleep is something many in Singapore as well as in this Chamber, struggle with.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Yet, Singapore bucks the trend, becoming a Blue Zone mainly because of stable governance, economic security, accessible healthcare and effective public health measures.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: So, in essence, being a Blue Zone was not something that came along organically for Singapore, but rather, through careful orchestration via policy and programming.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Indeed, we are living longer here in Singapore than many other parts of the world.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Does that mean then that all is well?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A significant 10-year gap between health span and lifespan exists.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: What this means is that Singaporeans spend the last decade of their lives in poor health, struggling with chronic illnesses, disabilities, or other age-related illnesses and issues.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: While Singapore has a high life expectancy, health difficulties have a substantial impact on quality of life in our later years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The answer does not lie in what we can do when we turn 60.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Let us examine the factors determining good health.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: According to the World Health Organisation, factors affecting one’s health are an individual’s social and economic environment, physical environment and their characteristics and behaviours.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is not merely how good or advanced a population’s healthcare system is that singularly determines the people’s healthcare outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In fact, social determinants of health play a much more significant role in ageing well than the state of the healthcare system alone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Therefore, a comprehensive approach to ageing well must consider various non-healthcare and non-medical components such as social connections, physical activity, dietary habits, cognitive engagement and employment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Social connections – strong community ties significantly support ageing well.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Conversely, research suggests that social isolation contributes to cognitive decline and poor health outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Physical activity – encouraging daily movement, natural movement, such as gardening or walking, rather than structured workouts, helps maintain long-term mobility and independence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Dietary habits – this is an obvious one, for we are what we eat.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We can almost see and hear the Health Promotion Board's various campaigns flashing before our eyes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Cognitive engagement – learning new skills, playing memory-enhancing games, engaging in purposeful activities reduce dementia risks, and from my own non-clinical experience, senior members of my extended family who played mahjong remained lucid throughout their golden years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Employment – continuing to work provides mental stimulation, encourages social interaction, adds to financial stability, facilitates a sense of validation, esteem and actualisation, all of which contribute to overall well-being.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our ambition for Singapore goes beyond what we had already achieved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In the words of our Health Minister, we are setting our sights to becoming a Blue Zone 3.0, moving beyond policy-driven longevity, to embedding healthier habits into everyday living.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As Singapore ages, it is essential to reframe the ageing narrative.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Negative descriptors that are often used today, like "Silver Tsunami", "has beens", "burden on society" should be immediately abandoned.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And we must shift our perception of ageing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: No longer should ageing be seen as a period of decline, but rather as a phase of life that represents opportunity, contribution and vitality.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: By fostering a society that not only values longevity, but also the potential and contributory role that seniors can play, we can create an ecosystem where older adults are empowered to contribute and to thrive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In Queenstown where I serve, nearly three in 10 residents are 60 and above.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I have been concerned about various aspects about our seniors in the community: their physical and mental well-being, their retirement financial adequacy, social isolation and the many associated downsides.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As our population ages, we must rethink senior employment in our society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Should retirement mean stepping aside completely, or can we reimagine a model where their experience and contributions continue to shape our community in a positive manner?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: How should we think about productivity, employment and social participation in our senior years?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For some insights, let us go back in time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For much of human history, retirement was not a formalised concept.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: People worked for as long as they were able to, and labour formed an integral part of an individual's identity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Now, the rest, from the late 19th century onwards, was history.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: An official retirement policy is arguably one of the best policy implementations that bolsters well-being in one's senior years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As people generally live longer, there is a growing sense of inertia in extending our working years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Some see the raising of retirement age as an obscene violation of their well-deserved rest after years of toil.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The real question is though: does employment in our senior years have to be cast purely as a binary, black-or-white construct: either you work full-time or you do not work at all?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In fact, I jokingly tell many of my Queenstown seniors that I meet that I would have to "check their IC" to be sure that they are telling me their real age!

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Many of them look way younger than their actual "NRIC age".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To be sure, many seniors find purpose, mental stimulation and social engagement in continued employment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Work is more than just an income source.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It provides structure, a sense of purpose and a continued role in society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Some seniors actively resist retirement because their professions define their identity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The challenge, then, is not merely extending work life but rethinking its structure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: How can employment be made more flexible, more meaningful and adapted to the strengths of an ageing workforce?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Also, what is the reality in our employment market today?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Do employers perceive the resumes of senior applicants they receive as prospective assets with decades of experience, or do they reflexively dismiss them on the assumption that senior workers would be a drag on efficiency and productivity?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: What changes can be implemented at the workplace to facilitate the reintegration of more seniors as part of our active workforce?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Would employers be willing to consider process automation, AI, redesigning full-time roles as micro jobs as ways to not merely hire more seniors, but also, to fulfil our manpower needs in a labour-tight market?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Among senior workers, many are rightly concerned about the perception of age discrimination at the workplace and many would also want to prioritise time for loved ones in their golden years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Concerns over physical and mental well-being also mean many are hesitant to re-enter or stay on in the workforce in their senior years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Clearly, mindset shifts and tangible action, on both the employer and employee ends of the spectrum, are needed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: If we are serious about our Blue Zone 3.0 ambition, then surely, we must lead the charge in reframing retirement and senior employment, among other issues.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: After all, to discriminate based on age, is merely the act of discriminating against our very selves – the future versions of ourselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As we strive towards being a Blue Zone 3.0, our goal is not just to live longer but to live well.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And to get there, we will be sailing through uncharted waters, where no one before us has gone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Our true measure of success lies not just in productivity, but in the collective well-being of every passenger on board this ship.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: After all, if there is any vessel that we can navigate all on board to the promised land of wholesome, empowered longevity, I have every confidence that that vessel's name must be Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Cost of living is a worry for so many families across Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is the money you spend every day to get by.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there are also other hidden costs of living – the time you spend navigating public services; time that you spend, and not just money that you spend.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The former Head of Civil Service, Mr Lim Siong Guan, once said, "Implementation is Policy", because the impact of policy, however well it is designed on paper, what matters is when you see what happens on the ground.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And in today's world, "User Experience is Implementation" – the resident's experience is the implementation of policy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Policy cannot fully help its intended beneficiaries if the resident cannot navigate the policy, or if too many of the processes are online and the residents themselves cannot quite get online to make full use of the policy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, again, what happens on the ground is the implementation, and implementation is policy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I met a young Clementi couple earlier these few weeks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because she has a lung infection, she needs to go to the polyclinic every day to receive medication, because the nature of the medication is that she has to take it in a supervised way in a medical setting at the polyclinic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She is not well, needs a wheelchair to get around.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, because her husband has to bring her in a wheelchair to the polyclinic every day, the husband has quit his job.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The family breadwinner has quit his job and now there is no breadwinner at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Home-based medical care, arranging for that treatment to be delivered at home could have saved my resident those trips to the polyclinic every day.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It might have been counted as healthcare expenditure, additional expense on MOH's bottom line, but by saving the caregiver's job, it would have saved on suffering for the family and saved on hardship and safeguarded the husband's ability to earn as a breadwinner in his existing job.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are similar challenges throughout Singapore – caregivers under stress when a loved one is sick.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In 2022, I asked in Parliament how many Specialist Outpatient Clinic visits a resident might need to go through in a single year.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That means 2,000 Singaporeans averaging three or more Specialist Outpatient appointments a month.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They share with me how hard it can be to keep a full-time job when the family is small; not many grown up children looking after a senior who has so many medical appointments.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also have Clementi residents, as well as sisters and brothers from Healthcare Services Employees Union and they share the challenges on the other end of care delivery as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They share about how much effort it takes to coordinate care to try and simplify the number of clinic visits, whether it is moving multiple Specialist visits to the same day, so the patient makes just one trip rather than four, or doing backend meetings to simplify the number of visits.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have been told by our sisters and brothers in healthcare that often this coordination work takes place outside of working hours.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Reaching out to colleagues, messaging, emailing, streamlining, working into the night sometimes behind the scenes – extra work, unrecorded, unmeasured.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because simplifying the care journey can help patients and caregivers stay employed, and not have to choose between maintaining their employment, and accompanying and supporting their ill relative through the medical journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is a cost to families, Mr Speaker, when a breadwinner can no longer maintain their full-time job.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is a cost to families when a caregiver who used to work part-time, leaves the workforce completely because of these stresses.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And when a worker leaves the workforce because they can no longer juggle supporting their sick loved one through the healthcare journey and at the same time, trying to hold down their job or employment, when a worker stops working because of this invidious choice, it is not just a loss of income, it is not just a loss of being a breadwinner.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because every month that a worker stays out of work, every month that a worker has sacrificed their career for, is also a month that their skills fade, become more out-of-date.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is another month when their networks, their professional networks, their workplace networks become more distant, less connected.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It becomes harder and harder, even as they make that sacrifice.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, anything we can do to streamline the care journey for our seniors, if it can help save a caregiver's employment and employability, it is something worth striving for and something that the Government can and should support even more, moving forward.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The importance of simplifying the journey, it applies to Government services as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In healthcare, the more apps there are, it also means the more logins, the more apps, the more notifications, the more processes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is not easy for caregivers and seniors.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are Government agencies which today, as a default, want the resident to login with Singpass, login online, to book an offline appointment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens to seniors who cannot easily go online, who have not kept their Singpass working?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has going digital made it harder for seniors to get help?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And what message do we send inadvertently when we ask someone who is not digitally-savvy to go online to get the offline appointment?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, even though our agencies speak of "digital first, not digital only", we must ask: what is the outcome on the ground for our seniors?
