speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I call upon this Government to study deeply how the implementation of digitalisation has affected the less digitally-savvy seniors.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In particular, we must look out for the risks of digital dropout.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As background, last year, April 2024, the Government set up the Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) for Pro-Enterprise Rules Review.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just as the IMC on Pro-Enterprise Rules Review aims to help SMEs better navigate Government rules and regulations, we should also do the same for citizens, especially our seniors who may be less digitally-savvy or who are afraid to go online, amid a world of digital scams.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because efficiency of access to services and the cost of navigating, the cost burden of time spent, it is not just a challenge for businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It affects any citizen who is facing difficulty navigating Government services, especially those who do not know how to go online.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Looking out for the less digitally-savvy is not just about social equity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is not just about making sure no Singaporean is left behind.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It also speaks to our social compact across the generations.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because these seniors, they spent their whole lives building Singapore up and yet, today, in the Singapore they helped build, the Singapore which is prosperous enough to go digital and have online services, there are seniors who feel left out, left behind.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must honour our seniors' contributions to Singapore, honour the seniors who made a digital smart nation possible by building Singapore in decades gone by, even as they face challenges, navigating a more digital world today.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because it also sends a message to today's middle-aged workers, today's workers who may be tomorrow's seniors.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It sends a message, if we include today's seniors, that tomorrow's seniors will also be included and not left behind when there is new technology, 10 or 20 years from now.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In 2018, during the Budget debate, I called for greater investment in AI, as well as quantum computing technology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I asked the Government as well, earlier in that year, 2018, to look at Asimov's Laws of Robotics, at that time in science fiction, but applicable in the event you have thinking machines that are able to engage and potentially even advise on human decisions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, from the US, we have ChatGPT, previously the GPT-4 model, now the o3 model AI model.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: From other companies, like xAI, we have Grok 3, new AI models from the US.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: From China, we have seen recently seen DeepSeek R1, advanced AI as well from China and many more AI models coming out.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In 2023 and 2024, I spoke again on AI.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Parts of the 2024 speech managed to get shared online.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One resident pointed out an overseas Instagram took a clip of the speech, eight million views.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Another resident mentioned some X accounts, one million views.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Another resident who is active on TikTok mentioned that there was an international TikTok sharing some clips, 1.4 million views.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But this is not about any individual MP's speeches.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The message is people are interested in Singapore and what Singapore MPs say, because Singapore is relevant to the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because Singapore has done well and it is relevant to the world, that is why people out there are interested in what we are doing, how we deal with today's challenges, how we plan for the future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: People around the world are interested therefore in what our leaders are doing but also what our back benchers are talking about, backbenchers of all persuasions, all perspectives.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And people around the world see what Singapore has achieved over the past 60 years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And because we are relevant, inventing the future, adapting to the challenges around us, that is why people around the world follow what our MPs say on the front bench, back bench and from all angles of this House.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I would say we must also allow AI to be accessible even to our home-based businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In Clementi, we have a young mother who looks after a very young family, while running a home-based business.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is not easy keeping track of accounts, doing supply chain planning, designing collaterals, publicity, doing business analytics.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: It should not be people bending to the technology but technology lifting our people up.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And so, with this, I thank my Clementi residents for their encouragement over the years, I stand proudly in support of this Budget.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It also coincides with SG60, the commemoration of 60 years of Singapore’s Independence.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the decades, we have weathered storms that could have broken lesser countries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: From Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) in 2003 to the unprecedented challenges of COVID-19, key Government systems in our country from healthcare, manpower, industry to education – and our social cohesion – were tested.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet, time and again, we have emerged stronger.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This resilience is a testament to our collective spirit and the leadership of this Government.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our journey has been marked by bold, creative measures to safeguard businesses, livelihoods and the interests of our next generations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These efforts, together with many post-COVID measures, rolled out consistently, reflect our Government’s commitment to supporting our people.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But as we approach SG60, our work is far from over.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Persistent challenges – like our declining fertility rate, the rising needs of a rapidly ageing population and the disruptive impact of AI on jobs and the economy – still demand urgent attention.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans look to the Government to lead in navigating these challenges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, this Budget is crucial as it addresses how we allocate our national resources, limited resources for the immediate and for the longer term; it is about resourcing a strategic plan to secure our future and it cannot be seen merely as an annual “goodie bag” giveaway but as a support plan to address our persistent challenges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To this end, Mr Speaker, Sir, I propose three focus areas where resources can be further directed to ensure Singapore remains resilient and inclusive in an increasingly complex world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Key focus area one: on jobs and skills in this age of AI.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: AI is transforming industries at an unprecedented pace.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: While it brings opportunities, it also threatens to displace workers and widen inequality.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In Singapore, sectors like finance, healthcare, logistics and customer service are already experiencing AI-driven changes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a stark reminder of the urgent need to reskill and repurpose our workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The latest World Economic Forum report cautioned that, and I quote: "Without appropriate decision-making frameworks, economic incentive structures and possibly Government regulations, there remains a risk that technological development will be focused on replacing human work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The trajectory of AI adoption could either help us collaborate with machines for outsized gains – or lead to greater inequality and job displacement, depending on how businesses and policymakers respond." In Singapore, Budget 2025 is going in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The SkillsFuture movement was started 10 years ago.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I remember when I first brought up at a Budget debate like this that MOE should look into adult training as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But I am glad that SkillsFuture Singapore has been established, put under the MOE and the Institutes of Higher Learning and other adult training providers are now part of the SkillsFuture adult training ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Few other countries have come close to the kind of systematic intervention for citizens that we see in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: ITM 2025 is our Government’s initiative to refresh and strengthen the Industry Transformation Road Maps over the next five years, focusing on seizing post-COVID opportunities and new strategies for jobs, skills, research and innovation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The short shelf life of technology and we can see AI’s impact on jobs and skills is tremendous.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I urge the Government to accelerate the review of the ITM 2025 and to treat the ITMs as living documents to be updated regularly, certainly not once in five years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us also go beyond the usual methods of Job Fairs and invest in channels to clearly communicate the required competencies to both current and potential industry entrants and stressing skills development over academic qualifications.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us prioritise working on the jobs that might be most at risk of obsolescence and develop action steps for these job families before they are axed.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: District offices like the Community Development Councils are ground partners who can support these efforts, since the Community Development Councils are already running hundreds of SkillsFuture Advice Workshops supporting MOE, SSG every year.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, let us define literacy for all age groups.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For such a time as this, the current definitions and the skills inventory of English, numeracy or Math and Digital Literacy should be updated and widely shared.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Everyone, regardless of age, should understand the specific skills they need to acquire beyond our traditional focus on English, Math and Digital Literacy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One of my young volunteers, sitting over there in the Gallery now, even suggested adding empathy and community spirit literacy in our fast-paced, polarised world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, is it possible for us to create a Literacy #101 Skills Inventory List, complete with suggested key learning solutions for all Singaporeans of all ages?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, to be more aggressive in driving upskilling campaigns.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The acquisition of new skills and literacies is no longer optional.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And, in fact, it is not just a pathway to promotions or career advancement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, key focus area two: on vulnerable groups and businesses.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The rapid use of technology presents significant challenges for vulnerable groups, especially the elderly, PwDs and low-skilled and lowly-educated workers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These groups, already at risk of marginalisation, face further exclusion due to the growing digital divide.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, some residents that I see in their 60s and 70s, they still want to work, they do not want to be at karaoke or bingo sessions whole day long.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They struggle and they want to work, they struggle to secure employment in the new economy, whether they want to work out of necessity or out of choice.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, I filed several PQs and Meet-the-People-Session appeals to different agencies before for seniors who are not proficient in English or matters that are digital and who struggle in accessing essential Government services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some cannot even read the English language responses that are mailed to them in response to my appeals for them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of them actually spend hundreds of dollars or share their Singpass information with parties or sometimes like agents outside the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority office, people whom they think can help them gain digital access to the services they need.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SMEs as well – traditional brick-and-mortar stores and low-margin industries are particularly vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: While many of these businesses should be more proactive in taking up the Government grants and schemes to automate, there is a segment of businesses that may not be easily automated or have a reason for sticking to its current business model.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One example, for example, is Wardah Books, a beloved traditional bookshop in Kampong Glam, which sells Muslim and Malay books.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It faces challenges in its current business model.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This initiative was announced recently during the official opening of the Kampong Glam Ramadan Bazaar, which was organised by the local business community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, we should establish task forces, focus groups, focused task forces for deeper dive, to assist these identified vulnerable groups and businesses.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: While the Government has implemented measures to assist these groups and individuals, the outcomes still remain to be seen.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Do this starting with the elderly, the disabled and businesses not so suitable for automation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I agree with the principle that not all solutions are best originated or implemented by Government.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the Government can play a crucial role in facilitating worthy community-driven initiatives or, at the very least, avoid creating adding obstacles to their initiatives.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to better encourage and support organic, ground-up initiatives.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I can think of several out of many needs I see on the ground that could do with better coordination and support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, school bus logistics and cost were mentioned throughout last year.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Could carpooling or escort services at the community level help families, for instance, affected by the manpower and cost constraints faced by school bus industry?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Elderly with dementia: for elderly residents with dementia who do not require nursing home care yet, but they lack caregivers who might be working, like people to escort them, to accompany them to day activity centres, could community-level solutions be better encouraged and developed and even scaled?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Families with special needs children: for caregivers of children with special needs who are emotionally drained and especially those with middle or lower income, could community-based support systems be established instead of just relying on ad hoc, acts of kindness?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In my constituency, Purple Hearts, and I know in Ang Wei Neng's constituency as well, a grassroots initiative has been formed, this is in Kampong Glam, to support families of children with special needs – children who maybe young or may already be adults in their 50s.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And this is also done, I think, by Ang Wei Neng.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Could these be scaled and looked at even more?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In his SG60 messages, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has called upon Singaporeans to actively become a part of community solutioning – to care and share, to look beyond themselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: By empowering community-driven solutions and providing some essential support, we can address pressing issues more effectively and inclusively – and not have everything done by Government which sometimes may be good or not so good.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us draw inspiration from the proverbial giraffe.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The giraffe, with its long neck, stands tall, not just to see farther but to reach higher, to nourish its herd and protect those around it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, let us be giraffes of our time – stick our necks for the common good.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We only need to look around us, to know that what we have got is highly uncommon and worth safeguarding.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While it is reasonable to question the accuracy of the Government's financial projections or debate how to best use the surplus, we, nonetheless, find ourselves in a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In his speech, the Prime Minister also framed the Budget statement in the context of the global realities at play.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We live in a time of persistent geopolitical uncertainty, where war rages on and global trade rules are being re-written.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Long-held principles are now being questioned or even renounced.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As citizens of the world, we are left to ask ourselves: what do we hold onto?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, even in these times, it is reassuring to see Singapore remain steadfast in our values.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: There is an inherent tension between securing our social ideals and maintaining financial discipline.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget has never been just about government spending or financial reserves.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: That is why I am happy to see "Nurturing A Caring and Inclusive Society" as a core tenet of this Budget, with meaningful initiatives for families, seniors and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: At its core, inclusion is not just about supporting specific groups in isolation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is about integrating them to strengthen our social fabric and unite us as one nation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When everyone, including the most vulnerable, has real opportunities to contribute and thrive, to participate in shared spaces and to engage meaningfully with the wider community, we build a stronger Singaporean identity.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In this debate, I hope to build on this and explore how we weave this naturally into the fabric of our society through two familiar avenues: the arts and sports.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: From a young age, we were taught to embrace people of different races and religions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We have internalised racial and religious harmony as a core Singaporean value, not only because we learn this in our textbooks, but because we have grown up, learnt together and played alongside friends, regardless of race or faith.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We bond as Singaporeans over shared experiences, whether it is our love of food, cheering for our national team, catching up on gossip or breaking down the latest Netflix drama.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Yet today, many still feel awkward interacting with persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We are still some distance away from more natural and meaningful interactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The arts create spaces where this change can take place, where people from all walks of life come together through a shared love for music, performance and culture.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Our SG Arts Plan 2023-2027 is a roadmap that guides Singapore's arts policies over a five-year period.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While the plan recognises the importance of inclusivity in the arts, there is room to further refine what this means in a holistic way for persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We can do more to harness the arts as a force for greater inclusion in our society.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve this, I propose a two-pronged approach: increasing participation and enhancing representation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: First, to boost participation, we need to make concerts, theatre performances and live music events more accessible.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, we were treated to a lineup of exciting, high-profile concerts, including Taylor Swift, Bruno Mars and Ed Sheeran.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But how many of those with mobility challenges or sensory disabilities actually get to attend?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Too often, the experience of booking tickets for major events can be stressful and anxiety-inducing for those with unique accommodation needs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The race of "fastest fingers first" leaves many excluded before the event begins.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Accessibility means more than simply providing wheelchair spaces or one-size-fits-all solutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It means recognising the diverse needs of individuals and adopting an end-to-end, user-centric approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While some productions do provide accommodations, it is not yet standard across the board.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, local theatre companies like Wild Rice and the Singapore Repertory Theatre have taken commendable steps in providing access performances at select showings.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These performances are accompanied by sign language interpretation, captions, audio descriptions and touch tours, to offer a fully inclusive experience.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Sign language interpreters translated the lyrics in real time, while fans used interactive vests called SubPacs, to feel the music through vibrations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These accommodations went beyond providing literal translations of the lyrics.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: They were about giving fans full access to the concert experience, immersing them in the rhythm, energy and soul of the music.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: There are actionable steps that we can take to understand and address the unique needs of individuals with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: First, could the Government consider commissioning a comprehensive survey to understand the participation of persons with disabilities in the arts and the challenges they face?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We need to make sure that when initiatives like this are rolled out to all Singaporeans, we do not inadvertently exclude others disproportionately.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Having such a survey will allow the Government to pinpoint specific barriers encountered by persons with disabilities and it could highlight areas that are under-addressed and ensure equitable participation even in the arts scene.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we should already recognise that persons with disabilities often have diverse needs, which require more flexibility and thoughtful planning.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Not everyone with mobility challenges uses a wheelchair.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Some can walk short distances, others may be able to manage a few steps.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, these nuances are often lost in the standard web-based ticketing experience.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A potential solution could be to establish a dedicated access and ticketing hotline for persons with disabilities to make enquiries and explore specific accommodations for arts events in advance.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This way, more people can be assured of a comfortable experience.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Government can take the lead by introducing such a hotline at venues it owns and operates, like the Singapore Indoor Stadium or Singapore Conference Hall.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This can serve as a model for private ticketing offices, allowing them to adopt similar practices, if proven effective.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When persons with disabilities can secure tickets as easily as everyone else and are then welcomed by trained staff on event day, this creates a smooth experience and facilitates participation in the arts scene without hesitation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is not just about putting more persons with disabilities on stage.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is about ensuring that the voices and perspectives of persons with disabilities are embedded into our cultural identity.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We already have dedicated groups to champion arts and cultural performances by persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: One great example is the Purple Symphony, an inclusive orchestra comprising talented musicians with and without disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Another organisation, ART:DIS, is a non-profit organisation that supports persons with disabilities in the arts by organising art programmes, exhibitions and performances.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Such groups offer training and resources to elevate the artistic standards of artists with disabilities by offering an alternative, accessible platform to hone their craft.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that the next stage for truly inclusive practices is when performances by artists with disabilities are no longer showcased in isolation but ingrained in our arts culture.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This means creating clear pathways for artists with disabilities to enter the mainstream.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: At present, persons with disabilities are a part of significant national performances, such as the National Day Parade and Singapore Youth Festival Arts Presentation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Their artworks are showcased alongside those of artists without disabilities and they perform as part of a larger collective.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But the question remains: how do we make this more of a norm?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I recognise that this shift is not easy.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: There are barriers to overcome still, both in infrastructure and in mindset.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps we can take inspiration from the successful strategies we have used in organising our ethnic and cultural festivals.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We have long celebrated our multi-cultural identity, hosting arts festivals that are rich in diversity, featuring both local and international cultural performances.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We do not even think twice about the cultural richness that these events hold.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The same can be done for performances involving persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Can we explore partnerships with international disability arts groups, to allow our artists to interact with peers from around the world?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we can proudly showcase the diversity of disability performances and provide greater exposure for local artists with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While I fully support these pillars and their initiatives, I have three complementary suggestions that I hope will further amplify their impact.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: First, we need to get more of the population to buy into the DSMP.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: If you read the master plan closely, you will find that achieving social inclusion through sports is actually a recurring objective.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is not about promoting disability sports exclusively for persons with disabilities or simply raising awareness among the general public, but it hopes to use sports to integrate society and normalise inclusive activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When someone without a disability comes across the DSMP, perhaps in the news, they may not instinctively see its relevance to them.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But this is not what the plan seeks to accomplish at all.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: If social inclusion through sports is a collective effort, then why not call future iterations the Inclusive Sports Masterplan?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Rebranding the DSMP in this way sends a clear yet subtle message: that sports should be for everyone.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It draws the attention of the general public and prompts them to consider the important role they play in fostering a truly inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Second, beyond awareness, we should take more active steps towards greater community integration, especially at a recreational level.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The first two strategic themes of the DSMP are to increase accessibility and enhance awareness of disability sports and inclusive sports activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These are great, targeted steps and I commend MCCY for actively listening to feedback and responding to engagement findings.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While it does not directly address integrating students with disabilities in mainstream schools via sports, it really does help to tackle the issue of awareness, which is the first step in overcoming preconceived notions about persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Though the overarching objective is awareness, I recognise it is also about integration as it enables PwDs to play sports together with the wider community.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While I personally find the competitive element fun and engaging, I do wonder if it may discourage those who prefer a more recreational approach to sports or exercise.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps in the next DSMP refresh, MCCY could consider engaging deeper into this area, to find more ways to integrate PwDs in mainstream schools and to introduce more pathways for recreational sports participation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Third, the end-to-end experience for PwDs to participate in sports needs to be seamless.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is encouraging to see that the DSMP is already working towards accessible facilities under Strategic Move 3.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Still, we must continue paying attention to the finer details to ensure an inclusive and uniform experience.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I have always appreciated that the OCBC Aquatic Centre at the Singapore Sports Hub has concession rates for PwDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is a clear signal that PwDs are welcome and supported there.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, while other gantries allow independent access, the wider, accessible gate for wheelchair users still has to be manually operated by a staff member, creating an unnecessary barrier.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These may seem like minor details, but addressing them is essential so that inclusive access does not feel like an after-thought but part of a proactive design.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I fully believe that we all recognise the importance of enabling PwDs to live independently.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As we continue making strides in enhancing our ActiveSG sports facilities, let us not overlook the small but important details to ensure complete accessibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Arts and sports hold a unique power to achieve this, by bringing people together in ways policies alone cannot.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: They create spaces where we see talent before limitation, ability before disability.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As the Prime Minister said in his Budget Statement, no one should be left behind.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But we must make this a lived reality, where dreams and aspirations are within reach for all, not just some.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Imagine a world where an artist is seen for their craft, a sportsperson for their skill – and not for their disability.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A world where access and opportunity are more than just ideals.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: That is the future we should strive for.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A Singapore we can all be proud to call home.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am glad to see further steps announced by Prime Minister Wong on nurturing a caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will touch on a few points on this, later in my speech.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will first focus on the longer-term investments in the Budget that look to strengthening Singapore's growth, giving Singaporeans quality jobs and helping Singaporeans be ready for the future of work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This gives hope for the future and will make Singapore a place where our people are proud to call home and want to nurture their families here.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In order to have opportunities, it is vital that Singapore continues to grow sustainably and is ready to handle future challenges.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is worth noting that Budget 2025 is allocating funds to signal the continued investments in technology and innovation engines as well as to address Singapore's resource constraints.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These are critical for Singapore to continue to grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While Singapore has strong fundamentals, being an open economy, global political tensions and escalating trade conflicts, and disruptions to supply chains pose challenges.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore must adapt to evolving conditions and uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is therefore important that we continue to create and sustain value for companies both local and foreign to want to anchor the businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The fund will support businesses as they drive initiatives and commit resources to adopt new technologies, modernise and upskill their workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It reflects the commitment to driving Singapore's energy transition and securing cleaner power sources such as hydrogen, electricity imports and the feasibility of nuclear.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Government has committed to sustained investment in R&D to about 1% of GDP.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: RIE2025 announced in 2020, with the $3 billion top-up in last year's Budget, totals to $28 billion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the additional $1 billion R&D infrastructure in this year's Budget, it will amount to $29 billion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is now almost five years since the launch of RIE2025 and given the importance of the investments in R&D for growth and in innovations, it would be opportune to have an update on the progress and achievements of RIE2025 and an understanding of the framing of the next phase of investments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Budget 2025 includes several measures to support businesses cope with rising costs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These include the enhancements to the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme, corporate income tax rebates and cash grant, and enhancements to the Enterprise Financing Scheme, the redesign of the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit Scheme from a reimbursement to a digital wallet with the additional 10,000 credits for companies that hire at least three resident workers, will definitely help companies offset out of pocket expenses for workforce transformation initiatives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It will enable businesses to access AI tools, computing resources, as well as specialised expertise from global cloud services providers, which would otherwise not have been available or be too costly, especially for our smaller businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But to truly reap the benefits of AI, businesses will have to do their part.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What will be key for them is not just the adoption of AI, but the transformation of their business processes and integration – and I think we need to recognise this is not easy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The schemes to support businesses announced in this year's Budget together with existing schemes are significant in helping them adapt and grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although I must say that in our meeting with business leaders, many did say not enough, but I think more importantly they did acknowledge after a little bit of reminder that there are loads of scheme.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The feedback from business leaders is that while support is available, it can be quite complex to navigate, to apply and utilise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are resources and support available to help businesses utilise these schemes, but the ease of utilisation does vary based on the specific schemes, as well as the businesses' familiarity with the process.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Business leaders are asking for streamlining of the support schemes and it would be of great help to companies if they could engage a single point of contact for more integrated and coordinated support as they apply and utilise the schemes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Why do we need sustained growth and successful businesses?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is really for quality jobs and opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The changes are impacting both companies and workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The demand for specialised skills, technology and innovation, such as AI, data, analytics, cyber security, digital marketing will continue to grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Companies are facing challenges in finding and retaining talent with the relevant expertise, especially in new and emerging technologies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Despite Singapore's high employment rate, the pace of change and technological changes has led to job insecurity and anxiety.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A recent Insight article in The Straits Times cited Institute of Policy Studies' 2023 report and a 2025 survey on economic sentiments by the NTUC, highlighting respondents' concerns of jobs not existing in the future or losing their jobs as companies transform and restructure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And most recently, we have also heard of companies talking about reapplying for even the jobs that you are in.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I do, however, worry about workers who lose their jobs due to disruptions, especially matured workers and their finding appropriate employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my engagements with residents during house visits and most recently last weekend during a dialogue on the Budget, concerns were raised about getting a job when their jobs are disrupted, especially among our matured workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many shared that they made multiple job applications and either did not get a response or an opportunity to interview.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the rapid changes and tech transformation that companies need to make.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Jobs will be disrupted, so while workers must continue to upskill and employers will train their workforce and build new capabilities, there still needs to be more direct job matching and more targeted industry specific reskilling to help workers transition when they are in their jobs, to new and growth sectors, and to address the challenges faced by both workers and businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, this is not going to be easy, but it is something that we all have to do because the disruptions will happen on both sides.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do welcome the setting up of the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment to conduct a comprehensive and longer-term review of senior employment policies to improve the employability of seniors and availability of jobs that better suit their needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do hope that the work will also consider senior employability in the context of an inter-generational workforce and how to tap the potential of matured workers in a diverse workforce, because they do not work in a vacuum.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not just about finding suitable jobs for seniors, but how our economy can tap this resource of talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For employers, hiring of seniors will require a mindset change.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While employers may not necessarily or consciously discriminate for age, there may be concerns or unconscious bias in the consideration of hiring of matured workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have received feedback from residents who have been retrenched that they face situations where potential employers inform them that although they are suitable for the jobs, they are reluctant to hire them, even when they are prepared to take a lower pay than their previous salary, because the concern is that the worker may not stay because they are so used to a certain level of jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This really requires both sides: one to say, "I'm prepared to do it", but the other has to be able to give the opportunity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And so it really is also not just about policies, not just about processes, not just about support, but mindsets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am heartened by the measures announced by Prime Minister Wong to nurture a caring and inclusive society to make Singapore a place where people aspire to call home and have families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many of the measures in the Budget will help the sandwich class as they care for both their children and parents.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are too many measures for me to discuss in my speech and I am quite sure Speaker will be happy that I am not going to touch on all of them because that will take too long, so I will focus on the enabling of our seniors to age well and long-term care services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Last year and the year before, I made the appeal in the Budget debate for the review and refinement of the means test criteria for senior long-term residential and non-residential care.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am now sounding like a broken record, but as Annual Value (AV) continues to be a means test criterion to determine eligibility for those with no per capita household income, I am asking for a refinement of how AV is used as the primary criterion to determine eligibility in this instance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not asking for no means testing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the increase in property value, most of the residents living in even small condo units and landed terraces in my constituency in Changi-Simei will not be eligible.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many are retirees who bought their homes long ago and are asset rich but may be cash poor.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The cost of eldercare services is not insignificant.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Nursing home from $2,200 to $4,200 per month, without subsidies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, indeed instead of 0% or no support for those with no per capita household income and they live in properties with AV greater than $21,000, could consideration be given, or at least a tiered support?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Over the weekend, I met one of my residents who is in her 70s, taking care of her mother who is in her 90s and she shared that it would really be helpful.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I thank the Prime Minister for including that, because they were very happy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In fact, many of my residents were very, very happy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is a Budget for all Singaporeans and I am confident it will help us move onward together for a better tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, I note that I am a social worker and educator currently working with the Singapore University of Social Sciences and the President of the Persatuan Pemudi Islam Singapura (PPIS), an organisation supporting women and families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: There is also increasing evidence that access to early childhood education is particularly beneficial for children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to consider the curriculum, the educator's qualifications and access and equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Effective early childhood education curricula should be child-centred and developmentally appropriate, give priority to play-based and hands-on learning and focus on social-emotional, not just academic, development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Early childhood educators also need to be suitably qualified, supervised and supported so that the sector attracts the right people and keeps the right people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Working with very young children is difficult work and important work, and the contribution of early childhood educators to the safety, health and well-being of children needs to be better recognised and rewarded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: There remain, in Singapore, strong personal and cultural perspectives that early childhood education is an unnecessary expense or a luxury, particularly when young children have historically been looked after by an elderly relative or helper.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to educate families about the benefits of early childhood education and ensure that services are geographically convenient, easy to access, affordable and culturally appropriate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Engaging children, including very young children, in activities that stimulate wonder and curiosity teaches them how to think creatively, critically and independently, how to problem solve and how to cooperate, share and resolve conflict.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It also improves physical development, including motor skills, balance, coordination and fine motor play.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to move away from seeing education as simply giving children facts and then assessing how well they remember those facts on any given day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by the philosopher Socrates, "Education is the kindling of a flame, not the filling of a vessel." Mr Speaker, part of the solution lies with parents encouraging their children to be children and to explore areas of wonders and curiosity at school.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, schools also need to play their part and implement individualised, experiential learning techniques in both teaching and assessment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Despite this, many families and schools give preference to traditional academic subjects, with the creative arts seen as something that children might do as a part-time hobby or as a non-essential skill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to provide children access to a wide of range of creative arts options at school and we need to nurture creativity in children just as much as we nurture literacy and numeracy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I dream of a Singapore where a young child who announces to their parents or school that they want to become an actor or painter or musician, is seen as no different to a child who says that they would like to become a lawyer, doctor or engineer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: His point is that we inherently value creativity in our children, yet sometimes forget to protect and nurture this creativity in our schools and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While Singapore has made significant progress in special education, there is still more to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Respectful and effective inclusive education for children with special needs promotes social integration and equal opportunities, and assists to break down barriers of stigma and discrimination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It also provides children with special needs better access to academic resources, peer support and tailored learning strategies, thereby helping them reach their full potential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Despite this increased attention to lifelong learning, we do, however, need to do more to ensure equitable access to lifelong learning opportunities, align educational offerings with industry needs and embrace experiential learning methods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important that employers and the broader community understand the importance of supporting students in their educational journeys.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Encouragement and understanding from both home and the workplace enables students to thrive and fully benefit from their educational endeavours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It would be a shame if Singapore's admirable commitment to lifelong learning becomes competitive and outcomes focussed and a source of personal stress and distress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is no secret that women and men in Singapore are delaying getting married and having children, and choosing not to get married and have children at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Studies, such as these, are invaluable, and can assist to inform targeted, evidence-based policy and procedure, which, Mr Speaker, leads me to my concluding comments about gender equality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, we have to have genuine conversations with women of all ages and backgrounds and, of course, with men.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Addressing stereotypes and biasness against older women is essential to ensure their continued well-being and contribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Providing resources and support systems to address these issues is vital for their empowerment and participation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to continue our discussions with Singaporeans, including those who may not normally have a voice or who are sometimes invisible, listen to their stories and ideas, and work together to co-create an affordable, equitable and long-term solution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by the Prime Minister: "Let us rally as one united people and move onward together for a better tomorrow."

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have filed question after question, made speech after speech, because the realities of an ageing society are not a distant problem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, I will focus on three urgent areas: keeping seniors meaningfully employed; expanding housing options so they can age in place; and strengthening support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, employment is not just about making ends meet.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many want to work – not because they have to, but because they feel healthy enough to contribute.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, despite all our rhetoric about senior employment, ageism is still deeply embedded in our hiring culture.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The unspoken belief that older workers are "less productive" persists.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And while policies, like the Senior Employment Credit help, they do not address the fundamental issue: workplaces are still not designed for an ageing workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, we need businesses to take the lead in creating age-inclusive workplaces.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Existing schemes, like the Productivity Solutions Grant, can be expanded to reward firms that redesign roles for senior workers – whether through flexible work, job-sharing or phased retirement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us introduce a "Gold Standard Certification" for age-friendly employers, with tax incentives or public recognition.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us reward companies that walk the talk.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme is a start, but let us get real – how many seniors will sit through generic digital courses?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need targeted modules in areas like caregiving and gig economy skills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, seniors can be trained as digital assistants to help SMEs onboard e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Training should be bite-sized, accessible in community centres, not buried under layers of red tape.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us run a national campaign showcasing seniors excelling in different sectors, not as an afterthought, but as an expectation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But our current housing policies may nort be keeping pace.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During Question Time last week, multiple Members raised this issue, and for good reason.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Yio Chu Kang, Blocks 642 and 648 at Ang Mo Kio Avenue 5 still have no direct lift access for some units.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The so-called "half-landing solution" from 2008 is no longer adequate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I acknowledge the Minister's concerns about cost-effectiveness and technical constraints, I have to ask: are these considerations more important than the daily hardship of our seniors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some say they feel "cheated" – paying for upgrades, only to find themselves still trapped in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Lift Access Housing Grant sounds good on paper, but in reality?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: No senior should be forced to relocate just to move freely in their own community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Projects like Kampung Admiralty and Bukit Batok's community care apartments are good, but they are just a drop in the ocean.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should repurpose unused public buildings, such as the former Henderson Primary School, to create new senior-friendly housing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Why not build inter-generational living spaces where seniors and young residents co-exist meaningfully?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: University students could get subsidised rent in exchange for community engagement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Older adults could mentor, share skills and build relationships with younger generations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many juggle work and caregiving, sacrificing their own well-being to care for ageing loved ones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We appreciate the enhancements to the Home Caregiving Grant, but let us be honest – it is a small step.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Imagine a place where caregivers can work remotely or upskill while their loved ones receive care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Co-located eldercare and co-working spaces can make this possible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: More funding to help caregivers gain professional certification in dementia care, physiotherapy and mental health support, so that they can provide better care, and even transition into new career paths.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A streamlined online hub where caregivers can access respite care, financial aid and training resources, all in one place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Caregivers do the heavy lifting, yet their sacrifices often go unnoticed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They built our homes, our industries, our institutions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They worked tirelessly, often without complaint, to give their children – us – a better life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their sacrifices shaped the Singapore we enjoy today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Now, as they enter their golden years, the question before us is simple: will we repay their dedication with policies that enable them to live with dignity, security and purpose?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Or will they be left behind, expected to navigate old age alone?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about the kind of society we choose to be.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we want to build a Singapore that truly respects and uplifts our seniors, we must act decisively.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Each of these proposals is not just a policy tweak.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are essential steps toward an age-inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And just as this Budget takes bold steps exploring nuclear energy for resilience, strengthening our economic foundations, we, too, must be bold in rethinking how we care for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because the question before us is not whether we can do better, but whether we will.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us not wait until we ourselves are old before we realise what we should have done today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us choose wisely and let us act boldly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us build a Singapore where every senior is valued – not as a burden, but as a pillar of our society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is the Singapore we must now build for them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Mental health, although not explicitly mentioned in Budget 2025, is directly impacted.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By alleviating the financial burden on families and individuals, we reduce stress and anxiety, which are major contributors to mental health issues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By investing in lifelong learning, we empower individuals to develop skills and resilience they need to navigate life's challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By supporting large families, we create a strong fabric that provides individuals a sense of belonging and support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And this paves the way for a healthier, more resilient, caring society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government has continually demonstrated unwavering commitment to supporting the mental health and wellness of every Singaporean.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We have made significant strides in improving awareness, education and public discourse on mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the study also reveals that many who are aware do not actively seek out for help when they need it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This gap between understanding and action remains a key challenge.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Although societal attitudes are improving, many still hesitate to reach out due to fear of judgement, particularly in professional or family settings.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And that is why we, as a society, must do more to equip ourselves with the mental health literacy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government has introduced many online and offline resources, but we can do more to ensure that these resources are well utilised, easily accessible and effective.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the very least, it acts as a simple introduction that could help more people understand this pertinent issue and take that first step towards seeking or providing help.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Ultimately, it is up to us to take this step, to practice what we have learned and build a more supportive, understanding community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our religious organisations have a unique ability to shape perspectives, offer guidance and provide safe spaces for open conversations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This can help bridge the stigma around mental health, ensuring that those who are struggling do not suffer in silence, but instead, find comfort and support within their communities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am glad to share that many religious organisations have taken this step.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They have taken up courses, equipping their staff with mental health knowledge, working closely with mental health organisations, like Club HEAL, Silver Ribbon and Social, Emotional and Mental Health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope we can do more by creating a structure for them to get easy training and support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some are unsure about what support is available, how to access affordable services or whether their concerns are "serious enough" to warrant an intervention.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And that is why the PAP Mental Health Group is currently recruiting and training our Mental Health Ambassadors who will be deployed to connect residents who need help to partners within the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The final challenge, Sir, is regards to financial and logistical barriers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We have heard this many times, there are long waiting times for consultations, we have affordability concerns and difficulties in balancing mental health care with work or caregiving responsibilities that deter individuals from taking the first step.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, we must ensure that mental health services remain accessible and affordable for all.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What this means is that we need to strengthen our community mental health services, integrate mental healthcare into primary care settings, like Healthier SG, and leverage technology to provide timely and practical support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I will expand on these points in the MOH COS debate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These people, with no formal training, provide therapy sessions for a fee.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Vulnerable individuals seeking help must receive qualified ethical and professional support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But we must be precise about the problem.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, psychologists and private counsellors play very different roles and our approach to regulation must reflect that.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For psychologists, registration is crucial to uphold the professional and ethical standards.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of them were in clinical settings, diagnosing and treating mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Regulation is about protecting patients from harm and ensuring they receive the care from trained professionals.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many operate wellness-focused services outside the medical system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Regulation should ensure transparency and ethical practices and prevent misleading claims so that those seeking help are not exploited.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we encourage people to seek help, we must also ensure they get the right help.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I will expand this further in my COS speech, discussing what we can do to enhance regulation and public safeguards in the mental health space.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond healthcare, mental health must be embedded in multiple domains.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is why my colleagues from the PAP Mental Health Group will be raising this issue across Ministries during the Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, under the Ministry of Defence, we will discuss how we can support our national servicemen (NSFs) and NSmen to receive stronger psychological resilience training and better mental health support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Under MOH and MCCY, we will look at how community health initiatives like HealthierSG and those under M3 Focus Area 5, can deepen engagement in mental health and wellness.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Under MSF, MOE and Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI), we will explore how to equip parents to better support their children's and youth's emotional and digital well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Also, for interest, is how can we protect teacher well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond providing short-term relief, this Budget also sends a clear message.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To truly thrive in a changing and dynamic world, lifelong learning must be the foundation of our economic future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet, while the Budget enhances SkillsFuture funding and support, barriers remain.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many Singaporeans struggle to upskill, not because of a lack of interest, but because of practical realities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many Singaporeans struggle to pursue further education while juggling family responsibilities and full-time work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The mental and logistical effort required to commit to long-term learning can feel overwhelming, even with financial support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could we explore more "Earn and Learn" models where training is embedded within current employment, allowing workers to upskill without taking extended breaks from work?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Companies could integrate structured training hours into their work schedules, supported by incentives for employers who participate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A common concern among mid-career workers is that whether upskilling will lead to better job opportunities or even higher wages.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many hesitate to seek help or take this leap because they fear that leaving a stable job to retrain, only to find that opportunities remain limited or their salaries do not increase.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And I have heard those in the new job face a much lower wage because they are starting afresh.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We could strengthen career mentorship and placement guarantees, where workers undergoing SkillsFuture-funded retraining receive structured job-matching support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers could also be encouraged to guarantee wage progression for workers who complete industry-recognised training.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While the Budget provides strong immediate support, long-term success requires more than just training credits.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To help Singaporeans transition smoothly into new or higher-paying roles, a comprehensive framework, including better career guidance, structured job placement support and policies to reduce the risks of retraining, is necessary.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could we introduce, what I call a "Lifelong Learning Hack"?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It would be a one-stop advisory service to help Singaporeans to map out realistic training-to-employment pathways, ensure that they select the right courses, knowing that they will receive long-term career guidance and assurances.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, many workers are still hesitant to continue their education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is not due to a lack of interest, but because of family responsibilities, work commitments, and financial concerns.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I left a stable job to continue my studies full-time for two years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: After returning to work a few years later, I decided to pursue further studies, also full-time, for five years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, I understand the concerns of those who want to learn but are afraid of any uncertainty that may arise.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The questions often asked is, is it worth it?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But I also know the immense value of lifelong learning, not just in building a career, but also in strengthening personal resilience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government has taken positive steps to alleviate these concerns.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we want to compete and thrive in an increasingly challenging economy, lifelong learning is no longer an option, but a necessity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I urge our community to view these opportunities as an investment for their future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is because, by having knowledge and skills that are constantly enhanced, we will not just be able to face challenges, we will be able to master them. : Sir, my final point is on large families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Raising a family is one of my life's greatest joys, but for many parents, it also comes with many financial and logistical challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As a father of four, I understand first-hand the rewards and realities of managing household expenses, education and childcare.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Budget recognises and strengthens support for all families, whether they have one child, two children, or more.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The increases in CDC Vouchers, rebates and subsidies will benefit families and ease daily expenses.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, I welcome the targeted enhancements that provide additional support for larger families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These policies do not take away from families with one or two children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead, they reflect the reality that household expenses grow exponentially with each additional child.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By ensuring that no family feels financially overstretched, we create a more supportive environment for all parents to raise and nurture their children with confidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Still, it is up to each of us, as leaders, communities and individuals, to make the most of them and contribute positively towards a compassionate, inclusive and resilient Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When we uplift our people, strengthen our families and prioritise well-being, we are shaping a Singapore that does not just move forward but thrive together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Building a Singapore made for families goes hand-in-hand with nurturing a caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will go a long way to further ease the financial burden on families, many of whom have been concerned with rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, I anticipate a challenge that may persist, that is, a long waiting time for enrolment and admission at Anchor Operator centres and Partner Operator centres located near homes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my speech delivered during the Motion which I moved last month, I shared with this House that many of my Woodgrove residents in Champions Court and Champions Green have been facing difficulties in securing a spot in a preschool for their toddlers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is pressing and distressing for families, especially those moving into new flats, which could be located in an unfamiliar area with no extended family support.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that one of the solutions is in increasing the number of Partner Operators.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would increase the supply of preschool spots and options for parents.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will make childcare more accessible from day one.
