speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Next, I move on to other support measures for families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During fourth session of the focus group discussion organised jointly by the PAP Women's Wing with Friendzone, which I had attended recently, where I joined close to 60 participants, aged 25 to 40 years, to have a heart-to-heart conversation, pertaining to the topic of parenthood.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have gathered that, while some participants may find the cost of pregnancy in Singapore, which is estimated to be in the region of $10,000, covering items from prenatal gynaecologist visits, hospital birth and confinement, nanny supports, and so on, to be a reasonable amount in comparison to the cost of planning for their wedding.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, larger financial assistance rendered to just this group is not enough.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Based on the other feedback and suggestions which PAP Women's Wing have gathered through our surveys, consultations with partners as well as focus group discussions, to encourage young couples to start and grow their families, I believe we must address a broader range of needs in which I have summarised into five key areas: one, fertility support to help couples start and pursue their parenthood journey; two, supporting first parenthood by equipping them with the necessary know-hows; three, readily available caregiving support networks to ease their load; four, more understanding workplaces with flexible work arrangements; and five, support for mothers to stay confident in the workforce with support systems such as enhanced tax incentives for working mothers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Pertaining to the point on fertility support, PAP Women's Wing Policy Group has received valuable insight from Fertility Support SG (FSS), a non-profit self-help group started by a group of ladies facing infertility and saw the need to create a community where couples facing infertility could get a right information as well as come together to share experiences and gain support through their difficult challenging times.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One of the founders of FSS, Ms Lin Shu Min had shared with me that the key areas where our Government can work on with partners to provide more support to are as follows.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One, upstream fertility education to help people plan their fertility journeys early.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: FSS can help to contribute by housing relevant resources and information on their website, making it easier for couples to access the knowledge they need.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Two, grants for pre-in-vitro fertilization (IVF) or general fertility testing to help identify issues early, improving the chances of success.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And four, private sector grants should also be considered, allowing grants to apply to treatments in private clinics, giving couples more options.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wish to take this opportunity to share a personal appeal, which my residents, Tina and Brandon, had confided in me just a few days ago at my Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The couple, both 32 years old, has been trying to conceive for the past four years.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From initially being given a clean bill of health at their fertility check-up to eventually being diagnosed with a blocked fallopian tube that resulted in them undergoing five IVF cycles since last year, which have yet to yield any success.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Despite emotional toll and financial strain, they remain hopeful to be under National University Hospital's (NUH's) care, whose advice to them is to not give up and to keep trying as each cycle brings the medical fertility team one step closer to finding the right combination of medication and timing to retrieve the best quality eggs and hope for eventual success.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the cost of medications, procedures and consultations are overwhelming and have pushed them to their limits.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The couple understands that public resources are limited and they do not expect full coverage.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, they believe that with the additional support that the Government can provide and consider to expend, it will go a long way towards easing the burdens of couples like them and sustain their dreams of becoming parents one day.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the next point of creating a smooth experience for first-time parents, we should consider to provide a new parenthood E-guide or a mommy's milestone booklet.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This can be personalised to each family's needs and with relevant information conveyed to parents to be by professionals at each milestone basis.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the risk of belabouring the point, having already asked for this in Parliament on numerous occasions over the years, most recently, actually, in my speech for my motion last month, I do hope that this booklet will help to track the expecting mother's physical and emotional development.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It contains helpful information regarding necessary preparation for each stage of their pregnancy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What are the list of support systems available to all parents, at least for the first year of their journey into parenthood?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What are the overview of vaccinations required for these expecting mothers, and what are the recommended estimated time, time and dates to sign up for prenatal classes, providing them with a checklist of items to prepare for the arrival of their baby, sharing tips with them on how to spot signs of labour and how to spot signs of postnatal depression?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To address this, I propose a small tweak to the policy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One is to retain the higher of the percentage base or fixed quantum relief.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This adjustment would ensure lower income working mothers to remain motivated to remain in the workforce and receive adequate tax deductions, while encouraging the higher earning ones to continue to pursue their career aspirations, while not forgetting the need to continue to expand and raise their families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This year, it has been announced that the SG Baby Gift will be given to all Singaporean citizens born in 2025.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is a meaningful gesture to celebrate our nation's milestone.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I recall my time as a grassroots volunteer 10 years ago, delivering the SG50 Baby Jubilee gift packs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Those packs included a suitcase with items like a special medallion, a multifunctional shawl, a baby sling, a set of baby clothes, a diaper bag, a scrapbook, a family photo frame and a set of baby books – thoughtful keepsakes and practical tools for new parents.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, babies grow and develop rapidly in their first year, with their needs shifting every three months or so.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since some SG60 babies were born as early as January this year, many will likely be past the three to six months stage by the time they receive the gift.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Moreover, many parents may have already bought the essentials like diaper bags before their baby's arrival, so to make this gift truly useful, I hope the items can vary to better suit the diverse needs of parents and their babies at different stages of their first year.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I support this initiative as it encourages us to engage with our rich cultural landscape.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, since the goal is to inspire participation in arts and heritage, why not extend this opportunity to younger Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I suggest lowering the age eligibility to include children from preschool onwards.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will mirror the approach of active SG credits, which promote family participations in sports and activities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A similar family focus design for the SG Culture Pass could help instil a love for culture from an early age while enhancing family bonding.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lastly, I am grateful for the Government's allocation of $800 in CDC Vouchers to every Singaporean household to help manage expenses.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On top of that, the SG60 vouchers available to every Singaporean and usable at all businesses accepting CDC Vouchers, add another layer of support.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This initiative showed a commitment to easing the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, during my recent house visits and routine walkabouts at our Fuchun Neighbourhood Centre and Triple 8 Plaza in Woodgrove, several residents and merchants have shared their feedback about the current E-voucher format.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They suggest switching to an E-wallet format like those used in the Life SG or GrabPay, which are already popular for purchasers and neighbourhood merchants.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This change could help make the vouchers more convenient and user friendly for everyone.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   In last week's 2025 Budget Statement, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of assistance measures to help families and individuals cope with rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These measures have also benefited many neighbourhood hawkers and merchants.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would make payment more efficient and convenient for both merchants and customers. : To conclude, I would like to share a few lines of assurance and encouragement that my husband recently said to me, a working mother who constantly questions if I have done enough for my six-year-old daughter and 15-month-old son amid my other commitments.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These words, though from an anonymous author, resonated deeply with the challenges and triumph of parenthood.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They remind us of the strength and resilience of mothers who are not only raising their children but also growing alongside them: "To the mum who has been through a lot lately, give yourself more credit.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You are raising children at the same time as you are raising yourself.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You are breaking cycles and doing it differently, even though you are exhausted.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You are trying to figure out who you are while helping little people do the same.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You are pouring all your love into your children while learning to love yourself at the same time. you are stronger than you can ever imagine.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let that be enough." These words capture the heart of what it means to build a Singapore made for families, a place where parents, especially mothers, feel supported, valued and empowered, and at a greater level, serve the team of SG60 Budget for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us continue to work hard and together to welcome SG60 and even better years to follow.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This year’s Budget is a Budget for all Singaporeans whereas Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said, "No one is left behind".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2018, I said in this House that then Minister Lawrence Wong which is my favourite Minister – I hope he remembers that I am the first to say that.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad he became Prime Minister and like my favourite Minister’s 2025 Budget is for all Singaporeans, my speech today is also for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is a long time to not improve a policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Whether you are a consultant for an MNC, a cashier at a convenience store, a cleaner at a coffee shop, we all have the same 24 hours in a day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We all need time from work to rest for our mental health and for our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My father was a model employee who worked extremely hard for the company he worked for, for 42 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He worked hard not just for his company but also for his colleagues and his family.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He looked forward to his retirement, when he could spend more time with his family and his grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My father never got to enjoy the fruits of his labour.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He was diagnosed with stage IV prostate cancer when he was close to retirement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our very first family holiday on a cruise was when my father was already dying.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the day I decided that I would take leave to spend more time with my father when he was in the hospital, he passed away, at the age of 67.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He lost consciousness before I made it to the hospital and so I never got a chance to say a proper goodbye.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I made a mistake and took too many things for granted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I wish I could turn back time and have more time with Daddy, but I know this is impossible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ten years on, I still live with regret.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are many Singaporeans just like my father.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They work hard their whole lives looking forward to more relaxing days with their loved ones, but they never make it there.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We go through life preparing for another life that we will eventually get to enjoy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We forget that there only is one life, and every day working is every day not being with the people we love most.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Budget, it is the vouchers, grants and financial goodies that will make the headlines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I hope this Budget, we can give something even more precious: time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The time that annual leave gives us is important for all and even more important for lower-income workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this speech, I will talk about how annual leave will help build a Singapore made for families and for our mental health, how annual leave is particularly important for the lower income and how it is not a zero-sum trade-off against business costs, productivity and competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, let me talk about how annual leave can help build a Singapore made for families and for mental health.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We now focus more sharply than ever on families and on mental health.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong made clear that mental health and well-being is a key priority.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He said, "So let there be no doubt: the Government is making mental health and well-being a key priority in our national agenda." Indeed, it is a key priority and we have been talking about reducing burn out, supporting couples on their fertility journeys, encouraging parent-child bonding, building family-friendly workplaces, encouraging a better work-life balance, supporting working caregivers and increasing family support for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can walk the talk on all these things we say are important by increasing the minimum annual leave entitlement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Annual leave is important and is needed for so many reasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Couples undergoing fertility treatments often tap on their annual leave for their treatments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Parents who use up their six days of paid childcare leave have to use their annual leave when their child falls ill or during school closures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many also take their annual leave to accompany elderly parents for their medical appointments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And let us not forget that annual leave is needed for rest and to spend time with your loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is for our well-being, the same well-being that Prime Minister Wong said is a key priority.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And just last year, the 2024 Gallup State of the Global Workplace survey ranked Singapore third in Southeast Asia for daily workplace stresses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I could go on with many more studies but I do not think we need any more data to prove how exhausted Singaporeans are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Take care of our parents, be there for our children, make more babies, work hard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For so many of us struggling to stay on top of a never-ending to-do list, it would sure help to have more annual leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For lower-income workers, annual leave is not a luxury and may not even be about rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For them, it is the only time they have to spend with their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon East, we have our Helping Hands programme to uplift lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A strong component of the programme is ensuring that they have family time and I have seen first-hand how parents struggle to find time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When I try to bring children from lower-income families out for outings with their parents, their parents simply cannot take leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One mother, who is a cashier, had only seven days of annual leave and has to work weekends every week with only one day-off a week, on a weekday.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another father, who is a cleaner, also had seven days of annual leave and just does not have time to spend with his children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both of them are single parents and their children need the precious time with their parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The data tells us that lower-income workers tend to have fewer days of paid annual leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: None of us sitting here would want to be part of that number.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps we are thinking, maybe this 8% of workers get to work from home or benefit from some other flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, with regard to annual leave, the Government has stressed that we are "looking at this from a more holistic way, by ensuring that there are avenues for other forms of work arrangements, including flexible work arrangements".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, this is not the reality on the ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Workers with the least amount of leave are also the ones least likely to benefit from FWAs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These workers are typically in frontline or labour-intensive jobs, such as cleaners, cashiers, security guards and service staff.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: FWAs are not a realistic alternative to having more annual leave for these workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our policies are supposed to ensure sufficient rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A week of rest from a year of backbreaking work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is that a humane way to treat people?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is our lower-income workers who are suffering the most from our annual leave policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope, we do not have to wait another 57 years to review this policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is that we do not need to lose productivity and competitiveness when we increase annual leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our economic conditions and workforce have changed drastically in that period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon replied to me in 2021 that there were no plans to review the annual leave entitlement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After a very good three years of break and no nagging Senior Minister of State Koh, I asked again in 2024 and Senior Minister of State Koh replied to me again that there were still no plans to review the minimum annual leave entitlements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Business cost was a concern stated by Senior Minister of State Koh and FWAs were again offered as an alternative to increasing annual leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree with Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon that work-life balance and productivity can be addressed from multiple angles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad we have made progress on other areas, such as FWAs, which I have fought hard for too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But for those who cannot access FWAs, increasing annual leave entitlement is one angle that we should not rule out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By keeping minimum annual leave entitlement at seven days for 57 years because we fear business costs and maybe losing productivity, we risk reinforcing the impression that well-being and productivity are trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This does not have to be the case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We do not lose out when we prioritise people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, I hope we can send the clear message that only by prioritising people, can we grow sustainably and healthily as a nation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are not less productive when we get more rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, I sincerely believe that a more well-rested workforce will be a more productive workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are also not any less competitive than our neighbours by increasing the minimum annual leave entitlement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am tempted to read out all 160 countries but I know Speaker will kill me, so let us just focus on the Asia Pacific region to give you a sense on how far behind we are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These countries all have a higher minimum annual leave entitlement: Afghanistan, Armenia, Australia, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, East Timor, Fiji, Georgia, India, Indonesia, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kiribati, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Laos, Malaysia, Maldives, Marshall Islands, Mongolia, Myanmar, Nepal, New Zealand, Oman, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Qatar, Samoa, Saudi Arabia, Solomon Islands, South Korea, Sri Lanka, Syria, Tonga, United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, Vanuatu, Vietnam, Yemen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All have a higher annual leave entitlement as compared to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of these countries also have a higher number of paid public holidays.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We pride ourselves on having a highly-skilled and professional workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our competitive advantage is our expertise and skills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely we are not competitive only because our workers are willing to slog for more days and for longer hours than other countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We believed it was the right thing to do for parents and we worked with businesses to ensure a smooth rollout.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For annual leave, we can do the same and work closely with businesses every step of the way too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should consult them, understand their concerns and challenges and provide the support needed to successfully implement the increase.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The business cost truly incurred is outweighed by the very clear message that well-being, mental health, family and rest are equally important for all workers and not just some workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They can only do their best when they are well-rested and have enough time for their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Importantly, the ability to rest and take care of our loved ones should not be a luxury.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It bears remembering that in 1955, MOM started as the Ministry of Labour and Welfare.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With my father, I lost time which I will never be able to get back and recover.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do not want others to have the same regrets that I have.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the iconic Dolly Parton said, "Never get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life." Many of us live as though we are rehearsing for a future life where we get to spend quality time with our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no real life other than the one we are living now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: On that note, I think we should all go back and rest.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister, would you like to adjourn the debate?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Budget 2025 is a Budget for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It provides immediate support for families and businesses amidst cost pressures, while advancing our growth frontier for the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This focus on tackling immediate challenges, while positioning Singapore for the longer term, has been a focus of this Government and has served Singapore well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: From a fledgling nation with limited resources, we have built a thriving economy, a cohesive society and a liveable city for our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our people are living longer and healthier lives in affordable and vibrant estates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our workers enjoy good jobs and rising wages in a modern economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our students learn and excel, and adults continue learning all their life.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As we enjoy the SG60 package in the Budget, let us express our gratitude for the hard work and sacrifices of earlier generations of Singaporeans, and for their support for political leaders to forge a path forward, to uplift all.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While we have done well over the last 60 years, changes will accelerate in the years ahead.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Prime Minister delivered the Budget Statement in a world that is moving towards a multipolar economic order.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Domestic politics in many countries are more polarised and fragmented, making rational policymaking harder.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Global political and security dynamics, and trade and investment flows, are shifting rapidly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Climate and demographic change are the warp and weft, weaving inexorable impact on the future of humankind.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Advances in science and technology are transforming our economies and societies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Imagine, the smart phones in our pockets today have more compute power than the Apollo 11 module that took the first man to the moon!

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Game-changing technologies like artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, 5G/6G, satellite communications, robotics, biotechnology, electric vehicles (EVs), autonomous vehicles and nuclear fusion are advancing rapidly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: All these will change how we work and live.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Chairman, I have been working with my teams at the National Research Foundation and the Future Economy Advisory Panel to stay on the pulse of these seismic movements.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: How can we ride these changes to create a better future for Singaporeans?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must stay creative and find opportunities in adversity and in times of major changes to emerge stronger, just as we did during the Asian Financial Crisis, the Global Financial Crisis and more recently, through COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must also invest in creating our future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, we must press on with our economic transformation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the last Budget debate, I outlined our latest phase of economic transformation, starting with the formation of the Future Economy Council in 2017.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Last year, we launched a report to take stock of our efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There are copies of this report in the Parliament library.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But change is inherently difficult, particularly when faced with near-term head winds.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Fewer companies, facing geopolitical uncertainties and higher costs, are launching transformation projects.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Let us build on the partnerships and structures we have established to support one another, whether through the tripartite platforms like the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) Company Training Committees (CTCs), or private-public partnership platforms like the Alliance for Action (AfA) on Business Competitiveness led by the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and the Singapore Business Federation (SBF), we will go further in our transformation journey by working together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I have spoken on pressing on with transformation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The second area is to continue to invest and double down on our investments in research, innovation and enterprise (RIE).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Science, technology and innovation are advancing at an accelerated pace.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These advances will reshape and disrupt industries, changing the competitive dynamics and transforming our lives and our societies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The recent buzz over AI, new generation of chips and 5G/6G communication is just the beginning.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Given the critical value of technology and innovation, strategic and economic strengths of nations and of companies will depend on who can make the breakthroughs and retain their lead.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The stakes have never been higher, and that is why Great Power rivalry is intensifying.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our investments in RIE will not only support our economic transformation but also benefit our people, directly and indirectly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, AI and robotics will automate routine tasks – augmenting our declining workforce and improving the quality of jobs; the science of learning, which explores how we learn, and the use of AI learning tools, can allow us to personalise learning for each student and worker; our National Precision Medicine Programme seeks to personalise treatments based on our genetic make-up; geriatric science, such as that being studied at the Queenstown Health District, seeks to keep our ageing population healthy and active for longer; and low carbon fuels and smart cities allow us to make best use of our limited land size, while reducing our carbon emissions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Unlike research and development (R&D) in a private company, the benefits from these public research expenditures accrue to the whole economy and society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Unfortunately, we are seeing a worrying trend where some governments are making cuts in these areas as they do not fully understand their value, risking great damage to themselves in the long run.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members, including Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Pritam Singh, have asked what progress looks like?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our RIE spending has supported our research talent and raised the quality of research in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our universities, research institutes and academic medical centres are well-regarded globally.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The National University of Singapore (NUS) and the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) are ranked among the top five universities in Asia.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is not a small achievement, considering that we have such a small population and there are so many universities in Asia alone.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Multinational corporations (MNCs), small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and startups alike partner our research ecosystem to develop new products and services through platforms like company R&D centres, over 20 corporate labs and Centres of Innovation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, as Members have raised, innovation is key!

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our agencies organise renowned innovation platforms, such as the Singapore Week of Innovation and Technology and the Singapore Fintech Festivals, the largest in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our RIE investments support entrepreneurship and incubation programmes in our universities, which generate a pipeline of startups.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In fact, the Global Start-up Ecosystem Index Report 2024 ranks Singapore first in Asia and seventh globally.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Neil Parekh also asked what else will we do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will finalise our investments from 2026 to 2030 later this year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But let me share two major new initiatives that we are working on for RIE2030.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I think Mr Henry Kwek made a good speech yesterday on the use of AI.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, our first initiative on Applied AI includes applying AI to major use cases in priority sectors, such as healthcare, education, finance, advanced manufacturing, connectivity, logistics and transport.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In October last year, we launched a $120 million AI for Science initiative, to support researchers in leveraging AI to accelerate discoveries in fields, such as advanced materials and biomedical sciences.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Applied AI sits at the intersection of AI and domain knowledge.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Building on the strong domain expertise of our practitioners and researchers in healthcare, education, finance, engineering and many others, we will invest more in developing "bilingual" scientific talent – researchers who can bridge between AI technologies and domain expertise.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The second new initiative is the development of new large-scale, cross-cutting R&D programmes called Flagships and Grand Challenges, to achieve greater impact. "RIE Flagships" will push for value creation in key economic sectors and "RIE Grand Challenges" will address national strategic priorities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These Flagships and Grand Challenges will pull together relevant research and translational capabilities across our universities, the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) and other research institutes, public agencies and private sector players, to form a suite of purposefully coordinated and synergistic programmes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The linkages between research, translation and commercialisation will be tightened, to advance key economic areas, produce new products and companies and address real-world needs and problems.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am pleased that work has started to scope and design these initiatives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The first Grand Challenge proposes to address the opportunities and challenges of healthy and successful longevity and the first flagship will be focused on advancing our semi-conductor and microelectronics R&D.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even as we do these, we must remember that while Singapore's research investments are significant, it is a small fraction of global R&D spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, we must work with like-minded partners from the region and around the world to achieve synergy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And even as a percentage of their GDP, they are far higher.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I think we must have a sense that even as we want to talk about value for money, that what we are spending is a tiny fraction, and I would say that even private sector players like Alphabet spent US$45 billion, Meta spent US$38.5 billion and Apple $30 billion in 2023, all in US dollars.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, we have to work with like-minded partners from the region and around the world to achieve synergy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In addition to what the Prime Minister announced in the Budget, we will also invest in new data and compute capabilities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I have spoken on economic transformation and investing in research.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To remain competitive, we must continue to maintain our outward orientation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Companies invest in Singapore not just for our market, but as a gateway to the region.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore has served this role well in the last 60 years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Today, Asia accounts for over half of the world's population and about 40% of global GDP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The projected medium-term growth rates of 4% to 5% is double that of the G7 developed nations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We can serve as a springboard for companies to venture to a new future, to a wider world market.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this regard, our regulatory agencies play an important role.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They need to fulfil their mandates to regulate safely and effectively, while staying on top of changes and facilitating new ideas and innovation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has embraced its dual mandate to supervise and develop the financial sector and is pushing the frontier in new areas, such as digital and sustainable finance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Singapore Food Agency (SFA) is the first in the world to approve cultivated meat for commercial sale.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Land Transport Authority (LTA) is facilitating trials of autonomous vehicles to transport goods and keep our public roads clean.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Talent is another key pillar of our innovation strategy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government is committed to helping every Singaporean achieve his or her potential.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When I was the Education Minister, we launched an Applied Learning Programme to interest the young in science and technology.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Earlier on, I supported Mr Philip Yeo, then Chairman of A*STAR, to send promising young Singaporeans to the top universities in the world to do their PhD under the A*STAR scholarship.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To date, almost 1,400 have completed their studies and returned, where they contribute to cutting-edge work in our research institutes and uplift our companies' R&D capabilities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the coming years, I encourage more Singaporeans to develop "bilingual" fluency in the languages of business and in science and technology.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Make full use of these Budget enhancements to build new skills.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, we must also welcome the best from around the world to be here.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Just as steel sharpens steel, strong minds sharpen one another.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Growing up in a diverse multicultural society, Singaporeans are well-placed to serve as bridges to connect ideas and talents across the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Together, we can learn from the best, work with the best and build a better home for future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In Mandarin):   This year marks Singapore's 60th year of Independence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is a significant milestone for our nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over 60 years, our people and the Government have worked together to overcome numerous challenges and created a remarkable economic miracle and a harmonious multicultural society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: However, amidst global uncertainties, intensifying geopolitical tension and rising trade protectionism, how can we maintain Singapore's economic momentum and create a better future for our people?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Science, technology and innovation are developing at accelerating pace, profoundly impacting countries' strategic strength and economic development.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As countries strive to achieve breakthroughs and maintain leadership in these areas, a competitive dynamic has emerged.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, many researchers worldwide are still willing to cooperate with researchers from other countries to address common challenges.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Therefore, we will continue to develop Singapore's research, innovation and enterprise ecosystem and strengthen international connections and cooperation to reinforce Singapore's position as a neutral, trusted Global-Asia node.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This enables Singapore to work closely with international partners to address common scientific challenges, such as ageing population and pandemic response. : Before I conclude, allow me a brief reflection on SG60.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A decade ago, I was chairing the SG50 Steering Committee, where we engaged with Singaporeans to express their love and hopes for Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was inspired and humbled by the hardy spirit of our Pioneers and the dynamism of our youths.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was then working on my first Budget and thinking hard about how to support Singaporeans to ride the waves of changes to come.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even 10 years ago, at SG50, we knew big changes would come.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We invested our resources, hopes and energies in building a resilient nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We never imagined we could be hit by a global pandemic that defined a generation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As I look forward to SG70 and beyond, my wish is for us to continue to invest in all Singaporeans, young and old.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In particular, let us continue to invest our time and energy to continue deepening our multiracial, multi-religious and multicultural society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we can forge our path forward, our youths today will serve as valuable bridge-builders, connecting ideas and talent across the world to solve pressing challenges facing humanity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Together, we can learn from the best, work with the best and build a better home for future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I trust colleagues in the House, and all Singaporeans, will support this call as we celebrate SG60 and grow towards the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Indeed, it is a proud milestone for a young nation and one that I believe many Singaporeans, including myself, celebrates with a smiling heart.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As a country that began with virtually no resources when it first became independent, we have certainly built our assets over the decades with resolve and dedication.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The 2025 Budget certainly sets the tone on what it means to look out for all Singaporeans and how we can create our country together in the years ahead.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One aspect of the Budget Statement that stood out for me is the human-centric approach and talent development.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Singapore has long recognised the importance of investing in our young, ensuring they receive the best education and opportunities to contribute as our country grows.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, as we navigate the complexities of a globalised economy, it is imperative that we equip our young Singaporeans with the skills and experiences necessary to thrive in an interconnected world amidst increasing tensions across countries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, I will focus my speech on the need to shift our approach towards talent development in Singapore’s current and future workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By collaborating with MNCs, we can create global rotation programmes where Singaporeans are hired and placed in various roles across the globe.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This initiative would provide our young talents with invaluable exposure to diverse cultures, markets, business practices and honing their leadership skills in order to broaden their perspectives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Many young Singaporeans aspire to work in MNCs given the global exposure, the career development opportunities, the competitive compensation package, the vibrant work culture that is in place, and the networking potentials that these companies offer.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By working with MNCs to hire and train Singaporeans, we can help our young Singaporeans meet their aspirations and gain the international experience that is much needed in order to excel in future senior leadership roles.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, we do acknowledge that MNCs will not automatically hire more Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This should be viewed as an investment in our local talent pool, which I believe can pay off in the long run.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Second, a differentiated look at the way we embrace talents and allocate resources to support their development.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The first, global talents with a much more local emphasis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is an issue that I believe is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Many cities across the world grapple with this and today find that increasing availability of competitive talents providing services from offshore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Over time, this will be a formidable threat to our local workforce without having the overseas talent to even be present in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We are also cognisant of a shrinking workforce locally given our low total fertility rate (TFR) and this implies the need to augment workers in different sectors through more options.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I totally agree with what Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat has just said.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need to have all these global bright minds with us, but we also need to find a way in order to create opportunities for Singapore to become the bridges and connectors that he referred to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The question is how best do we do this such that Singaporeans continue to have equal opportunities to get good employment for a much longer period and also the opportunities to participate in the global arena.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Taking a reference from this company called Atos, an international information technology services company who successfully implemented a global talent policy that aligns with their global and local talent management strategies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It has certainly proved to be effective for the investments they have made.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Being in the digital space, Atos certainly faces the challenge of dynamic market trends and the constraint that needs to retain their own talents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Yet, they are focused on the skills development of their employees, ensuring development pathway and positive employee experience which translates to positive customer experiences that help sustain their business.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need an equivalent framework that encourages MNCs and large local corporates to provide similar approach in incentivising the development process and retention of talents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Next, shifting the implementation approach for MNCs and our local SMEs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We are committed to support both the MNCs and our local SMEs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By differentiating Employment Pass quotas and providing targeted incentives, we aim to create such a balanced ecosystem where both sectors can thrive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Businesses thrive when there are economies of scales; and MNCs bring to Singapore important business flows, not only in terms of the scale of business but they also serve a broader region beyond Singapore, with a natural opportunity that allow SMEs to provide goods and services, which in turn help Singapore's economy to be more resilient.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To make this implementation possible, I would like to suggest a few measures to be considered.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This way, the SMEs can hire more talented foreigners without increasing the overall number of foreign workers in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This merits the opportunity to develop a sizeable local workforce with time that will enhance the capabilities which can value-add to the company and support rotational roles when the opportunity arises.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Likewise, we need concrete steps need to be in place to ensure that Government-linked companies provide ample internships for the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) and polytechnic students, while we establish the mechanisms for accountability to ensure the initiatives can be successful over time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Not everyone who undergoes a global job rotation programme will continue to work in MNCs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We should create a pathway for some of these trained talents to be able to flow into our SMEs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By making them available for the SMEs, they will bring their valuable experiences and skills to strengthen our local businesses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Such talent flow would benefit both the individuals involved and yield significant advantages for Singapore as a whole.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By cultivating a pool of experienced global leaders, we also enhance our ability to retain the MNCs within our borders.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These leaders, equipped with a deep understanding of international business dynamics, will be better positioned to drive innovation, foster economic growth and ensure that Singapore remains a hub for global commerce for a long time to come.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Many of these students eventually go on to enrol in our ITEs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This would allow them to begin skills development over a longer horizon and discover their niche in the various trade crafts that are suitable to their own abilities which can be useful, as they explore their future careers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Further, we can consider expanding ITE to have a stronger focus on technical skills development and if they can excel in some specific areas, for example, like cross-skills capability development in our youths, this will prove to be very valuable for the future unpredictable work environment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These initiatives, as much as I have said, will need to be implemented in phases, allowing us to evaluate and refine our approach that is based on feedback and outcomes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This will ensure that we can address any challenges and make the necessary adjustments in order to make sure they will become successful in the implementation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And, Sir, lastly, a healthy and successful career pathway must be balanced with one’s well-being and one that caters for their mental health and work-life balance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These are integral to our vision of a happy and thriving society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While economic success cannot guarantee a person’s well-being, expanding the options and pathways available to all Singaporeans for their career choices will help more people achieve their dreams, thus creating a more inclusive and cohesive society for future generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Providing diverse opportunities for our citizens not only empower them to excel in their potential, it also fosters a greater sense of fulfillment and purpose.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When individuals feel supported and valued, it boosts their overall happiness and contributes to a stronger and more resilient community at work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While we do not have infinite resources to double down and resolving all challenges, we should have faith that investing in Singaporeans will pay off in the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We must believe that every Singaporean is capable and responsible and should be given every opportunity that the country can afford.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To enable the future where equity and inclusivity are strong values that anchor this country, we need to commit to ensure that opportunities are accessible to all Singaporeans, regardless of their background.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This includes implementing fair and transparent selection processes and providing additional support to those who need it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is a long-term commitment and a topic we should focus on investing when we have Budget surplus.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We have many assets that our forefathers and the current generation have built together as a united country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These are rare assets in a fractious world today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I consider this a blessing to have and one we should treasure to preserve and enhance for future generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It exists before and will only be more rampant in the years ahead.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, I advocate that we begin to emphasise on our goal of providing more pathways for success.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By diversifying our talent development strategies, by offering broad opportunities for exploration from young, we aim to reduce the pressure and allow individuals to find and pursue their unique strengths and interests.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By investing in our young talents and providing them with opportunities for global exposure, we not only secure their future but also fortify our nation's position as a leader in the international arena.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Through our investment for individuals to understand the necessary skills to develop building upon their strengths, our workforce can truly live up to a continuous learning and adaptation mindset in the ever-changing global landscape.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This will, over time, result in a more innovative, balanced and sound economy, enabled by the creation of the economic growth destiny that our citizens are a part of.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With this, I rise in support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, you have a clarification to make?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will also add, at the outset, that I am fully supportive of increases to our national R&D spending, having called for this in Budgets past.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will include here social sciences as well as areas in the humanities and liberal arts, such as design, linguistics, psychology, history and, of course – I am being a bit self interested here – economics as these areas can also indirectly contribute to our more techy or sciencey endeavours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Lest we forget, Steve Jobs, for example, was a liberal arts major who brought Apple from a pure tech company into a global consumer lifestyle juggernaut.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Jack Ma, founder of tech giant Alibaba was also an English major.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The National Research Fund oversees the part that is largely related to science and technology.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But beyond science and technology, where there are parts that are related to how science and technology may be deployed; we also fund some of those research.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For instance, in the field of ageing, it is not just the biomedical aspects of ageing, but also the behavioural aspects of ageing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: How do we nudge people towards healthier lifestyle, healthier behaviour.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, where it is closely related, we do fund those projects as well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At the same time, there are also many different pots of research funding.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When I was at the Ministry of Education (MOE), we have and we still have the Academic Research Fund at different tiers that is administered by MOE.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The question is, how do we bring all of this together?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I think for individual researchers, do apply for that, look at what may be relevant.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: My personal appeal to researchers is that I know there are some who love to look at just the basic research of it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Budget builds upon past Budgets, providing immediate support for today's challenges, investing in our growth and securing Singapore's long-term future while maintaining fiscal prudence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The fact that it has gone smoothly with no distractions is no easy feat.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Political stability has been the cornerstone of Singapore's success, shaping our economic growth, social policies and diplomatic standing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is our "secret sauce" – the ability to plan, think and most importantly, execute for the long term while still tackling the challenges of today.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, as we plan for the future while tackling today's challenges, we must stay engaged, listen actively and adapt swiftly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Understanding the powers of our people is key, ensuring that we refine our approaches, improve our policies and respond effectively to evolving needs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With deep respect and gratitude, we recognise the seamless handover of leadership from Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong to Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The transition reflects the hallmark of Singapore's governance – continuity, foresight and stability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we look at the world around us, Singapore's political stability and mature leadership transition is an anomaly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many nations struggle with uncertain transitions, political instability and abrupt policy u-turns, leading to wasted investments, stalled progress and loss of public trust.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Take, for example, the US saw political turmoil during the 2020 transition, culminating in the 6 January Capitol riot and repeated policy u-turns across administrations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some Asian countries experienced drastic shifts in economic and diplomatic policies with each new leader, causing instability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In just three months, one Asian country has seen a president and an acting president impeached.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The United Kingdom (UK) continues to face instability with frequent leadership changes, leading to uncertainty in trade, immigration and economic policies, particularly post-Brexit.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), repeated leadership changes have resulted in policy reversals such as the abolition and reintroduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST), causing economic uncertainty and deterring long-term investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In contrast, Mr Speaker, Sir, Singapore has shown that leadership transition can be done right.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This stability has been the bedrock of our economic growth, our social policies and diplomatic standing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It allows us to focus on long-term plans while tackling today's challenges, even amidst geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is something that we must protect and strengthen to uphold the values that have guided our progress.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, Mr Speaker, I am pleased that this Budget reflects this continuity and consistency.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It builds on the past Budgets while adapting to new challenges and reinforces our commitment to a resilient and forward-looking Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In an era where countries are turning inwards, onshoring businesses and shifting away from global collaboration, Singapore must stay ahead.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Developing Singapore into a leading air hub requires more than expanding our airport capacity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As regional airports modernise rapidly, we must scale productivity, enhance global connectivity and strengthen Singapore's position as a premier travel and business hub.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond the airport, our broader air hub ecosystem must grow in tandem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Industries such as aerospace maintenance, repair and operations (MRO), logistics and airside services are critical in keeping Singapore competitive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Their growth requires a coordinated strategy, aligning infrastructure expansion, workforce readiness, sustainability strategy and industry development.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must also strengthen collaboration among key ecosystem players such as Singapore Airlines, Changi Airport Group, the Singapore Tourism Board and the hospitality sector to enhance Singapore's value proposition as an air hub.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Its airline, tourism and airport operator are strategically aligned to position the city as a premier travel destination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, as Changi Airport continues to expand, how can we optimise urban planning and resource allocation in our east and north east areas like the Loyang Industrial Estate, Changi Business Park, Pasir Ris, Punggol, in particular, Punggol Digital District and Seletar to reinforce growth and strengthen Singapore's overall aviation sector?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is not just an investment in technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is an investment in energy security, economic resilience and environmental responsibility.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The key question is, how will this fund be used to deepen our understanding of alternative energy feasibility for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To make real progress, we need to strengthen research efforts to assess viable alternative energy sources, ensure regulatory readiness, preparing Singapore to govern and implement new energy solutions; build a strong talent pipeline, equipping Singaporeans with the expertise needed for this transition; and engage with international partners to accelerate learning and preparedness, ensuring we lead rather than follow.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More importantly, we must move with urgency from technology exploration to pilot programmes and ultimately, to full-scale industrial deployment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that Singapore transitions at pace and does not lag behind?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I look forward to hearing more about the whole-of-nation approach to developing Singapore as a leading air hub and the details of the Future Energy Fund during the Committee of Supply (COS) debates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, as we plan for the future, we must stay engaged, listen actively and remain adaptable to solve today's problems.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is essential to understand the pulse of our people, refine our approaches and continuously improve our policies, ensuring that we build a stronger, better future together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A good example of this is the cost-of-living support through the U-Save, and service and conservancy charges (S&CC) rebates, Climate Vouchers, MediSave and Edusave top-ups and SG60 Vouchers, which provides much needed relief.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some Pasir Ris residents suggested receiving Community Development Council (CDC) Vouchers in cash for greater flexibility, including overseas spending.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the CDC Voucher system is well-refined, helping Singaporeans while also boosting local businesses, especially our smaller neighbourhood shops.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our stallholders, such as Mrs Wee and Eric at Pasir Ris Drive 4 and 6 wet markets have shared that they have seen their business increase during voucher disbursements.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Keeping spending local ensures that support reaches Singaporeans while strengthening small businesses and hawkers, a vital part of our community and economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my 2022 speech on the White Paper on Singapore Women's Development, I shared the story of Mdm Neo, a Pasir Ris resident caring for her bedridden husband.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Budget reaffirms the Government's commitment to building a Singapore made for families, with stronger support for vulnerable families, seniors and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Measures such as the enhanced Fresh Start Housing Scheme, higher ComCare rates and initiatives to help seniors age well are welcome steps.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, retirement adequacy remains a concern, particularly for seniors with insufficient Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But are we truly moving the needle on employment opportunities for those with special needs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While SkillsFuture grants support workforce upskilling and Senior Employment Credit incentivises hiring older workers, workforce transformation remains slow in hiring seniors and PwDs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we move beyond incentives to truly shift workplace culture?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What more can be done to ensure employment inclusivity is not just a policy goal but a reality for all Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, beyond the grants, schemes and vouchers introduced, there are three important points we need to ponder.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, this is the first Budget under the new leadership of Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and the 4G leadership team.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This achievement is no mean feat, especially when we look at what is happening in other countries including the US.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, the importance of political stability for Singapore's progress.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many countries experience turbulent leadership transitions, resulting in uncertainty, political instability and squandered investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ultimately, it is the people who bear the consequences.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Political stability is a cornerstone of Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It shapes our economic growth, social policies and diplomatic standing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The ability to plan, think and most importantly, implement for the long term while addressing current challenges, is the secret to our success and we must protect it for the sake of our children's future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, we must prepare for the future by taking a flexible approach.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In planning for the future, we need to continue to listen, understand the people's wishes and make swift adjustments to policies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The people, leaders and businesses must work together to continuously refine and improve policies to shape a stronger and more resilient Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Only through unity and efficient leadership can we continue to progress as a stable and successful nation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore must continue to lead in green finance and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Businesses that purchase voluntary carbon credits to manage their emissions targets would benefit from enhanced tax deductions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would encourage more businesses to participate in sustainable investments globally.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The shift towards electric mobility is crucial for our sustainability goals.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government allow businesses to claim input tax on GST incurred for expenses related to EVs?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will support early adoption and accelerate fleet transitions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Enterprise Singapore administers numerous grants and schemes to support SMEs in their green transition.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, these are largely based on a reimbursement model, which creates uncertainty in capital recovery.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a result, many SMEs hesitate to invest in expensive equipment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To improve accessibility, I propose that Enterprise Singapore offer upfront financial support, especially for vendors who have cleared the agency's onboarding criteria.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, the Government, leveraging its data on registered businesses, could use AI to prequalify SMEs for relevant assistance schemes and grants, and then inform these companies that qualify and welcome them to submit their applications.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To further encourage sustainable investments, Enterprise Singapore could support the leasing of energy-efficient equipment like electric cranes, allowing SMEs to claim these expenses instead of requiring outright purchases, followed by applications.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SMEs require targeted funding support to invest in carbon pricing models, value-chain emissions management and decarbonisation projects.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
