text: I propose further tax deductions or co-funding mechanisms, with a limited implementation window of two to three years to assess effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also welcome the Government's expansion of the Partnerships for Capability Transformation (PACT) scheme in 2024, which fosters deeper collaboration between MNCs and SMEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could the Government provide insights on the utilisation rate of this scheme?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should start with ourselves by encouraging large local buyers, such as GLCs and NTUC FairPrice, to join the scheme and help their SME suppliers with green transformation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Sustainability is an area where SMEs and MNCs can work together.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MNCs, as "queen bee buyers", can guide SMEs towards meeting global environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, ESG reporting applies only to listed firms, but many countries are mandating sustainability compliance across entire supply chains.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SMEs should start identifying and reporting their carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can the Government help these SMEs master the business opportunities in this area?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, I highlighted the shortage of heavy vehicle parking near drivers' residences, forcing companies to cover additional transport costs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could the Government convert vacant premises, such as unused schools or JTC sites, into temporary parking lots or allow these heavy vehicles to park overnight?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, inclusivity hiring requires additional workplace training for supervisors and colleagues.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To further incentivise employers, I propose: one, tax rebates for businesses that adopt inclusive hiring practices; two, higher foreign worker quotas for companies hiring persons with disabilities; and three, bonus points for inclusive companies in Government project bids.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also urge MOE to provide more Edusave Awards opportunities to children studying at Special Education Schools.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, families with more than one special needs child face immense financial strain, as one parent often has to stop working to provide care.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government offer enhanced financial assistance to such families? : Enterprise Singapore administers numerous grants and schemes to support SMEs in their green transition.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, these are largely based on a reimbursement model, which creates uncertainty in capital recovery.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a result, many SMEs hesitate to invest in expensive equipment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To improve accessibility, I propose that Enterprise Singapore offer upfront financial support, especially for vendors which have cleared the agency’s onboarding criteria.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, the Government, leveraging on its data on registered businesses, could use AI to pre-qualify the SMEs for relevant assistance schemes and grants.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To further encourage sustainable investments, Enterprise Singapore can support the leasing of energy-efficient equipment like electric cranes or electric generators, allowing SMEs to claim these expenses instead of requiring upfront purchases.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SMEs require targeted funding support to invest in carbon pricing models, value-chain emissions management and decarbonisation projects.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government provide insights on the utilisation rate of this scheme and any potential areas for improvement?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can we also encourage the local "queen bee buyers", like NTUC Fairprice and the Temasek-linked companies to be part of this scheme and help embark key SME suppliers on this green journey?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Sustainability is an area where SMEs and MNCs, as well as the local large corporations, can work together.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These “queen bee buyers,” can guide SMEs towards meeting global environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, ESG reporting applies only to listed firms, but many countries are mandating sustainability compliance across the entire value chain.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Government can help the SMEs to start tracking their emissions now, so as to avoid future trade barriers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, I highlighted the shortage of heavy vehicle parking near the drivers’ residences, forcing companies to cover additional transport costs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government convert vacant premises, such as unused schools or JTC sites, into temporary parking lots to allow these drivers to park overnight?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, inclusivity hiring requires additional workplace training for supervisors and their colleagues.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also urge MOE to provide more Edusave Awards opportunities to children studying at special education (SPED) schools.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, families with more than one special needs kid face immense financial strain, as one parent often has to stop working to provide care.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government offer enhanced financial assistance to such families?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has many social support schemes for lower-income families, but eligibility criteria can be complex.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Essential workers, who need help the most, often lack time, knowledge, or digital access to navigate these schemes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, they may struggle to identify suitable upgrading opportunities, especially with rising job and training scams.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Government to develop a systematic framework to proactively reach out and guide these workers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I strongly support these measures and urge the Government to further refine tax policies, expand SME support, accelerate sustainability efforts and simplify access to social assistance.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With this, I affirm my support for the Budget.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: On behalf of residents of Sembawang group representation constituency (GRC), I thank the Government for the generous support provided to all Singaporeans and for the forward-looking Budget, which further invests in our economy, our infrastructure and most importantly, our people.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It demonstrates a robust approach to tackling financial crime.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In this context, I would like to ask the Prime Minister: did the confiscated funds contribute to the reported surplus?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This question is pertinent given the devastating impact of scams on many Singaporeans, some of whom have tragically lost their entire life savings.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, would the Government consider utilising a portion of this confiscated money to provide much-needed assistance and support to Singaporeans who have suffered such devastating losses.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Such a measure would not only provide crucial financial relief but also demonstrate the Government's empathy and commitment to supporting citizens affected by financial crime.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Together with many fellow Members of Parliament (MPs) in this House, I have expressed concerns about our heavy reliance on natural gas and the need to explore diversified energy options.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, I spoke about the potential of nuclear energy for Singapore back in 2009, during my first term as an MP, before the unfortunate Fukushima incident.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, I am particularly pleased to hear the Prime Minister addressing the possibility of deploying small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) during his speech.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These reactors are touted as being significantly safer and present lower risks compared to conventional nuclear reactors, like those in Fukushima.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, understandable concerns remain among Singaporeans, primarily regarding safety and the potential locations of these reactors.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I therefore pose these questions: will these SMRs be situated on one of our offshore islands, as far as possible from our population centres?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Or might they be located deep underground, within our granite bedrock, offering potential for easier containment in the event of any incident?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Furthermore, the high capital cost and long gestation period associated with nuclear reactors are well-known.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the estimated cost for these SMRs and how does the Government propose to fund this significant undertaking?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Next, understandably, with the talk of general elections approaching, the media has been very busy trying to speculate where will be the hot spots.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am pleased that my cut at the Ministry of National Development (MND) Committee of Supply debate in 2016, urging the Government to consider building a hot spring park on Ministry of Defence (MINDEF)-owned land, ultimately led to the creation of Sembawang Hot Spring Park and, now, a space for all to enjoy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, hot springs are a natural phenomena, subjected to change, shifts and new formations due to ground movement.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, I hope the ongoing construction of the North-South Corridor expressway adjacent to the Sembawang Hot Spring will not adversely affect this valuable resource of ours.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Furthermore, a few years ago, a dormitory operator in Sembawang reported the discovery of another hot spring on their premises.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I understand the leases of these dormitories are not being renewed, as the land is slated for redevelopment.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I urge the Government to prioritise the preservation and protection of any new hot springs that may be discovered in the area.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The potential of geothermal energy generation using underground heat in Sembawang has also been discussed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This presents a promising source of renewable energy and a valuable opportunity to diversify our energy sources.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on this project?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Specifically, I would like to know the exact location of the geothermal exploration and what is the potential impact it may have on our environment, more importantly, on the existing Sembawang Hot Spring.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Another important element in our pursuit of energy resilience is solar.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Despite our limited land size, Singapore has made commendable progress in incorporating solar power into our energy mix.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The SolarNova programme, launched in 2014, has successfully deployed solar panels across Government buildings, public housing and key infrastructures, proving that the solar panel deployment is both cost-effective and scalable.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many buildings and houses still possess untapped roof spaces suitable for solar panel installations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I urge the Government to further incentivise and encourage these building and homeowners to embrace solar energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: One potential approach is to incorporate solar panel installation requirements directly into our Building and Construction Authority (BCA) building code, ensuring all future buildings contribute to our power grid.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Furthermore, like the climate vouchers initiative, could the Government consider providing grants to private property owners to offset the cost of solar panel installation?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This would not only accelerate the adoption of solar energy, but also empower individuals to contribute directly to our national sustainability goals.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Let us now turn to the heart of our nation's strength: our people.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: People are Singapore's most valuable resource and our adaptability and unity are hallmarks that we must safeguard.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In our early years, the kampung spirit fostered strong community bonds.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Extended families lived together, often with limited Government support, relying on local village or clan associations for mutual aid.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Everybody knew their neighbours, creating a tightly-knitted community.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's rapid development over the past 60 years has transformed our living landscape.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Today, most reside in Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates with modern amenities, served by Residents' Networks under the People's Association (PA).

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While these networks organise beneficial programmes and events, it is an unfortunate reality that neighbours living on the same floor can remain strangers even after many years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Distressing incidents, such as residents passing away unnoticed until the discovery of a foul smell, highlight the gaps in our modern social fabric.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Clearly, we need to create more opportunities for connection and strengthening of bonds between neighbours.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: PA excels at organising large-scale community events that foster unity and raise awareness amongst hundreds or even thousands of attendees.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But the nature of such events means that they are less effective in cultivating close neighbourly ties.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have seen relationships blossom and a renewed sense of community emerge.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We capture these moments with a group photo of the whole entire floor and encourage neighbours to exchange contact information, recognising that in emergency, neighbours are the first line of support.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have witnessed heartwarming instances whereby neighbours offered to drive their neighbours to hospital during emergency, working together to extinguish fires before the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) arrival, and cooking and delivering meals to those living alone and facing mobility challenges.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This strong community spirit shone brightly during challenging times, like the recent COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The resilience of our people must be continuously nurtured.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I urge the Government to invest more in initiatives that promote neighbourliness and strengthen our bonds within our community, building a more resilient and interconnected society.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are undeniably facing increasingly unpredictable and extreme weather conditions, a trend that is projected to worsen.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Government plays a pivotal role in bolstering our resilience through comprehensive policies and initiatives.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Sustainable Singapore Blueprint and the Singapore Green Plan 2030 outline ambitious yet necessary goals for sustainability, including reducing carbon emissions, increasing the use of renewable energy and promoting waste reduction.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Beyond national efforts, promoting individual actions, such as the 3Rs – reduce, reuse and recycle – is crucial.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I recall when I first entered politics in 2006; there was only one recycling bin for every five blocks of HDB.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While we encouraged the residents to recycle, the limited infrastructure presented a significant challenge.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And in this very House, I advocated for increased recycling bins and dedicated recycling chutes in new HDB developments.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This project proved highly successful and paved the way for islandwide adoption later.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Now, new HDB projects incorporate dedicated recycling chutes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Building upon this progress, I encourage individuals with innovative ideas and a passion for contributing to this vital green industry to step forward.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Collaborative efforts between all stakeholders and the Government are essential for achieving the ambitious goals outlined in the Singapore Green Plan and ensuring the environmental resilience for our nation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They built the foundation upon which our nation stands.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Let us honour their legacy by continuing their work, strengthening our resilience across all vital sectors – energy, people and environmental – and securing a brighter future for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Lim, you can go back to your hot seat.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will address three critical areas: one, budget marksmanship; two, the concept of affordability; and finally, the challenges faced by some vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As highlighted by fellow Members, the Ministry of Finance's (MOF's) budget forecasting this year has been notably inaccurate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To put this in perspective, $8 billion equates to $8,000 million, a substantial underestimation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Additional increased contributions came from Statutory Boards, stamp duties and personal income taxes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In September last year, midway through the fiscal year, Prime Minister Wong responded to a Parliamentary Question (PQ) from Workers' Party (WP) MP Louis Chua, reiterating the projected surplus of $0.78 billion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Was there an awareness at that point of the significant deviations from projections?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If so, should an updated estimate have been provided?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If not, why was this discrepancy not identified earlier?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Escalating cost of essential items, such as food, are particularly concerning.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister aptly noted, "Singaporeans are still adjusting to these new price realities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some have had to tighten their belts, rethink spending habits or make difficult trade-offs to manage their expenses." While external factors contribute to inflation, it is important to recognise that COE and GST are outcomes of domestic policies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Offering ad hoc vouchers and handouts in response to the cost of living, may come across as missing the wood for the trees.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government's approach to easing cost of living pressures and ensuring public housing affordability warrant scrutiny.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Current measures suggest that Singaporeans can only manage expenses with the aid of vouchers, subsidies and grants.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Reliance on rebates and vouchers indicates that, without such assistance, basic necessities may be out of reach for many.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On public housing, the necessity of substantial housing grants, which were further increased in 2023 and again in 2024.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This implies that, without them, most citizens would struggle to afford HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On childcare and education, the dependence on subsidies and fee caps suggested that, without these interventions, these services might be unaffordable for the average family.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In 2023, then-Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong noted that the Singapore dream was no longer about the five Cs – cash, car, credit card, condominium and country club; but it was about fulfilment, meaning and purpose in life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could it be that the five Cs simply hold no relevance today as they are no longer attainable to many?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, the growing dependence on housing grants prompts questions about future affordability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Parents today are understandably anxious about the housing prospects for their children.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such reliance on Government transfers raises concerns about the sustainability of such support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a Straits Times opinion piece on 24 February, Professors Linda Lim and Pang Eng Fong queried this approach for the long term.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They observed that, "The persistent need for subsidies for basic goods and services like food, accommodation and utilities in one of the world's richest countries, indicates that prices are too high and wages too low to enable a substantial segment of Singaporeans to make ends meet." Sir, such a concern is not confined to this House, nor to economists.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier this week, a member of the public named Joe called into a CNA TV programme to pose a most pertinent question to the Government, "Can the Minister reassure us that the Government is looking into the rising cost of living and not just providing handouts?" Sir, looking ahead, I also wonder how much more the Government will collect from Singaporeans every year in taxes to fund these handouts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will there be an endless upwards spiral in prices and increased handouts, in the name of affordability?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As we commemorate 60 years of Singapore's Independence, it is timely to reflect on the challenges faced by certain groups, particularly homemakers, whose financial security requires attention.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Currently, CPF members have the autonomy to nominate beneficiaries for their CPF savings upon death, even to the exclusion of immediate family members.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This poses a potential risk to non-working spouses, typically wives, who have dedicated themselves to managing the household and consequently have limited CPF savings of their own.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For families with fewer resources, CPF savings constitute a significant portion of liquid assets upon a member's death.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This highlights the importance of CPF savings in retirement planning.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In situations where a CPF member nominates non-family beneficiaries, a surviving spouse and any children could be left without a financial safety net.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Notably, during divorce proceedings, CPF monies accumulated during the marriage are considered matrimonial assets and are subject to division.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This could be implemented by mandating the spouse as a necessary witness to such a nomination.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a measure would acknowledge CPF funds as shared assets within a marriage and ensure that both parties are aware of and agree to the distribution plans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Ministry will give this proposal some consideration during that debate.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is what gives Singaporeans confidence in the future and what continues to attract investments, create good jobs and secure prosperity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This stability is about good governance, a responsible fiscal approach and a united people.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we want to continue finding stability in a world of flux, we must continue making the right decisions and not just the popular ones.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of the biggest tests of our stability today is the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As an MP for Zhenghua, I have witnessed first-hand the challenges that residents face.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While data indicate that inflation has eased, prices remain high and families continue to feel the pinch.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singaporeans are adjusting, tightening their belts and rethinking spending habits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is reassuring that these concerns are reflected in Budget 2025, with measures, such as the CDC Vouchers and LifeSG credits, offering timely relief.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But while short-term relief is necessary, we must also address structural cost issues to ensure that the rising cost of living does not erode Singaporeans' quality of life.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One area where the Government has taken a bold structural step is preschool education.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a significant step forward, ensuring that every child, regardless of their background, have a good start in life.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, Sir, affordability must not come at the expense of quality.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Preschool teachers play a vital role in shaping our young minds and their work must be fairly compensated.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Affordability, wages and social support all intersect at one issue – fiscal management.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And that brings me to my next point.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some argue that the tax burden on Singaporeans is high and we have sufficient surpluses to reduce the tax burden.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But let us set the record straight: Singapore's tax burden remains one of the lowest in developed countries.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unlike other nations that rely heavily on personal income and consumption tax, our two largest revenue sources are corporate tax and the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And as Prime Minister Wong shared in his Budget speech, Singapore expects a budget surplus in FY2024 and FY2025.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are encouraging figures, surpluses give us the confidence and resources to invest in our people and secure good jobs for everyone.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The reality is that the Government spending has increased significantly, not just for social and healthcare support, but also for initiatives that will secure Singapore's economic competitiveness and protect our island from the impacts of climate change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A budget surplus today does not mean we can spend recklessly tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, we must remain disciplined and focused on delivering real outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ensuring that economic growth translates into good jobs and higher real wages is one key measure of success.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2023, I raised a PQ on real wage growth trends and projections, as I was deeply concerned about whether Singaporeans' wages rise in tandem with living costs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thankfully, Singaporeans experienced real wage growth in 2024 in tandem with higher-than-expected economic growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Economic growth must continue to translate into real wage growth, good jobs and meaningful opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But how do we exactly go about doing this?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One initiative I championed last year in my Budget 2024 speech was the adoption of Employee Stock Ownership Plans (ESOPs).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ESOPs grant employees the option to purchase shares at a set price upon meeting performance goals, aiming to retain key staff long term.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Crucially, ESOPs instil a sense of ownership, boosting motivation and performance.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This also translates into high real incomes and enables employees to build their asset base.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The promotion of ESOPs can complement the new Global Founder Programme announced in Budget 2025.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we encourage global founders to anchor and grow more new ventures in Singapore, we should ensure that the investments also benefit employees of the investee companies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will anchor talent in Singapore and help Singaporeans grow their income and asset base.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It can complement the Global Founder Programme by driving investments in start-ups, attracting top talent and giving employees a stake in asset appreciation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But beyond ESOPs, we need a comprehensive, multi-pronged approach to sustain real wage growth and meaningful job creation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, we must leverage the announced Enterprise Growth Investment Fund and the $1 billion private credit growth fund to include blended capital solutions that drive impact investments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By aligning financial instruments with corporate purpose and societal impact, we can support businesses that prioritise innovation, sustainability and meaningful job creation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Blended capital, combining grants, recoverable grants and equity from diverse sources, such as foundations, bridges philanthropy and impact investments, unlocking additional funding streams.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To accelerate this, agencies like EDB and the National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre (NVPC), which have developed the Company of Good framework and accreditation, should collaborate to develop programs that expand blended capital deployment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond mobilising resources, blended capital can reduce financing costs while enhancing social and economic outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It strengthens corporate purpose, fosters sustainable business growth and creates meaningful employment opportunities, ensuring that enterprises contribute to both economic progress and societal well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whether it is foreign talent or multinational enterprises (MNEs), the concern is that foreign talent and MNEs compete with local jobseekers and local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such concerns are valid only if it is a zero-sum game.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, the reality is that it is a non-zero-sum game.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Maximising the complementary advantage for the individual would mean the Government's consistent support in skills upgrading, so that Singaporeans always boost their capabilities and seize new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For local enterprises, we need to strengthen the enterprise ecosystem and the network effect between local enterprises and MNEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Despite the high cost of operating in Singapore, MNEs stay committed in Singapore due to the relevant enterprise ecosystem that provides MNEs with high quality supplies and expertise.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Local enterprises can collaborate with MNEs to innovate, create new products and services, and grow internationally by leveraging the MNEs network and referrals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As globalisation trends shift toward localisation and onshoring, there is a growing risk that MNEs may relocate key manufacturing, R&D and corporate functions away from hubs like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To build economic resilience against such external shocks, we must strengthen the nexus and integration between our local enterprises and MNEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As one CEO of a large local enterprise aptly put it, "MNEs may adjust their investment focus based on global geopolitical trends, but local enterprises are here to stay.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is our home base." By fostering the growth of strong local enterprises, we can anchor critical capabilities, sustain high-quality jobs and ensure long-term economic stability for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By strengthening the complementary relationship between local and foreign workers, as well as between local enterprises and MNEs, we can create a synergy that drives shared growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This ensures that the partnership is a non-zero-sum game, but a collaborative effort that generates greater opportunities and benefits for local workers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, we must continue powering ahead with workforce upskilling.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers play a critical role in aligning workers' skills with the evolving demands of industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is imperative that we provide them with stronger support to ensure Singapore's workforce remains future-ready.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The NTUC CTC Grant has been instrumental in co-funding employer-led initiatives that boost productivity, redesign jobs and enhance career development.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The SkillsFuture Workforce Development Grant further strengthens this by increasing funding support while streamlining the application process, making it easier for businesses to invest in talent development.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By serving as an intermediary that links industries, training providers and employment facilitation partners, JSIT ensures that training programs are directly aligned with market needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can the Government share how these schemes complement each other in supporting businesses and workers to adapt to evolving industry demands and skills requirements?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, work-study programs are critical in bridging the gap between education and employment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I fully welcome the expanded support for work-study programs under the SkillsFuture Level-Up programme, particularly the introduction of the Part-Time Long-Form Training to cater to part-time upskilling.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The opening of Singapore University of Social Sciences' (SUSS's) new city campus is another positive step, making work-study opportunities more accessible to working professionals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On this note, I would like to ask the Government if there are plans to encourage more employers to offer work-study arrangements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What policies can be introduced to minimise workplace disruptions while ensuring workers can upgrade their skills without compromising productivity?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By aligning workforce upskilling with employers' transformation needs and industry trends, we enable both businesses and workers to seize new opportunities and drive growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A strong focus on growth and top-line expansion ensures that companies have the resources to invest in talent development, fostering continuous learning, innovation and sustained wage increases.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourth, we need to take AI by its horns and improve its adoption among enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This integration allows students, researchers, and businesses to work closely together, accelerating innovation and ensuring the real-world application of research.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Internationally, successful models demonstrate the impact of such integration.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Stanford University’s close ties with Silicon Valley have fostered groundbreaking startups like Google and HP, while the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s (MIT’s) Industrial Liaison Program connects companies with faculty and researchers, ensuring innovations translate into commercial applications.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Budget 2025 builds upon the Government’s consistent investment in our economy and our people.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have been able to deepen these commitments while keeping individual tax burdens low compared to many developed countries.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, the true impact of these investments depends on effective execution.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In an increasingly volatile world, Singapore’s stability is our foundation, giving us the confidence and conviction that we can deliver on these policies and secure a better future for all.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most importantly, Sir, our unity as Singaporeans remains our greatest strength.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have witnessed this firsthand in Zhenghua, where residents often tell me they would rather let others benefit from local assistance schemes, such as the monthly $1 Deal and Project Sama Sama.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This selfless Spirit of looking out for one another, of caring for our neighbours, is what defines us as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is this collective sense of community that will see us through any crisis and propel us towards an even stronger Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, Government handouts have become regular.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has become a national past time of sorts to monitor the timetable of handouts each month, which is also publicised in the media and in the HDB lift lobbies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can this really be healthy for our society?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Comments are already circulating on social media that the new 5Cs of today are Cash, CDC Vouchers, Climate Vouchers, CPF top-ups and Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) cards.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure that the first generation PAP leaders would never have allowed this to happen.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the PAP Government's vouchers may help many Singaporeans deal with rising costs in the short term, they are not enough to help Singaporeans in the long term or solve Singapore's structural economic issues.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) supports some short-term financial assistance in the Budget to help deal with the high and rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, over the past four Budget debates, we have also argued that instead of giving out short-term ad hoc handouts, we should have long-term permanent schemes to strengthen the social support for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The schemes proposed by PSP over the years, including a Minimum Living Wage, Affordable Homes Scheme, National Healthcare Scheme with MediShield and CareShield premiums paid by the Government, and Caregivers Allowance will create financial security for Singaporeans and empower them with the resources to pursue their career aspirations, form families and build a better life.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, is the SG60 Voucher which will benefit the billionaire living in a good class bungalow and a 1-room rental flat resident equally, truly a good and fair use of our fiscal resources?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the PAP's patchwork of scheme of handouts and vouchers that will breed dependency among Singaporeans and not PSP's proposals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP's recognises that it is unrealistic to expect living costs never to increase, but we maintain that the PAP's current budget approach and policies around taxes, Reserves and property prices are the main driver of the high cost of living in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Long before the Ukraine War and supply chain disruptions, Singaporeans have found it difficult to cope with the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a persistent structural problem caused by the PAP Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has collected a lot more revenue from GST, COE and land sales over the past few years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will eventually increase the cost of living for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PAP Government has always claimed that there is tight fiscal headroom, but if year after year surpluses are always bigger than what is estimated, then it really calls into question why the Government decided to inflict so much pain on Singaporeans by raising GST in 2023 and 2024 amid high global inflation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I questioned Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on budget marksmanship at the debate last year, he said before COVID-19, our fiscal marksmanship was not too bad, and our forecast accuracy was not as good now because of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Prime Minister expect our budget marksmanship to be better this year?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or will we end up having a larger surplus than we anticipated again?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Budget marksmanship is important so that Parliament and Singaporeans have a clear view of the fiscal resources available to us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the debate on the Public Finances Motion last year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I explained that the Government transfers a large part of the surplus Budget resources arising from the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) each year to many endowment and trust funds that are intended for future spending over the long term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has camouflaged our huge structural surplus Budget position.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also questionable whether so much of today's resources should be used for certain projects.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the Government has parked another $5 billion in the Changi Airport Development Fund, even though over the years we have already put $6 billion there.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe such a large infrastructure project should be funded by the Significant Infrastructure Government Loan (SINGA) framework so that we can evaluate the commercial viability of such projects better.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our country's fiscal position is extremely strong, much stronger than what the PAP Government would like to portray.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yesterday, Ms Foo Mee Har claimed that Singapore could face fiscal vulnerabilities like Hong Kong, if we use land sales to fund our expenditure like what PSP had advocated.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has only proposed that if a piece of land is sold on a 99-year lease, the proceeds should be recognised as revenue spread over 99 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is unlikely to create the fiscal vulnerabilities Ms Foo suggested.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would remind Ms Foo that last year, even Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong said our proposition was not unthinkable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's financial position is strong, but ordinary Singaporeans financial position is weak.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An OCBC survey in November 2023 found that fewer Singaporeans are able to comfortably spend on things beyond the basics.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In March 2020, the Government tabled the Resilience Budget, which was aptly named, because there is a need to make Singaporeans more resilient.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all the CDC Vouchers and short-term schemes from the Budgets of the over the last five years, have Singaporeans become more financially resilient?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Judging from the conversations that PSP has had with many Singaporeans, the answer is no.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why PSP believes there is an urgent need to reimagine our Budget approach and public policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our objective is to empower Singaporeans so that they can be financially resilient without relying on ad hoc handouts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to better utilise the NIRC and our budget resources to benefit Singaporeans so that they can become truly resilient.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are more and more of such funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There needs to be more scrutiny over the use of these funds, as many will not directly benefit Singaporeans in the short term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of parking funds in endowment funds and spending on special transfers that do not create long-term financial security for Singaporeans, we can fund PSP's four main policy proposals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can implement the Affordable Homes Scheme without reducing the reserves, unlike what Minister Indranee has repeatedly claimed, but will empower Singaporeans in the following ways.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans of all generations will enjoy affordable public housing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As AHS flats cost less, Singaporeans will not have to deplete their CPF balances to pay off HDB mortgages.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They will have adequate CPF savings for retirement without having to downgrade to smaller flats in retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yesterday, Mr Henry Kwek suggested that our schemes will put a downward pressure on resale values.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will not happen, because Singaporeans who sell their Affordable Homes Scheme flats will have to repay the land cost with accrued interest to the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will maintain stability in the resale market and allow Singaporeans to continue upgrading to private properties if they choose to do so.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Kwek pointed out that many of his residents see their HDB flat as a key pillar of their retirement planning.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP's Affordable Homes Scheme will empower Singaporeans and free them from such concerns.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our second proposal is to effectively create a national healthcare scheme by having the Government pay the MediShield and CareShield premiums for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, the national healthcare scheme will empower Singaporeans in the following ways.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All Singaporeans will be able to enjoy a basic level of benefits when they need hospital treatment or certain outpatient treatments free of charge, paid for by the state, without having to worry about rising insurance premiums in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans will have more MediSave balances to pay for other healthcare costs not covered by MediShield Life, freeing up their cash for other purposes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also support progressive wage increments up to the median wage of $4,500.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These policies will empower lower-income Singaporeans with the financial resources to attain a minimum standard of living in a high cost-of-living environment more quickly than the Government's Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporean workers will also enjoy further wage increments when they improve their skills.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our fourth proposal is the PSP Family Plan, which will reimagine our policies to support families.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the Population White Paper Debate in 2013, Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean said, "I hope our birth rate can increase to at least 1.4 or 1.5, which was our birth rate not so long ago, around the late 1990s and the early 2000s." We are not sure if Senior Minister Teo still has these hopes, but PSP certainly does.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why our PSP Family Plan is a whole-of-society approach to better support family formation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our two most important proposals are the enhanced Job Sharing Scheme and the Caregiving Allowance Scheme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These proposals will benefit all parents, including single parents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The enhanced Job Sharing Scheme will empower parents to opt for flexi-time work.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will allow them to remain in the workforce while spending more time to care for the child.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, employers will benefit from retaining their workers with children and employ more workers with Government subsidies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will empower families to explore different childcare arrangements and strengthen extended family bonds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, more problems have emerged in the lives and livelihoods of many Singaporeans in the last 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not want a first-world Singapore where the next generation has to live in smaller and smaller flats that are also more and more expensive relative to income.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not want a first-world Singapore where public transport only seems to be more and more crowded, expensive and unreliable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the first world we should aspire to create this SG60.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the first world Singapore that PSP will fight for.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We urge Singaporeans to think beyond the short term and dream bigger than the PAP Government.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At its very core, this Budget is a pledge to every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It places our people at the heart of our nation's progress.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Indeed, no matter the global uncertainties that swirl around us, it is a reaffirmation that the fruits of our progress must be shared widely with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Budget is also an expression of our readiness to face a more contested and fragmented global landscape.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We see economic fault lines emerging: new trade barriers, shifting alliances, competitive races in technology.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are a small city state, but we refuse to be overshadowed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have proven repeatedly that our size is our advantage.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our agility, our openness and our resilience are the defining factors that keep us ever relevant.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I attended an international forum post-COVID-19, where large powers were competing to dominate the narrative.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By pure alphabetical happenstance, Singapore found ourselves sitting in the midst of some of these heavyweights – "U", "R".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While they sparred, we quietly worked with fellow small states to give the conference, ultimately, a coherent and balanced outcome.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This story reminds us that size does not define our relevance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A small state can indeed be nimble, collaborative and innovative.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our resilience lies in adapting swiftly, building trust and championing a rule-based order.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When others falter or become mired in rivalry, we must step up to facilitate real progress, not just for ourselves but for our region and the world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The reality is that this year is an election year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we have seen elsewhere and as we have experienced during this Debate and outside of this House, passions will naturally run high.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A lively debate is part of a healthy democracy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, let us remember that when the dust settles, we must remain, first and foremost, Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Each of us is entrusted to safeguard and advance our nation's interests.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our survival ultimately hinges on our unity as a country.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: No matter the electoral outcome, we must close ranks, striving together for a stronger and more cohesive future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Indeed, it is this unity that has propelled us from the turmoil of our founding years to the globally connected Singapore that we know today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the Prime Minister highlighted, we must invest in our people and our industries, especially in areas of semiconductors, biotechnology and digital services, amongst many others, to stay at the frontier of economic opportunity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must not forget this fact – the world eats small states for breakfast.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us not serve ourselves on a platter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In tandem with all these economic strategies, we must also preserve and strengthen our social foundations, especially the family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must remember that the cornerstone of a strong, cohesive society is built on families, on marriage.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In its most fundamental sense, marriage is about commitment – about forging a lifelong bond that nurtures love, respect and responsibility.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When a husband and wife come together in this union, they form the primary building block for stable families, which, in turn, form the bedrock of a flourishing nation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Children benefit the most and most profoundly when raised in a context where love is modelled daily, where values are imparted through the constancy of caring adults who look to each other in partnership, very much like the relationship we have with our people and with one another.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Equally important, of course, is that every child must be valued, never to be cast aside as some inconvenient economic liability.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Children are gifts we welcome into our world, each with immeasurable potential, not just for our families but for a stable society and a strong nation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When our society affirms the priceless worth of every child, whether in the womb or in the classroom, we safeguard not just our demographic future but the moral core of what it means to be a nation that truly cares.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These measures in the Budget reflect these values on two critical fronts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a father of four lively youngsters myself, I know firsthand how swiftly grocery bills can mount and how quickly shoes can wear out.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is even more so for families with lower incomes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Budget continues to support marriage and parenthood and affirms our belief that families remain the anchor for Singaporean life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the local level, we have seen similar measures take root.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While Little Steps is funded through a generous donation, I urge the Government to consider making the national scheme more generous and extend support beyond the age of six to include those below 12.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let us consider how best to support those who choose to have large families before any incentives were introduced so that they, too, may benefit and feel that their contributions have not gone unnoticed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many Members, over the course of the last one and a half days, have also spoken about helping working mothers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, on the other hand, want us to be able to look beyond the working label.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All mothers make significant contributions and deserve our recognition and support.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Every mother, every parent, contributes immeasurably to our nation's future, and no mother or father should be penalised for putting family first.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As I stated earlier, lively debate is part of a healthy democracy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is to be expected that in the cut and thrust of politics, there will be disagreement on policy directions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it is always all too easy to score points by latching onto popular sentiments and making grandiose statements to grab the headlines.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But we must remember that true leadership is not measured by how loudly we speak or how dramatically we posture.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: True leadership shines through in the quiet, consistent and determined pursuit of policies that genuinely serve Singaporeans for the long term, even when policies are complex and unwieldy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Anyone can cast aspersions and claim to have all the answers; far fewer are willing to endure the gruelling work of finding real solutions that can withstand time and turbulence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Governing a nation is always challenging, but it is doubly so in a rapidly evolving global landscape.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It requires foresight to anticipate risks, prudence to steward our resources, and courage to stay the course when decisions are unpopular, or even detrimental to electoral support.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is the real test of leadership for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the turbulent world that we live in, not only do I think we need marksman, but marksman do not win wars on their own.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need an entire budget arsenal at the ready for the storms that would come in the future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is easy to say that is all we need for now.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But for a country with little resources except for the precious asset of our people, we need to prepare for the long term.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We, therefore, cannot grow complacent, for many nations today are torn by polarisation and discord.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Indeed, SG60 reminds us of how our founding generation defied the odds.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Contrast this with a poll of private sector economists in Singapore in an article run by The Business Times with a headline that goes, "Budget 2025 may run generous deficit of up to $6.6 billion after FY2024 surplus." The combined fiscal surplus of $13.2 billion for FY2024 and FY2025 was also surprising in the context of questions in Parliament towards the end of last year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The combined fiscal surplus of $13.2 billion for FY2024 and FY2025 was also surprising in the context of the sizeable $41.6 billion in top-ups to endowment and trust funds in these two years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We can say that, look, these are resources set aside to meet real needs in the future, but it does not take away the significance of these surpluses that are generated within just these two years alone.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, the amount drawn down from our Reserves to combat COVID-19 amounted to about $43 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It was previously said that we have drawn on our Reserves equivalent to over 20 years of past Budget surpluses.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We have used a generation's worth of savings to combat a crisis of a generation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the amount of additional resources we can set aside for endowment and trust funds in just these two years alone is close to $42 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Higher than expected surpluses are also not a recent phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: FY2021 was estimated to record a deficit of $11 billion but ended up as a surplus of $1.9 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: FY2022 was estimated to record a deficit of about $3 billion but ended up a surplus of $1.7 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do not deny that uncertainty is a fact of life and, yes, revenues and expenditures can go up and down with the economic cycle.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The point of all these observations, Mr Speaker, is that if the Government consistently collects more than it needs and runs huge surpluses year after year, it leads one to question the wisdom of raising the tax burden on Singaporeans, such as via the higher GST and the urgency in implementing them, especially as many are struggling with high inflation rates and the cost of living in the past few years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On this note, last year, I touched on the importance of structural changes instead of one-off handouts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Cost of living concerns are front and centre of Singaporeans' minds, and any additional support to tackle cost pressures are no doubt welcomed by many.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This year appears to be the year of vouchers, be it in the form of CDC Vouchers, Climate Vouchers or the new addition to our list of vouchers, SG60 Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given the record surpluses that the Government is enjoying, it is only right and appropriate that this is being shared to Singaporeans who have also contributed directly to the Government coffers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the General Elections around the corner, it is only natural for Singaporeans to be cynical where these are seen as election handouts tied to the political cycle rather than the economic cycle.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I believe that, firstly, it is important to put in place structural levers in our system, as opposed to relying on one-off schemes, which may be politicised, incur a lot of administrative costs and resources to operate on the part of the Civil Service, and create much unnecessary uncertainty on the part of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure many Members have seen the viral video where Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's Budget 2025 speech announcing the CDC Vouchers is being juxtaposed against an election rally speech by Minister Chan, where he put it quite elegantly, "If we give everybody the same – rich or poor – how are we helping the poor?" Take the CDC Voucher scheme, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I am sure many Singaporeans appreciate cash handouts amid the cost-of-living crisis, the CDC Voucher scheme evolved from one aimed at helping Singaporean lower-income households defray their cost of living in 2020 to one where all Singaporean households are eligible for the same amounts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The amounts given have also varied quite significantly over the years, and it remains a question whether the scheme will be a permanent one and, if so, whether all households will continue to qualify, and just how much are the vouchers going to be worth?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should this be a recurring feature of the annual Budget, this would effectively raise the tax threshold from the current first $2,000 of chargeable income.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The move is, however, abandoned as part of the SG60 package.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead of a run-off rebate, we are better off raising the bottom brackets of marginal resident personal income tax rates and increasing the tax-free threshold for the first $20,000 of chargeable income to reflect inflation over time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was what I raised in a PQ back in 2022, and also in my Budget 2024 speech last year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially so when, based on my estimates, close to 80% of resident taxpayers would only receive the $200 tax rebate cap and does not sound as generous as the 60% headline rebate level highlighted.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Next, I would like to now focus on how the Government can implement structural reforms to our CPF system to enhance the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans, an issue that I have frequently raised, and would only grow in importance due to our rapidly ageing society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is also a topic which I have repeatedly pleaded with the Government to take urgent action, as there are significant opportunity costs with the Government's inaction.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How should one save up prior to their retirement?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A recent DBS report provided several ballpark figures based on one's spending habits and lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the other end of the spectrum, should a retiree seek to enjoy an aspirational lifestyle with a monthly expenditure of $4,000, they would need approximately $1.3 million in their nest egg.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, someone aiming to enjoy a balanced lifestyle with $2,800 in monthly expenses would need to accrue $950,000 in retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: No matter one's preferred lifestyle, I am sure most, if not all Singaporeans would like to kick back and enjoy as they enter their retirement years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, many Singaporeans face difficulties in building up a sufficient retirement nest egg for them to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is largely attributed to financial difficulties, such as increased household expenditures and debt repayments, that hinder them from saving up for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the percentage goes up to 74%, if you only consider active CPF members, I am sure we all will agree $60,000 is a very low bar to cross.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I have been going on like a broken record, I hope we can urgently implement the Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS), which was first accepted by the Government back in 2016.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is also something which I have been repeating in each of the last four years so that we can better support Singaporeans' retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For sure, CPF returns are guaranteed by the Government, but is it sufficient in today's context?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yes, CPF members have the option today to enhance their returns via the CPF investment scheme, where members can invest their Ordinary Account (OA) and Special Account (SA) balances in a selection of investment products by external providers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But can we assume that everyone is confident and capable of making sound investment decisions?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I, therefore, read with interest a recent interview by Lian He Zao Bao with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, where he, too, noted that the Government has been studying the scheme for some time, and I quote, "The challenge is, can such a fund produce returns that are better than the very generous risk-free guaranteed returns that the Government already provides?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And would it still have some volatility which would expose CPF members to financial market risk, especially when they retire?" I have three simple answers to this question posed by the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, this has already been studied extensively by the CPF Advisory Panel about a decade ago, and they have, in my view, given a considered solution with the LRIS.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, think about the difference to the amount of Singaporeans' retirement funds almost a decade on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I hope that the Government is cognisant that the longer the delay, the higher the opportunity cost and the real cost to Singaporeans' retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe the deepest divisions in our society today is not based on race, language or religion, but based on socio-economic status.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we do not take a concerted effort to address this issue head on, as we have done with racial and religious harmony, these divisions will only deepen over time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In this 2025 Budget Statement, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned that income inequality after Government taxes and transfers is at its lowest since 2000.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, if measured by the Gini coefficient, after accounting for Government transfers and taxes, income inequality appears to be trending down.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is however, on the back of various short term and one-off transfers, such as the GST Assurance Package, CDC Vouchers and other temporary grants.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, much can be said about how median and average household incomes have been growing over the years, but there are several interesting statistics which I wish to highlight from the latest key household income trends report published by SingStat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After more than a decade since the Progressive Wage Model, which was launched in Singapore, our minimum wage equivalent, the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS), there still appears to be a significant number of households whose household income is less than the equivalent of what is estimated to be the average living wage per worker of $2,990 per month, as estimated in a study in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Based on the average household size today, this group of locals represent close to half a million people.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Can we truly say that all Singaporeans will be able to adequately pay for just their basic needs?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us also contrast this with the other end of the spectrum.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From 2014 to 2024, the total number of resident households in Singapore has grown by close to 263,000, from 1.2 million households in 2014 to 1.46 million households in 2024.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Behind the Gini coefficient statistics lies a stratified reality where we are seeing a widening income and wealth disparity in our society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, beyond income in inequality, we must also address wealth inequality, which has widened in recent years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To quote from the same report, in markets where average wealth growth strongly exceeds median growth like Singapore, it appears that much of the rise in wealth has benefited the upper-income brackets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as we welcome family offices and high net worth individuals to our shores, we must also explore bolder policies, such as stronger minimum wage frameworks, further enhancements to wage supplements and more aggressive redistributive measures on a sustained basis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should also examine how wealth taxes can play a greater role in narrowing the gap and ensuring a more equitable distribution of resources.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond income and wealth, we must also look at other forms of inequality: educational access, job opportunities and social mobility.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
