text: While we have taken steps to improve the inclusivity in our education system, more must be done to ensure that every child, regardless of background, has a fair shot at success.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And this begins all the way in primary school, where it should not matter as much as today who your parents are and what school they went to in determining primary school placements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to conclude in Mandarin, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   First, when the Government has consistently been collecting more than it spends year after year and generated substantial budget surpluses, Singaporeans cannot help but to question the wisdom and urgency of the tax increases, such as raising the GST, during a period of high inflation and cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many Singaporeans are deeply concerned about whether they will have sufficient retirement funds.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope we can address this issue head on and explore bolder policies, such as strengthening the minimum wage framework, further improving wage subsidies and continuing to implement more proactive redistribution measures.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 triggered a trade war, leading to a collapse in global trade.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses faced uncertainty as supply chains were disrupted and access to foreign markets became increasingly difficult.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The lack of international cooperation left economies vulnerable to shocks.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fast forward to 2025 and the parallels are striking.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While not on the brink of war, the world is similarly fragmented, marked by rising protectionism, economic nationalism and a lack of trust in multilateral institutions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses must navigate external challenges and domestic constraints in land, manpower and carbon.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These headwinds underscore the need for resilience, adaptability and readiness to seize emerging opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2025 provides a critical roadmap, introducing measures to strengthen economic foundations and enhance enterprise and workforce capabilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A recent SBF dipstick poll found that eight in 10 business leaders expressed satisfaction with the Budget and seven in 10 noted increased confidence in Singapore's business environment.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We are also encouraged that many recommendations from the business community, including those from the SBF's AfA on Business Competitiveness and SBF Pre-Budget Recommendations together with PwC Singapore, have been incorporated into the Budget.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses are reassured that the Government has their back and has reaffirmed the importance of long-term economic growth.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A key focus in Budget 2025 is ensuring that support is accessible not just to large corporations but also to SMEs, which face global uncertainties, domestic cost and manpower pressures, as well as the need for transformation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Equipping them with the right tools and resources is crucial for their survival and growth in this evolving landscape.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The enhancement of the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit, now operating as a wallet system rather than a reimbursement model, reflects the Government’s responsiveness to SMEs' cash flow concerns.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This practical adjustment will significantly benefit smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with other Members of the House that other Government schemes can also be reviewed to adopt similar cashflow-friendly models to better support SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of new CDC Vouchers and SG60 Vouchers will benefit households and will boost heartland enterprises and local retailers, potentially driving domestic retail sales, especially in areas where many SMEs operate.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Sustainability is also a key focus, with the transition to a green economy opening new avenues for innovation and growth.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Heavy Vehicle Zero Emissions Scheme and Electric Heavy Vehicle Charger Grant will reduce the cost of transitioning to clean vehicles.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, to maximise the impact of these schemes, SMEs must be able to access them easily.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Simplifying applications and providing clearer guidance will be key.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I encourage the Government to continue collaborating with trade associations and chambers to streamline access and advisory support.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, businesses should actively tap into the resources available through organisations like SBF, which play a key role in administering some of these schemes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, longer-term solutions require more than temporary wage offsets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We need job redesign and workplace transformation to fully leverage the experience and capabilities of our senior workers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The planned increase in CPF contribution rates for workers aged 55 to 65 is necessary for retirement adequacy but presents cost considerations for businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While the CPF Transition Offset provides relief, businesses will eventually bear the full impact of higher contributions and rising healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses recognise that seniors bring decades of experience, institutional knowledge and mentorship capabilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, to unlock their value, we need a fundamental shift in how work is structured for them.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That is why the upcoming Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment is so important.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It must go beyond financial incentives and tackle the fundamental issue of job redesign and workplace transformation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: First, flexible work arrangements must become the norm for senior employment.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Many older workers want to stay active in the workforce, but rigid work structures prevent them from doing so effectively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We therefore need more job-sharing, hybrid work models, staggered hours and part-time roles that allow seniors to remain productive without overextending themselves.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The skills landscape is evolving rapidly, and while seniors bring valuable experience, they must be equipped to stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Enhanced Training Support Package should be expanded with practical digital and technical upskilling to help seniors transition into roles that are less physically demanding but still leverage their expertise.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Third, businesses need clearer industry-specific guidelines on how to integrate seniors effectively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Not all industries have the same needs, and we should be looking at sector-based strategies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In knowledge-intensive sectors, seniors can mentor younger employees and provide advisory expertise, like in areas of risk management and succession planning.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In service industries, their experience and interpersonal skills make them well-suited for customer-facing roles.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In technical fields, they can focus on quality assurance, training and oversight.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, I urge businesses, especially SMEs, to see senior employment as an opportunity, not just a necessity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: With manpower shortages, seniors offer stability, knowledge and mentorship, making them a valuable, untapped resource.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond senior employment, I also welcome the Budget’s enhanced support for PwDs transitioning from school to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Like our senior workers, PwDs represent an underutilised talent pool.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Companies that embrace inclusivity will not only benefit from diverse perspectives but will also build more resilient and innovative teams.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But inclusion for seniors and PwDs alone is not enough.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses must also prepare for the seismic shifts brought by technology.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The rapid pace of technological change is reshaping industries and making skills obsolescence a growing concern, not just for rank-and-file workers, but increasingly for professionals.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: AI and automation are redefining job roles, forcing businesses to reassess how they value human capital.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Enterprise transformation and workforce transformation must therefore go hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses adopting new technologies need workers with the right skills, and workers upgrading their capabilities need jobs that make full use of them.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Without this alignment, talent risks being underutilised or displaced.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Rather than focusing primarily on formal courses at IHLs, there should be stronger support for workplace-based training, where skills are immediately applied and training directly addressing business needs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This can be developed in collaboration with trade associations and chambers and can help workers make informed training choices and guide businesses in investing in relevant skills development.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I urge MOE to revisit this proposal and integrate it into the MySkillsFuture portal.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Another refinement is raising targeted subsidies for future-relevant skills.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A tiered subsidy model should also be considered, where an initial batch of trainees receives full funding, provided they complete the course and meet a high passing grade that could also encourage uptake while ensuring accountability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond tapping into our local workforce, we must also recognise the critical role of foreign manpower in sustaining business operations and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has always thrived by remaining open to global talent, and this must remain a key pillar of our economic strategy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Initiatives like the Global Founder Programme, and the Overseas Networks and Expertise (ONE) Pass reflect a clear understanding of the need to attract top talent to drive innovation and growth in key sectors like biosciences, medtech and semi-conductors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Global Founder Programme encourages seasoned builders, operators and innovators to establish their next ventures in Singapore, helping to develop a stronger pool of globally competitive startups and enterprises.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the ONE Pass ensures Singapore remains a top-of-mind destination for high-skilled professionals, securing the expertise needed to maintain our competitive edge.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is equally important to calibrate and track the right skills transfers and innovation to our local workforce and enterprises, enhancing local capabilities and alleviating concerns from Singaporeans about the role of foreign professionals in our economy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Government to continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we push forward in these high-growth areas, we must also address the acute shortages of skilled and semi-skilled workers in foundational sectors like manufacturing, which support these advanced industries.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, I propose four refinements to our foreign manpower policies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, expanding the list of non-traditional source countries for work permit holders to address the drying up of traditional sources like Malaysia and China.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Third, expanding traditional support for companies undergoing transformation, such as conditionally expanding foreign workers dependency ratio ceiling and extending the duration of support under the Manpower for Strategic Economic Priorities Scheme.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Current manpower restrictions prevent businesses from optimising foreign workforce allocation, even when there is clear economic justification to do so.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Government can consider piloting cross-deployment between majority-owned entities across sectors, enabling businesses to re-allocate workers where they are most needed.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Also, by facilitating movement between firms with strategic contractual relationships, such as those in supply chain partnerships or ecosystem clusters, will allow businesses to share manpower resources more effectively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These proposed refinements will not undermine the Government's broader objectives of workforce localisation, but instead, help businesses better utilise existing resources and stay competitive without unnecessary bottlenecks.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While Budget 2025 did not announce specific measures to address this, it is crucial to ensure that industrial land policies continue to support business competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These adjustments would help mitigate the impact of rising land costs and support companies in sustaining their growth and transformation efforts Mr Speaker, Sir, nothing excites the business community than dollars and cents.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Government to consider the management of these funds with private sector players, so that these funds can be deployed effectively to support both large local enterprises as well as our SME ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: He once said, "The political problem of mankind is to combine three things: economic efficiency, social justice and individual liberty." A good Budget is not just about numbers on a spreadsheet.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is a statement of our priorities, a reflection of our values and a commitment to our future.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I am not a politician and do not understand the difference between an election Budget and a non-election Budget.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But I do know this; a good Budget must be fiscally responsible, inclusive and future-ready.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is prudent without being restrictive, supportive without being excessive and strategic without being short-sighted.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It provides immediate relief where needed, invests in long-term competitiveness and ensures that Singapore remains strong, resilient and ready for challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Most importantly, it does all this without compromising the stability of future generations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Let us embrace it, act on it and work together to build a Singapore that continues to thrive, far beyond SG60.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 2.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 2.25 pm until 2.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The world is growing more complex and the impact of global developments are bound to have a significant impact on Singapore, given our dependence on international trade and investment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am heartened by the proposal, such as the increased assistance levels under schemes such as ComCare and the increased Government support under the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, I once again urge the Singapore Government to review the need for a statutory minimum wage to be introduced to ensure that the lowest earners in Singapore will be able to cope better.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They will always worry about bread and butter issues first.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The rising cost of living have been felt more keenly by all Singaporeans in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Taken together, it is clear that Singaporeans want the Government to look beyond the disbursement of payouts to help Singaporeans cope with the cost of living and consider structural changes to existing schemes towards keeping cost of living affordable for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues in the Workers' Party (WP) have floated several proposals in this House on previous occasions – most notably, when we table a Motion calling for the Government to review its policies, so as to lower cost of living pressures on Singaporeans and their families.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There is also a particular subset of this group, one defined by their age, that leaves them in an unenviable position of bearing responsibilities of caring and supporting aged parents as well as young children.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For example, one resident needed legal assistance in a matter involving his brother's insurance claims.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He was deemed ineligible for assistance from the Legal Aid Bureau, but the cost of hiring a lawyer was prohibitive for his family and him.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Another individual informed me that because his household income did not satisfy the means test threshold, his mother was not qualified for MediFund scheme.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He compared himself to his relative, whose elderly mother lives in a rental flat and receive MediFund assistance, even though his relative is more financially secure than he is.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He remarked that by having his mother staying with him and caring for her, he feels that he is being penalised for his filial piety.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In situations like this, Singaporeans in the middle class are like a sandwich without fillings.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They are left with choices they find neither savoury nor sweet.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Trade-offs have to be made and assistance has to be directed to where it is most needed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I also acknowledge that instances such as the ones I have cited may not be representative of the bigger picture.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Even so, when such cases do arise, I hope that the relevant agencies will be able to exercise flexibility and review each case more holistically in assessing an applicant's eligibility for assistance.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The ability to cope with the cost of living is not just a function of the price of goods and services, but also the ability to afford them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A report published by The Straits Times on 8 February 2025, covered the experiences of several Singaporeans who had faced employment disruptions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The report noted that residents' unemployment and long-term unemployment rates remain low and the incidence of discouraged workers was also at a low point.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Economists interviewed for the article noted that even so, there were plausible reasons for job insecurity among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: News of an retention exercises, the increased prevalence of contract work, disruptions caused by technological changes are some of the factors fueling job insecurity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am not against the notion that our workforce needs to remain attuned to the needs of the job market and adequately trained.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I believe we need to take a more proactive approach.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These are worrying statistics and if the downward trend persists in subsequent years, will continue to fuel insecurity among Singaporeans beyond fresh entrance into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I call upon the Government to consider offering incentive schemes to companies that employ more Singaporeans than required by dependency ratio.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This incentive could include tax breaks, reduction in Government charges, or preferential access to state incentive.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On a related note, as the Government invest in making Singapore more attractive to global companies, it should also consider encouraging such companies to play their part in nurturing and developing our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Speaking broadly, Madam, my concern is the mental burden borne by the middle class in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Members of the House would recall the Motion on Mental Health and Well-Being, which was passed in February 2024.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government has also acknowledged the importance of mental health and well-being and have announced several measures to address the matter.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At that time, we would not have been able to withstand the complex global environment without instilling order and efficiency in our society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When people think about Singapore now, what are the images that usually come to mind?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Clean streets, a safe city, strict laws and a stable national system.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In just 60 years, we have transformed into a modern metropolis.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What will be the dreams, aspirations and choices of our people today that will shape our country's future in the next 60 years?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To face our future, I would like to emphasize two things.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, we must also form a new social compact.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This spirit should celebrate the differences in our society and also further strengthen the bonds between all communities, as our pioneers did when they started to build this nation. : Madam, just 60 years ago, it would have been hard to imagine Singapore as the city we are today.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This country was built on the dreams and pragmatic choices our Pioneers made amidst a challenging world order.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We would not have survived the chaos if we did not build order and efficiency into our society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When people think of Singapore today, what picture comes to mind?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Clean streets, safe city, strict laws, stable systems, but what are the dreams, aspirations and choices that will build our next bound?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must ensure that we continue to be a Singapore that can dream of hopeful opportunities, endless possibilities and a future where no one is left behind.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must cultivate a new social compact – one that welcomes diversity and strengthens the bonds between all communities, no matter how different, just as our Pioneers did when they built this nation together.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, we are living longer with innovations in technology that seek to make life better.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In his Budget Statement, the Prime Minister talked about how we ended 2024 on a strong footing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But somehow in coffee shops and online, some sentiments would indicate that life feels otherwise.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans continue to feel the pinch from higher prices, an epidemic of stress plague students and workers and the daily grind somehow does not spark that much joy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The promise of the Singapore dream seems out of reach.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the changing of the guards to our 4G leadership, I hope for a renewed vigour, a cautious optimism amidst the global contest of might, a version 4.0 of the Singapore dream, if you will, where our people can increasingly define success by their own measures, where Singapore can hold multiple versions of life and success that we each want and that there is space for each one of us here; where we lean into our strengths rather than be caged by how society sees weaknesses.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not everyone will start from the same place in life, but having tailored support that can help meet people's needs where they are, in a timely way, is critical and must sit at the centre of the schemes that we design.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Take for example, the dream of a large family.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some young couples in Singapore, this feels out of reach due to the costs associated with raising a child.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every parent wants the best for their child.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also grateful that implementation was immediate, a fairly unusual timeline, but necessarily decisive in the face of our declining TFR.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope we can also do more to support grandparents who often play an important role in caregiving, in terms of learning new skills and forming care networks.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While financial support is important, it is equally crucial to address the underlying issues that makes starting and growing a family so challenging.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I touched on some of these points in my recent speech for the Motion on families: for couples, with fertility health and treatments, as many are getting married later at a later age.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And secondly, while the Government provides significant grants and subsidies for housing, education and healthcare beyond financial costs, the most precious resource of all time is scarce for daddies and mommies to spend with their little ones.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Surveys also reflect that long work hours and stress from work are the top obstacles couples face in getting pregnant.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, we must work towards creating an environment where families feel empowered by the decision to have children.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will not be resolved in one Budget or by the Government alone, but will take a shifting of mindsets in society, support from employers and a redefining of what success looks like beyond the corporate ladder, followed by the ability to live that life on our own terms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As industries evolve and technology becomes more integrated into every sector, middle-aged workers are increasingly finding themselves at crossroads.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some global companies have also decided it no longer makes financial sense to operate some roles in Singapore and instead choose to move to regional neighbours with cheaper labour costs or replace labour with automation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There may be someone else who is cheaper, but given our nimble size, we can be faster, and with Singaporeans' talent, we can be better.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those who lose their jobs, the fear of being left behind is overwhelming.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not just their dreams which are paused, but that of their whole families deferred.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we ensure they are empowered to rejoin the workforce with relevant skills quickly?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a good step, which acknowledges the reality where not everyone can afford to take full-time off.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond structural unemployment and displacement due to cost pressures, some are also forced to slow down due to caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By 2030, around one in four Singaporeans will be 65 and above.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that over time, we can look into doing more for caregivers' mental health and financial well-being, recognising the key role they play.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This leads me to my final group – our seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some are struggling with a reality that they did not foresee.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the idea of life after leaving the workforce was perhaps once associated with relaxation, many find themselves battling poor health and limited financial resources.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A 2023 study by the Singapore Management University's Centre for Research on Successful Ageing revealed that only half of the respondents surveyed felt there was at least a 50% chance they would have to lower their standards of living.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also glad that we have geared up to focus on preventive health to encourage longer health spans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must also extend our reach to those who are isolated, ensuring they have access to the resources they need.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whether that means bringing services to their doorsteps or encouraging them to come out and participate in more inclusive community activities, outreach efforts cannot be touch and go as some seniors may be tentative at first.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope we can find solutions to offer active ageing programmes, mental health services and daily rehabilitative exercises to our seniors in private estates, where the space to build centres is often difficult to find.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would love to see an active ageing centre in a park or utilise a container concept, for example.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These seniors may be deemed asset rich but cash poor and feel left out of various schemes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to hearing more about how the Ministry will be rolling this out and hope we can also increase awareness on support schemes such as the Home Caregiving Grant.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Globally, we see people fragmenting into us versus them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We grow intolerant of different perspectives, focused on the needing to be right and someone else wrong, and in our frustration forget that society is stronger because of diverse views, that the collective pull is stronger than the sum of its parts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Against the odds, we have built a society where different cultures, perspectives and backgrounds have coexisted in relative harmony.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Harmony is not the absence of differences, but what prevails in spite of it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our harmony can only be sustained if we recognise that we are interconnected by the same collective responsibility and have an active citizenry which trusts not just in the Government, but also in each other.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that in the spirit of SG60, more can be done to encourage ground-up activities and programmes in local communities and between different groups.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A social compact is not something bound on paper, nor does it come with an expiration date after a single Budget cycle.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a living, breathing commitment – one that transcends generations, upheld by every government and every citizen.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Budget 2025 is a reaffirmation of this commitment – a promise that the Government is striving to build a society where every individual can thrive regardless of age and circumstance.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For those who laid the foundations of Singapore, for all of us who call this nation home today, and for the generations who will inherit this legacy, we must renew our shared promise and reignite the Singapore dream – to protect and steward the progress we have made, to provide stability and security, even in the most uncertain times, and to break new ground so that future generations can dream even bigger than we ever thought possible.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is the vision that we carry forward for Singapore's future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to participating in the COS debates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the union ground, we see a mixed picture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the one hand, some companies are hiring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the other hand, companies are also doing restructuring and laying off employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, the aerospace industries, while seeing a robust recovery since COVID-19, are also grappling with some of the increase in operational cost as well as difficulty in hiring people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the service sector, unions have reported a more cautious outlook in the domestic F&B as well as retail sectors, citing increasing operational costs as well as competition with our neighbouring countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Even manufacturing companies in some unions are taking a wait-and-see approach, depending on how international trade and tariffs pan out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is therefore reassuring to see a responsive Budget this year that empathises with what our people and our businesses are going through on the ground and tackles them head on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But more importantly, I feel it is also a responsible Budget because it presents long-term strategies for our businesses and our economy, ensuring that they remain competitive and our workers' skills remain up-to-date and relevant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Prime Minister in his speech mentioned that to achieve 2% to 3% annual growth will require us to continue to uphold some fundamentals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One of them is to deepen the tripartite partnership as a cornerstone of economic stability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As Singapore approaches SG60, it is a fitting time to reflect on the pivotal role that NTUC plays in fostering industrial peace and economic stability and in promoting workers’ welfare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Born in the turbulent 1960s, NTUC emerged as a unifying force amidst chaos, rallying unions to prioritise long-term interest and stability over short-term disruptions and gains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Despite being outnumbered by pro-communist unions, NTUC, under leaders like Devan Nair and Ho See Beng, focused on workers' welfare, eventually winning over unions and laying the groundwork for industrial harmony.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Post-Independence, NTUC played a critical role in navigating crises like the British military withdrawal, persuading workers to accept difficult but also necessary changes, such as the Industrial Relations (Amendment) Act, which prioritised stability and investment for the long-term good of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The 1969 Modernisation Seminar marked an important turning point, redefining unions as partners in progress and establishing Singapore's unique tripartite model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Though the COVID-19 crisis seems like a distant memory, it was a severe test of our tripartism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Both our workers' lives and livelihoods were in great danger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC was at the very forefront, securing job stability, wage support and training opportunities for thousands and thousands, particularly in the aviation and aerospace industry as well as retail and for self-employed persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In a recent media article titled "Do Singapore Unions have a PR problem?", my unionists and I acknowledged the image issue that NTUC has and the scepticism shared among some members of the public towards the Labour Movement in view of a spate of high profile layoffs in 2024.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While some of these cases were addressed publicly, the majority, in reality, was negotiated behind the scenes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: After spending nearly three years in NTUC and working alongside many, many union leaders and staff, I am really in full admiration of the relentless, often behind-the-scene, and effective work that goes on and is put in by our union leaders and our NTUC staff – unheralded but nonetheless vigilant bargaining and consensus building to secure the best outcomes for workers of all collars, ages or nationalities while ensuring at the same time that our business and our economic pies continue to grow and expand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Going forward, geo-economic divisions, economic volatility, demographic changes and technological and sustainability advancements will reshape the global labour market, driving changes in job creation, skill demands and work patterns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In this rapidly changing landscape, one thing is clear – the skillsets that brought us success yesterday may not be sufficient to secure our future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To remain competitive, both as individuals and as a nation, we must embrace a culture of innovation, learning and continuous upskilling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These findings reflect the growing recognition of the value of upskilling and reskilling among workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I believe our advocacy for greater training opportunities and the support of the Government on this front have yielded positive results.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I urge more employers to prioritise training initiatives for your employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I hope employers should not be afraid to lose an employee because the employee is better trained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is essential to look beyond the short-term disruptions or losses and invest in the long-term growth and development of all our workers and employees, which ultimately will benefit the entire industry and our economy as a whole.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For SMEs, the increases are slightly lower, from 3.5% to 4.2%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: SMEs cited reasons such as the lack of need for AI due to the scale of their business and perceived high costs of implementation vis-à-vis the return of investment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This raises an urgency for higher AI adoption among local SMEs to reap the benefits of AI and for Singaporeans to be upskilled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The CTC initiative is NTUC's response in 2019 to navigate these rapidly evolving and changing landscapes, supporting our enterprises through enhancing their business productivity and upskilling our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A general manager, Chew Zi Xuan, from Chew's Agriculture, a company that is unionised under my union, the Singapore Industrial and Services Employees' Union, said, "The CTC Grant has been a lifeline for us, ensuring that our older employees retained their jobs while receiving training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They have learned to operate new machinery and conduct quality control checks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This support has made our senior employees feel truly valued and empowered." I am always heartened to hear stories of such positive feedback from the employers of how CTCs has not just benefitted their businesses but also their employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: STMicroelectronics, a global leader in semi-conductors, has been a pillar of Singapore's manufacturing sector since 1969.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Operators at STMicroelectronics were required to manually load and unload wafer cassettes, each weighing up to five kilogrammes, throughout 12-hour shifts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The physical strain led to fatigue, slower production speeds and high turnover rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Recognising the need for change, STMicroelectronics partnered with the United Workers of Electronics and Electrical Industries through the CTC to implement five robotic systems to take over these manual tasks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The robots now operate 22 different machines, running efficiently 24/7, leading to a productivity gain of no less than 10%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But more importantly, workers were not displaced, they were trained in robotic operations, maintenance and Industry 4.0 technologies, preparing them for future higher-value roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The impact on their growth has been very significant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Operators are now progressing to become technicians, technicians to become assistant engineers and assistant engineers to full-fledged engineers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This structured Career Development Plan ensures that workers experience career progression.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the end, 111 employees have benefitted from this initiative, 91 of them PMETs and 20 rank-and-file workers seeing career progression and wage outcomes and directly benefitting from them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are therefore very thankful for the Government to acknowledge our effort in the CTC and announced a top up of $200 million for CTC Grant in the Budget and also extending CTC Grant 2.0 to support employer-led training that leads to formal qualifications and certifications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I urge more companies to come on board, to partner with NTUC, to join us on the CTC journey and leverage on the grants available to accelerate your business transformation and upskill your workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The success of CTCs encouraged us to expand our reach and explore how CTCs can benefit more companies, more clusters or even the entire sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One such example is the formation of the tripartite partnership between NTUC, SkillsFuture Singapore and one company, ST Engineering.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The partnership draws on the synergies between SkillsFuture Singapore's "Queen Bee" programme and NTUC's CTC initiative to deliver comprehensive support for ST Engineering Land Systems and its ecosystem of suppliers in business transformation and workers upgrading.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is also backed by the ST Engineering Staff Union.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is what the CTC is all about: regardless of whether we are supporting a company or a cluster of companies or a sector, future-proofing businesses while uplifting our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Another initiative NTUC have had in place for quite some time to promote upskilling and reskilling is the NTUC-Education and Training Fund Collaborative Fund (NCF) and Union Training Assistance Programme (UTAP) through defraying the cost of training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Unionised companies enjoy an annual $50,000 NCF funding support while union members get to utilise up to $250 or $500 UTAP training credits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One of the workers who benefitted from NCF is Brother Phil, Manufacturing Manager, Operations at Hamilton Sundstrand Pacific Aerospace Pte Ltd.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: At 35 years old and with 11 years of experience in the company, Brother Phil has always been committed to operational excellence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, to take his leadership capabilities to the next level, he needed to strengthen his coaching skills, conflict resolution and performance management skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through the NCF co-funded training, Brother Phil has acquired new soft skills and enhanced his ability to lead teams, foster a positive work culture, and drive innovation and productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the past two Budget speeches, I have called for greater support for mid-career workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We are hopeful that this initiative will encourage mid-career workers to pursue lifelong training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I feel for this group of workers, partly also because we have quite a number of them in Pasir Ris, who are going through a mid-career transition and experiencing both job placement as well as skills upgrading challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I hope that we will continue and NTUC will continue to push for this group to help them pivot their career and also have relevant skillsets to move into a new career.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We have also developed and are using stronger AI platforms to guide jobseekers in their career search.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Ms Angela Guo sought a career switch from F&B to human resources (HR) for better work-life balance and more time with her child.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Despite lacking HR experience, she approached NTUC’s e2i for help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Her career coach, Mr Wang, guided her through an employability programme, providing industry-specific mentorship, resume advice and encouragement to upskill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Angela now is pursuing a part-time HR degree and successfully transitioned into a HR role, achieving her goals while building skills for her new career path.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Job security is key amid technology and industry changes as it provides the stability and the confidence for our employees and our workers to adapt and to grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC will continue to support our workers with initiatives to expand training and upskilling opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Prime Minister Wong's "Onward Together for a Better Tomorrow" Budget not only addresses current challenges but also establishes long-term growth strategies, helping workers upgrade their skills to prepare for the future and ensuring our economy remains competitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Budget has received positive feedback from workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Government has introduced various measures to support mid-career workers, platform workers, freelancers, low-wage workers, young workers and families, middle-age workers for their retirement adequacy and help Singaporeans with the cost of living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These measures and schemes have taken into account workers' views and concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This year, our economy faces many uncertainties, such as inflation triggered by global situations and the impact of disruptive technologies on companies' manpower needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the employment front, businesses are sending mixed signals: some companies are conducting phased retrenchments, while others are actively recruiting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Facing these uncertainties, workers should take the initiative to strengthen themselves and seize economic opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC provides various upgrading and training programmes and I encourage everyone to make full use of them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Since 2019, NTUC has promoted the establishment of the Company Training Committee (CTC) within companies, to enhance employee skills in a targeted manner and facilitate transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We hope that more employees will initiate CTCs to upgrade their skills and strengthen their ability in the future economy and enterprise competitiveness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Another initiative is the NTUC-Education and Training Fund Collaborative Fund (NCF) and the Union Training Assistance Programme (UTAP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Companies that join the union can receive up to $50,000 in NCF funding annually to support training programmes, while unionised employees can receive UTAP training subsidies of $250 or $500.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Fellow workers, these programmes and subsidies are tailored for you, so please make good use of them to upgrade your skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As the saying goes, "30% is destiny, and 70% is hard work".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This hard work includes constantly seeking innovation and change, and learning new skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Let us unite, continue to work hard, upgrade ourselves and create a better future! : As we look ahead, the challenges of the next decade will be unlike those we have faced before.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Yet, the strong foundation of tripartism built by generations of government, employers and union leaders, are well-equipped to navigate this future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC and the Labour Movement remain steadfast to support all our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Whether you are a delivery rider battling the elements on the streets or a mid-career professional adapting to AI, or a senior worker seeking renewed purpose, the Labour Movement fights tirelessly to uplift your voice, to secure your livelihood and to future proof your potential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And on this momentous year of SG60, in solidarity with our tripartite partners, the labour movement will march forward with our workers for our country, Singapore.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We have moved from third world to first world and we have seen our economy improve from a state of bare survival to one of resilience.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Most of us have our basic needs met in housing, education, healthcare and employment.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the continuing global and external uncertainties, we are well positioned to face these challenges together.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Our multiracial and multi-religious society remains cohesive and harmonious and we continue to enjoy political stability, peace and security despite external tensions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We must treasure all this and preserve what has taken decades to build.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I described last year’s Budget under three broad themes.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In Budget 2025, we continue fiscal prudence and good stewardship.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In Budget 2025, we enhance help for many groups.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, being a blessing to one another, sharing as we ourselves have been blessed and how we have also shared beyond our borders.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In Budget 2025, we enhance the spirit of giving.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This year’s forecast surplus is extremely helpful to navigate local and global uncertainties should the need arise.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2025 will enable many to continue to thrive and, at the same time, move others forward to not just survive, but also to thrive.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, we need to recognise there remain vulnerable groups that our current and future policies need to address.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget provides for avenues of support for such persons post-18 years of age and, more specifically, in the area of employment.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must also find avenues for those who may not be in a position to work.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: These individuals also deserve to have access to an acceptable level of quality of life.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It would not be appropriate to see them as a burden to society just because they may not be considered economically productive.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Persons with mental illness are also a broad vulnerable group.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Much has been debated in this House on mental health and well-being and the many interventions we have and continue to introduce.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In previous speeches, I have put to this House specific consideration for better employment support for persons in recovery from mental illness.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Government reconsider the position for support for persons in recovery both by way of some form of disability allowance or support during treatment and rehabilitation when they are unable to work and be gainfully employed, particularly if their financial situation warrants such support?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, would the Government reconsider support for employers of persons in recovery in ways similar to the Enabling Employment Credit and SG Enable grants as it relates to persons diagnosed with a mental health condition?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: And here I would just like to add my appreciation to many employers who are already providing this support by employing persons in recovery.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In some cases, the mental illness may be so debilitating that these individuals require a very long recovery time.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Can we better support them, so no one is left behind?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget continues the advocacy for lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Should we take a closer look at the options and consider where we may need to tailor these for vulnerable groups so that they, too, can benefit?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Persons with intellectual disability or autism may need tailored courses in their adult life.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some may need to, or desire to, to reskill.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we will provide these options, especially where the levels of learning may need to be moderated.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, Mdm Deputy Speaker, may I suggest we provide or expand appropriate skills and other courses for these special groups?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I am pleased to see the inclusion in the support of caregivers.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we will comb through all caregivers progressively and comprehensively and, over time, give them the necessary support.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Suicide is tragic and a most painful encounter, whether by family, friends or communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the increased risk of suicide amongst the elderly.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Suicide cuts across all age groups and all strata of society.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: One suicide affects many, many others, including family, friends and communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There are many who attempt suicide and need support.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Families and friends who care for individuals with suicidal ideation also need support and help.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Project Hayat is a community-led effort guided by a work group comprising policymakers, suicide experts, researchers, community workers and helping professionals, religious leaders, corporate leaders, representatives from the media, and people whose lives have been impacted by suicide.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Project Hayat presented a White Paper to the Government in late-September 2024 covering 23 recommendations for a national suicide prevention strategy in Singapore under the S.A.V.E.L.I.V.E.S framework, using the acronym, each highlighting a specific course of action.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The research conducted for the White Paper included direct interviews with key stakeholders from countries with national suicide prevention strategies, such as Indonesia and South Korea; focus group discussions with people in Singapore who have been directly and indirectly affected by suicide, including parents, youths, educators, first responders, healthcare and emergency services personnel, religious leaders, media representatives; and the first phase of public consultation with more than 500 respondents sharing their views on suicide and suicide prevention.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I understand the Government has provided an initial response to the White Paper through the Minster for Health.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I will expand on three of these groups.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: First, the youths and adolescents as a vulnerable group.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: More than half of the patients had “ambivalent intent”, that is, confused about whether they truly wanted to end their own lives, which highlights impulsivity and the lack of emotional regulation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The study found a predominance of female patients, in this case, 85.5% over male patients.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, focusing on risk factors for females, such as eating disorders and past history of self-harm, can inform risk management strategies in schools and in communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In a 2021 study of non-resident suicides which occurred in Singapore between 2011 and 2014, it was found that most resident suicide cases did not have a known physical or mental health issue, prior to suicide attempts or suicide notes.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Based on the analyses of available suicide notes, relationship and health problems emerged as the top two suspected triggers for suicide.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The researchers, therefore, hypothesised that the unique situation of working abroad may increase non-residents’ vulnerability in general, while adverse life events, such as relationship and health issues, may be too overwhelming to bear, especially when support services are not readily available and accessible.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The third vulnerable group identified in this White Paper, the neurodiverse population, I will just share an anecdote from the parents who lost their child who had autism spectrum disorder (ASD) to suicide and recounted this in the focus group discussions: “I don’t think he can understand why he cannot seem to get along as well with other children as maybe his classmates can, so I think there’s also the feeling of rejection….

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I always thought that if he had managed to live to COVID, perhaps he would still be alive, because we are all just in our safe little space, he doesn't have to go out and socialise.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I always wish that he had that two extra years,   just didn’t happen.” Three other vulnerable groups identified in the White Paper include the elderly, caregivers and lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBTQ) community.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: A key feature of suicide prevention efforts across the world is to ensure that people who have been affected by suicide are involved in all aspects of suicide prevention, including policymaking, implementation, research and advocacy.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Involving individuals who belong to communities at greater risk of suicide, survivors of suicide, and those who have lived experiences of suicide is essential in bridging gaps in suicide prevention.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We need to value data and research: investing in research on the upstream determinants of suicide amongst the vulnerable groups, and to conduct further research to determine additional priority groups in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There is a strong link between upstream factors and social determinants that heighten suicide risks among vulnerable groups and those who are experiencing loneliness or hopelessness in their lives.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: More research is required on priority populations that are at greater risk of mental health challenges, self-injury or suicide and to develop evidence-based interventions that are tailored for these respective communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Another recommendation is to involve families and communities: strengthening family support initiatives to manage mental health and suicide prevention, and strengthening collaboration with religious and community leaders.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Family-focused programmes should be developed to equip families with the knowledge and skills to recognise early signs of distress, facilitate open and supportive communication, and offer practical strategies to assist loved ones facing mental health struggles.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As trusted figures within communities, religious and community leaders hold significant influence and are often seen as sources of support and guidance, making them well-positioned to promote mental health awareness and reduce the stigma surrounding suicide.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Leaders can foster an environment of compassion, understanding and acceptance to reduce stigma, as well as play a key role in identifying individuals at risk and providing timely support.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: And this would involve equipping school staff with the tools to recognise early signs of distress, intervene appropriately, and provide ongoing support to students facing mental health challenges.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I have covered those with mental health conditions, persons with disability and special needs, caregivers and proposed for more to be done to prevent suicide.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We will need to work together, Government and society, to ensure no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Just like our nation, this will have taken time, most likely decades of tireless efforts of dedicated individuals and the supporters, including Government and private donors —

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Chua, you have one and a half minutes, so I would ask you to round up.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Our charities, both large and small, continue to form part of our social support network, providing daily care to many beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: We are an increasingly caring and generous society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is a Budget that prioritises uplifting all Singaporeans, including our lower-wage workers, by strengthening social safety nets and ensuring sustainable economic growth.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we move forward, it is crucial to reinforce our commitment to these workers, ensuring that they receive fair wages, improved working conditions and the respect they deserve.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore's approach to uplifting lower-wage workers has never relied on a single measure, but rather a comprehensive suite of interventions, including the PWM, the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS), Workfare Skills Support (WSS) and the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS).

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These policies form the foundation of our commitment to ensuring sustainable and inclusive wage growth for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Today, I want to focus on the following three areas to strengthen the protections for our workers, especially lower-wage workers: one, enhancing Workfare to boost retirement adequacy of older lower-wage workers; two, improving working conditions for lower-wage workers, especially outsourced workers; and three, empowering workers via M3 Focus Area 4 (FA4).

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As economies evolve, workers, especially those in lower-wage roles, must be empowered with better protections, stronger financial security and opportunities for long term stability.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Enhancing Workfare schemes can provide older, lower-wage workers with greater retirement adequacy, ensuring that they can transition into later years with dignity.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, improving working conditions, particularly for outsourced workers, is crucial to fostering fair and sustainable employment practices.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Together, these focus areas aim to build a resilient and inclusive workforce that can thrive in a rapidly changing economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: WIS plays a crucial role in supplementing the income and retirement savings of lower-wage workers while encouraging regular employment.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am also heartened to note that most of these enhancements are targeted at vulnerable groups, such as our older workers and PwDs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As the Government regularly reviews Workfare, I seek an assessment of how effective WIS has been in improving the wages and retirement adequacy of lower-wage workers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We must also do more to secure the long-term financial well-being of our older lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many lower-wage workers retire with significantly lower CPF savings, affecting their ability to afford healthcare and daily necessities in their later years.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I urge the Government to introduce additional age tiers beyond 60, with progressively higher WIS payments, to better support older workers who remain active in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Additionally, the minimum WIS payout, in both cash and CPF, is just $10 per month.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Given the rising costs of living, I urge the Government to review and raise this amount to provide more meaningful support for workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: LQS ensures that local workers are employed meaningfully, rather than on token salaries for firms to access foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, I call on the Government to update on the effectiveness of LQS since it was introduced and whether its implementation has led to unintended consequences, such as job losses.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In particular, I hope that LQS has truly contributed to raising wages for lower-wage workers across the board and that the data does reflect this desired trajectory too.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Relatedly, it would be helpful for the Government to clarify its broader policy approach towards LQS implementation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For instance, the wage percentile of which LQS should be set at to effectively support our resident lower-wage workers while balancing against business costs and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While we have made progress in uplifting wages, we must ensure that lower-wage workers have good working conditions and are not taken advantage of.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One critical issue is the need for proper, accessible rest areas for outsourced workers, such as the cleaners and security officers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many of these workers still struggle to find adequate spaces to rest during their breaks.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The lack of rest areas can result in them working beyond their maximum cap of overtime, which is 72 hours every month for security officers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I ask the Minister for Manpower whether a review of the criteria and eligibility for the WorkCare Grant has been conducted?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Would the Government consider upstream policy measures, such as exempting dedicated rest areas for outsourced workers from the Gross Floor Area (GFA) calculation for new developments?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This could incentivise building owners and developers to incorporate proper rest facilities at the planning stage.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Another persistent issue is the leave resetting for outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many of these are lower-wage and outsourced workers, such as cleaners and security officers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This creates instability, as workers may repeatedly lose accrued benefits despite continuing in the same role.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay): The evolving global economy and rapid technological advancements demand that we equip our workforce with the necessary skills and career mobility to thrive.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Focus Area 4 (FA4) on Employment and Employability of M3 provides a structured framework to achieve this goal through several strategies.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: First, FA4 connects workers by facilitating access to job openings, understanding industry needs and providing career guidance.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It ensures that individuals are matched with suitable career pathways for long-term growth, not just filling job vacancies.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Through initiatives, such as job fairs, career counselling, workshops and industry partnerships, we can help workers transition effectively into sustainable employment.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Second, skills upgrading and lifelong learning are key.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In recognising that the skills required in today's economy are constantly evolving, especially in the green, digital, and care sectors, we must empower individuals to adapt to changing job requirements and remain competitive in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Training programmes and upskilling initiatives must be designed to bridge skill gaps and prepare workers for emerging industries.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
