text: FA4 also focuses on helping individuals navigate changes and build resilience.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This includes digital literacy training, promoting competencies relevant to the digital economy and providing support for workers transitioning to new industries.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Allow me to outline our key priorities which will focus our efforts and resources on three crucial workforce groups namely: platform workers, mid-career switchers (PMEs) and senior workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These three groups represent vital segments of our economy, each with unique needs and challenges.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We recognize the valuable contributions of platform workers, the potential of our PMEs navigating career transitions and the wealth of experience that our senior workers bring.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is imperative that we support and empower each of these groups to thrive in our evolving economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By doing so, we can future-proof our workforce and ensure every worker has access to meaningful employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): Madam, "Onward Together for a Better Tomorrow" is more than just a theme; it is a vision for an inclusive and progressive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This year's Budget lays a strong foundation for uplifting lower-wage workers, strengthening retirement adequacy and improving working conditions.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It also reinforces the values of dignity, respect and fairness for all workers, regardless of their job.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Beyond lower-wage workers, the Budget also addresses the needs of families, businesses and our economy, ensuring that Singapore continues to thrive in a rapidly changing world.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is a comprehensive plan and supports many facets of our society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: With unwavering dedication, the NTUC stands ready to champion the needs and the interests of our Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC continues to advocate for our lower-wage workers, to better their lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC cares and is taking action to enhance their working conditions and welfare.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Rest assured, NTUC will take action for you and with you.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For these reasons, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some are in industries that are shrinking or being disrupted, where jobs are disappearing faster than new ones are created.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Others see their roles changing because of automation or AI.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some even face the anxiety of being told to reapply for their own jobs as part of restructuring exercises, effectively forcing them to compete with their colleagues or external candidates for roles they have already been performing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such practices not only create stress and uncertainty but also serve as a way for companies to bypass retrenchment obligations while reshuffling their workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While overall employment levels have continued to rise in tandem with the growing population, some displaced workers face difficulties transitioning into a new job at the same skill level and salary.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many struggle to break into growth sectors despite efforts to reskill, as employers often favour candidates with industry-specific experience or are younger.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While most employers prioritise merit, some hiring processes may still be influenced by informal networks, creating additional challenges for mid-career jobseekers trying to break into new industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The data also shows that long-term unemployment affects PMETS more than non-PMETS.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These PMETS are workers who have spent decades in their industries, built up expertise and contributed to the economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many have significant financial responsibilities, including housing loans, children's education and elderly parents to care for.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When these PMETS get retrenched or step away from the workforce for a period due to caregiving responsibilities, re-entering the job market becomes a daunting challenge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even those who are currently employed may be preoccupied with day-to-day operational work and get blindsided by technological changes that make their skills obsolete.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A worker who has spent years in corporate operations, for instance, may find it difficult to transition to a technology-driven role without a structured pathway to bridge the gap.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even if they secure interviews, they are often offered roles at significantly reduced salaries, making it difficult to maintain their financial obligations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some are forced into contract or gig work, with little stability or opportunities for development.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The longer they remain unemployed or underemployed, the harder it becomes to re-enter the workforce, as employers perceive them as outdated or overqualified, rather than seeing the value of their accumulated skills or experience.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some may drop out of the workforce completely after years of discouragement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government has introduced several schemes to help workers upgrade their skills and transition to new jobs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On top of that, career matching services run by Workforce Singapore and its partners help jobseekers refine their resumes and prepare for interviews and, in the future, as announced in this Budget, there will be an expanded network of job placement centres at all CDCs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are important steps, but more needs to be done to ensure mid-career workers secure meaningful employment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Training and reskilling alone do not ensure job placement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For mid-career workers facing immediate job displacement, waiting years for the benefits of these programmes to materialise is not a viable option.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many are unable to afford the temporary drop in income that often comes with switching sectors, often making it difficult for them to commit to full-time training programmes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While some industries are shrinking, others, including healthcare, sustainability and advanced manufacturing, are expanding.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mid-career PMETs should have clearer pathways to transition to these high-demand sectors through structured job placement and industry partnerships.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Career Conversion Programme (CCP) is designed to help mid-career individuals transition into new jobs or sectors with better long-term prospects through training and salary support.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, there still remain deeper structural barriers that make it difficult for these workers to secure new jobs at comparable skill levels and salaries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need a more structured and targeted job placement programme, where mid-career jobseekers can have their applications and CVs reviewed and refined by specialists in their field.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These specialists can then actively match and recommend them to employers, including those enrolled in the CCP, increasing their chances of securing a placement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Once hired, these workers can then benefit from the CCP to receive the necessary training and salary support for a smoother transition into their new roles.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They have spent years contributing to the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many have built businesses, trained younger colleagues and helped shape their industries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us give every Singaporean who wants to work, retrain and contribute, the best possible chance to do so.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is the second Budget advancing Forward Singapore to renew our social compact for a stronger and more united society, with Prime Minister Lawrence Wong at the helm.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: By reaffirming Singapore’s resilience and unity as we celebrate SG60, Budget 2025 has outlined key strategies to uplift livelihoods, strengthen our economy and reinforce our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As Singapore sails ahead in increasingly choppy waters, it is imperative that we remain resilient in uncertainty and find strength in unity.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To this end, I wish to highlight three key themes related to Budget 2025: first, upholding fiscal prudence in a volatile world; second, growing Singapore’s economy; and third, doubling down on social resilience and safety.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A recent OECD report commended Singapore’s robust fiscal framework, which has given us the strength to navigate uncertainties more effectively than other nations.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Especially for a small country like Singapore, the Ukraine situation is a stark reminder that we can only count on our own people and financial resources in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This principle is now set against the backdrop of an external environment fraught with risks, intensified geopolitical rivalry and evolving trade wars.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Recognising cost of living concerns faced by Singaporeans, I welcome the additional measures to provide relief, such as the enhanced CDC Vouchers, as part of the Assurance Package that continues to make our GST scheme a progressive one when viewed holistically.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Taken together with the SG60 package, this is akin to a “Singapore Dividend”, where every citizen shares in our nation’s success, with those who need more help receiving greater support.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A basic financial planning concept is that in the long run, certain expenditures must be matched with equally certain revenue streams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Hong Kong’s challenges in balancing its budget is due to its narrow tax base and reliance on tax collection from its cyclical real estate sector.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To criticise the GST increase because of recent fiscal surpluses misses this fundamental point and takes only a limited view of the overall GST scheme.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As a finance professional, the fiscal surplus, whether expected or unexpected, speaks to a prudent and conservative approach, which I believe all sensible financial experts, with a heavy responsibility of a stewardship role, would adopt.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is the basic value system of not spending more than one has.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To me, the more important question is how we will use these surpluses to further enhance our infrastructure and capabilities for Singapore to be an even more vibrant financial centre, compelling tourist destination and flourishing metropolis.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond Terminal 5, there are many, many exciting plans shared previously that can be accelerated, such as redeveloping Paya Lebar and the Jurong Innovation district, revitalising Clarke Quay and boosting our arts scene to achieve what London is to Europe.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to the Prime Minister’s sharing of his insights on these aspects and would like to ask if there will be enhancements to Forward SG’s plans, given a global landscape that is now more complex than when it was first launched, and what is the Government’s thinking to realise those plans faster.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given prevailing global uncertainties that may slow long-term returns, and the already modest GDP projections for 2025, can the Prime Minister share his insights about MOF’s assumptions on why this is so?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Also, if indeed surpluses are expected to continue, are there opportunities to recalibrate the pace and amount of taxation to allow markets to be more efficient, and to ease rent and labour cost pressures while still upholding fiscal prudence?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It enables job creation, social mobility and sustained prosperity.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I am glad that Budget 2025 has introduced several initiatives to support businesses and enhance our financial markets.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: SMEs remain the backbone of our economy, contributing nearly half of GDP and employing 70% of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond financial incentives, it is essential that SMEs are uplifted with the know-how in the advent of AI and have a clearer commitment and path towards sustainability.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Workers, too, need to adapt as the world rapidly transforms.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While Singapore has made strides in digital adoption, many SMEs still face resource constraints and expertise gaps.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, can the Prime Minister provide assurance on stronger safety nets to support SMEs and workers who face challenges in keeping pace with technological advancements?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Aligned with Forward SG’s plans, how may we better ease such anxieties and increase effectiveness in upskilling?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: At the upcoming COS debate, I plan to seek clarifications if more support will be provided to SMEs to accelerate AI adoption, develop customised AI solutions and facilitate collaborations with research institutions to pilot new innovations.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On sustainability, while Singapore is committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, we must balance this with shifting economic and political realities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Significant changes in global trends, including the US’ withdrawal from the Paris Climate Agreement and major banks pulling out of the Net-Zero Banking Alliance, highlight the complexities of decarbonisation commitments.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While I agree with the Government’s directions to play our part to decarbonise, global developments are confusing.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses will wonder if these costs will eventually pay off, in the face of mixed signals on the world’s fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Against this shifting backdrop, can Government clarify its stance on our green transition; whether there will be a recalibration to our earlier planned pace and trajectory so that SMEs can manage the associated costs better and be incentivised to progressed on their decarbonisation journey?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I will at COS, seek additional support for business to do so and clarifications if revenues collected from carbon tax will be reinvested to assist SMEs in adopting decarbonisation practices.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In strengthening financial markets, I strongly support the Government’s moves to revitalise the Singapore Exchange (SGX) to further enhance our status as an international financial centre.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, I strongly advocate the adoption of an ecosystem approach in this endeavour.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This could include: one, plugging in specific high-growth sectors that the Government is already supporting, like pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and precision engineering; two, encouraging Singapore-based flagship companies, or companies owned by Singaporeans or new Singaporeans who are on the Forbes list, to list or dual-list on SGX; and three, urging family offices and high-net-worth individuals to list or dual list their businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore must also stay flexible to seize emerging opportunities amid volatility.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone exemplifies this strategic flexibility, aiming to enhance economic resilience and deepen bilateral relationships.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, we must ensure this collaboration does not compromise Singapore's competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Learning from the experience of Hong Kong and Shenzhen, the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone should complement Singapore's strengths, so that it is a win-win situation for both countries.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Today, threats such as scams, drug abuse, fire hazards and radicalisation pose growing risks to our communities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While our nation remains one of the safest in the world, recent trends highlight areas where more measures are necessary.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Particularly troubling is that over 80% of scam cases now involve "self-effected" transfers, highlighting how criminals exploit human psychology and AI-driven deception.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, the increasing prevalence of youths’ engagement with harmful substances necessitate stronger mitigating strategies.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is despite enhanced measures by our agencies.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This trend is compounded by the emergence of harmful vapourisers which contain drugs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government to step up inter-agency collaborations, such as among the Central Narcotics Bureau, Health Sciences Agency and schools to guide our youths towards healthier paths.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Regarding community cohesion, neighbourhood disputes continue to be high, with monthly noise-related feedback at over 2,100, and this number remains more than five times that in 2019.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is deeply concerning that some of these neighbour disputes have escalated into violence, with a few having serious outcomes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This highlights the critical need for robust resolution mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The passage of the Community Disputes Resolution (Amendment) Bill that has now come into law will strengthen mediation and community engagement efforts.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to its early pilot and hope we can scale the measures island wide faster so more residents and neighbours, including those at Nee Soon, can benefit sooner.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Building a safer and more cohesive Singapore is a shared responsibility and I look forward to speaking more on these at the COS debates.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Amid turbulence, Forward SG charts our path ahead, ensuring that every Singaporean has a meaningful stake in our future.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As we mark SG60, Budget 2025 is a reminder of how far we have come as a nation, built on the collective determination of our people.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As it is said, we cannot direct the wind, but we can adjust our sails.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We can confront challenges ahead with confidence, knowing that Singapore has always found resilience in uncertainty and strength in unity.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Let us remain steadfast and bold in shaping a brighter and more inclusive future.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Let us move Onward Together for a Better Tomorrow!

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In this 14th Term of Parliament, our Government has also consistently kept young workers at the centre of our national policies.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate that Budget 2025 would enhance existing programmes and introduce new initiatives, such as the Large Families Scheme, that respond to Singaporeans' changing aspirations and needs as well as the SG Culture Pass, an ActiveSG credit top-up that will boost interest and careers in arts, heritage and sports.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It will set our sails to catch favouring winds as we forge ahead in an uncertain economic climate.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Even then, social and economic changes are uneven and unsettling, for vulnerable Singaporeans more so than others.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A 2022 Harvard Business Review article on perceived job insecurity among American workers sets the impact in context, "Whether you've been laid off, downsized, forced to take early retirement, or seen contract work dry up, losing your employment is one of life's most stressful experience.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Aside from the obvious financial anguish it can cause, the stress of losing a job can also take a heavy toll on your mood, relationships and overall mental and emotional health." In Singapore's context, who are the emerging groups of vulnerable workers where we must lean forward?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Two groups come to mind: those who could be hit hard by layoffs when their employers re-organise or restructure and those would be hard-hit by market shifts, such as freelancers and agency workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Both groups see the same overcast on the horizon – that of possible job loss.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, those who could be hit hard if companies re-organise or restructure and take the decision to lay off staff.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A mother and daughter sat close to me at a crowded food shop.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I caught this remark by the daughter, a lady in her thirties. "我最怕的就是裁员", which translates to "I am most fearful of being retrenched." Retrenchment is a heavy topic for mealtime conversations.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is a topic that is increasingly par for the course as firms push ahead with merger and acquisition (M&A) and business reorganisation and restructuring.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: No age group of workers is immune to retrenchment.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us strive for immunity by working harder, often at the expense of our health.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: If the Government, employers and unions fail to recognise and respond to the prevalent perception of job insecurity, workers can become increasingly stressed and disillusioned.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, those who would be hard-hit by market shifts.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In July 2024, Hollywood video game performers went on strike to seek fair artificial intelligence regulations for the gaming industry because performers asserted that gaming companies had condoned replicating of performers' likeness and voices without informed consent and fair compensation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because performers were largely freelancers and paid by the hour, their incomes took a hit when companies reduced contracted hours in favour of exploiting AI as a substitute.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: If service buyers fail to respect and uphold fair use of AI, creative freelancers will become increasingly vulnerable to diminishing earnings and prospects.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from creative freelancers, agency workers could be hard-hit when user firms respond to market shifts.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: User firms hire agency workers on temporary basis for projects and specific roles where these workers' skills are needed.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many agency workers service hotels, F&B, supermarkets, e-commerce logistics and banks.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike in the past, when companies turned to staffing agencies as stop gaps, companies are increasingly hiring agency workers as a shortcut to organisational flexibility and fluidity.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In a 2021 article by The Bureau of Investigative Journalism, Matt Creagh, a UK Trades Union Congress employment rights policy officer said, "It's easy for employers to hire agency workers because you don't have the fixed costs of a directly employed workforce and it's much easier to fire an agency worker.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The pace of change is accelerating and will hit home for workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: How might we lean forward to protect and uplift this emerging vulnerable workforce?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Separate reports from the World Employment Confederation and the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs point to two trends taking root this year: one more companies will strive to build flexibility into the workforce; and two, more companies will seek to exploit AI at functional levels.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Together, these trends will disrupt how work is done and valued.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, Singapore must press on with innovation and growth to counteract the demographically-driven reduction in innovation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In 2010, Japanese inventors were the biggest producers of patents in 35 global industries.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Economist linked Japan's decline in disruptive innovation to its demographic decline, which, in turn, was an outcome of falling total fertility rate and limited immigration.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore must press on with innovation efforts to counteract demographically-driven reduction in innovation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation raises productivity and, ultimately, standards of living.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Progressive, because the Budget allocates significant funds to reinforce innovation and technology as engines of growth for the economy and enterprises.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget also offers financial incentives and tax perks that encourage businesses to grow strategically through M&A and significant grants to transform jobs and upgrade workforce capabilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Protective, because the Budget also allocates significant funds for various employment credit schemes and the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme that reinforce employment of vulnerable segments, including lower-wage workers, senior workers, persons with disabilities and ex-offenders.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Budget also defrays cost of part-time long-form training programmes for Singaporeans aged 40 and above and enhances the training allowance for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Together with the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme that was announced in 2024, Budget 2025 will improve employment and employability outcomes for these groups.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, the paradigm of job security is changing.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us, including the lady I met at the food shop, are still struggling to make sense of it.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We struggle because being uncertain about our job security makes us feel helpless.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Feeling helpless goes against the ethos of self-resilience ingrained in Singaporeans from young.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Our ethos compels us to show that we can deal with all curveballs, to the extent that we might hold ourselves accountable if our jobs are made redundant.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We pride ourselves in taking tough times in stride, but this ease is built up when we endure hardship.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It is not easy holding ourselves up when life deals us a low blow that knocks the wind right out of us.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, it does not matter whether we lose our jobs because of a layoff or, in the case of freelancers and agency workers, cancellation of assignments.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Job loss is a blow that inflicts extended psychological, emotional and financial pain.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because we extol self-reliance, even in such situations, we hesitate to seek help.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We can do more to lean forward to protect and uplift Singaporeans who are emerging vulnerable workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Alongside clarifications, I would like to offer three suggestions of how we could lean forward as a country.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, reframe self-resilience so that seeking help is not a sign of weakness but an affirmation of courage and determination.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The experience of losing a job is distressing, especially when dependents look to us for finances, care and support.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Some who lost their jobs have to care for aged parents.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Government consider applying flexibility to the income criteria of the basket of support for families schemes?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This would allow a worker who is involuntarily unemployed or a freelancer who can prove significant loss in average monthly net trade income compared to the past two years to still qualify for the schemes if they fulfil all other criteria sans the income criteria.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Doing so could further encourage retrenched workers to apply for the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme, particularly professionals, managers and executives.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It would be helpful if scheme applicants could be concurrently linked with other assistance, such as subsidised counselling support as well as workplace advisory for those who exited on unfair terms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, reframe shared accountability so that enterprises and workers are committed to upholding the social compact.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, agency workers often slip beneath the radar when it comes to upskilling.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because agency workers are hired by staffing agencies but report for work at user firms, agency workers' training needs are often overlooked.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, as a unionist interacting with firms, I observed that firms expressed enthusiasm when discussing the use of the CTC Grant for new systems or technology but needed more persuasion when the union broached job redesign or training.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In response, I share my takeaway from the book "Good to Great" by business researcher Jim Collins.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Grants can help firms to bring in the right technology to jumpstart productivity.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To scale and sustain, businesses must "have the right people on the bus".

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: My pitch to bosses: tap on the CTC grant.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Through this approach, we can encourage more firms to practise fair and reasonable employment and hiring, redesign jobs to raise job worth, train lower-skilled workers, including agency workers in the firm as well as start programmes to attract and develop Singaporean talent.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Doing so would reinforce shared accountability to develop and value Singapore workers and uplift the workforce across the board.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, reframe shared responsibility so that the lead Government agencies are motivated to co-shape development roadmaps with unions, employers and relevant fellow agencies as core stakeholders.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, as a unionist representing workers in the food sectors, I note that stakeholders in the food sectors must contend with concurrent developments in the food space, such as the new Food Safety and Security Act and developments in the manpower space, such as the Progressive Wage Model for the food services sector, foreign manpower regulations, Workplace Fairness Act and flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As agencies' priorities do overlap, it would be helpful for lead agencies to engage the core unions and employer groups from the outset when the agencies set goals and design regulatory implementation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Doing so would ensure that workers' interests are equally valued.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A similar approach could apply for areas that impact broad swathes of workers across sectors including PwDs, agency workers and freelancers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As the economy evolves, these groups might become even more vulnerable if they lack updated work protection and training.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, lead Ministries and agencies could initiate multi-stakeholder workgroups to discuss protection and provisions for emerging vulnerable groups.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Agency workers too count on the Government to look out for them, particularly those engaged by user firms that fall under the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Strengthening legal protection for these emerging vulnerable workers would provide them with a peace of mind.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, allow me to share a verse by 19th century American poet Ella Wheeler Wilcox titled “The Winds of Fate”. "One ship drives east and another drives west With the self-same winds that blow. ‘Tis the set of the sails And not the gales Which tells us the way to go.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Like the winds of the sea are the winds of fate, As we voyage along through life, ‘Tis the set of a soul That decides its goal And not the calm or the strife." We are at the turning of a chapter in Singapore’s journey.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: If we unite as a people, SG60 can be one defined by resilience that is empathetic as well as a shared accountability and responsibility for the growth and well-being of fellow Singaporeans, particularly those who are more vulnerable.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Whether we are the Government, business owners, employers, unions or workers, the choice is upon us to be the heroes of our own story.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For the past 60 years, through solidarity with workers, Singapore has overcome economic hardships, achieved higher wages, stronger labour protections and expanded opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This unity remains key to our success and shared prosperity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Amidst global trade tensions, rising costs and rapid technological change, we must remain steadfast in our commitment to ensure that no worker is left behind but instead equipped with the skills and protections needed to thrive in an evolving economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is therefore critical that this momentous 3C Budget recognises that sustainable growth is only made possible when workers are fairly compensated, their rights are protected, and their well-being is prioritised.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To this end, I will focus my speech on what I call strengthening the 3 "Cs": core, competency and capability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, strengthening the Singaporean Core; second, strengthening the workers' compact; and third, strengthening human capital capabilities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The first "C" – strengthening the Singaporean Core, is a call I have persistently made since my maiden speech in Parliament in 2011.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Since then, I have had many conversations with Singaporean workers and have heard their fears and anxieties about growing competition with foreign manpower, especially the PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They worry about job displacement, stagnant wages and having fewer opportunities to advance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These sentiments were echoed during NTUC’s engagements with about 10,000 Singaporean PMEs through the Joint NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce, which I co-chaired with the Singapore National Employers' Federation (SNEF) in the midst of the pandemic from 2020 to 2021.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Act also strengthens unions’ capabilities to represent our members by conferring an expanded suite of individual remedies and penalties for discriminatory employment practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The current economic climate is an uncertain one and challenges lie ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Last year, we saw many high-profile retrenchment exercises impact local PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Following trends like generative AI and geopolitical turbulence, we can expect the same this year.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must take a proactive approach to protect local jobs and invest in skills training so that our workers remain ready, relevant and resilient.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Ready with the new skills, relevant to the new jobs and resilient to the new changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC has always continued to work closely and do more for PMEs to enhance their job security and ensure fair job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In 2020, NTUC proposed a Fair Retrenchment Framework outlining three key principles to guide companies on responsible retrenchment practices, the first of which is "Protecting the Singaporean Core" by helping Singaporeans keep their jobs while due considerations are given to foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This Framework was then incorporated into the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Foreign manpower can help fill critical skill gaps and support sectors facing labour shortage, but we cannot over-rely on external labour.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must also take a concerted effort to build our local bench strength.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A stronger Singaporean Core means a stronger economy for Singapore, one that is more competitive and less reliant on external labour.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Beyond fair opportunities, we also need to ensure quality opportunities for Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This means good wages, good welfare, good work prospects, workplaces free from discrimination and harassment and more meaningful tasks at work so that we fully maximise the true potential of every Singaporean worker.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Supporting local employment must be a strategic priority for the Government to help Singaporeans, especially Singaporean workers earn a better living and live a better life.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The second "C" I want to highlight is strengthening the workers' compact.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In 2023, after a year-long engagement with over 42,000 workers through the #EveryWorkerMattersConversations, NTUC released its renewed workers' compact with recommendations for five groups of workers, including mid-career workers, older workers and vulnerable workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One of the recommendations from the workers' compact as well as the NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce was short-term unemployment support for the involuntarily unemployed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Amongst PMEs, those aged 50 to 59 were most likely to be concerned.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I therefore continue to call the Government to consider extending the Jobseeker Support Scheme eligibility to mid-career and senior workers in the broad middle.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Mid-career PMEs is a worker segment that I have consistently advocated for.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This group faces unique challenges but can receive less support from the Government in view of their higher income.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Mid-career PMEs often struggle with stagnation in career progression, or job instability as industries transform.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While they typically have more dependents to take care of as part of the "sandwiched generation", they can take a longer time to find a new job when they become unemployed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Upon re-entry to employment, there is also an increasing propensity for them to suffer from wage loss.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: NTUC’s 2022 #EveryWorkerMatters Conversations Survey had revealed that mid-career workers, defined as aged 30 to early 50s, experienced a relatively higher level of anxiety about jobs as compared to younger and older age groups.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The same report also found that six in 10 Singapore firms have identified skills gaps as a potential barrier to their business transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The SkillsFuture Level-Up programme is thus a positive step towards enhancing career mobility for mid-career PMEs, enabling them to deepen their skills and pivot into new growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A next step could be expanding career conversion programmes tailored specifically for experienced professionals transitioning into new industries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Workers could also be given the option to tap on SkillsFuture credits for career coaching and mentorship, which would benefit mid-careerists navigating upskilling or a career transition.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this regard, NTUC is innovating, together with PMEs, to tailor support needed for job placements and career coaching.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With regard to older workers and vulnerable workers, I recognise the Government’s efforts in enhancing the Workfare Skills Support scheme for lower-wage workers aged 30 and above, as well as the extension of the Senior Employment Credit for older workers, uplifting Employment Credit for ex-offenders and Enabling Employment Credit for Persons with Disabilities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I hope the Government continues to strengthen the workers' compact by empowering these workers in their upskilling aspirations and transition into more resilient career pathways by creating support ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: My third and final "C" is strengthening human capability, which is critical as we adapt to the "new normal" of work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Last Thursday, I had an opportunity to speak to and engage with a group of senior HR leaders and head honchos during an event organised by the Institute of Human Resource Professionals (IHRP).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Collectively, we agree that HR and human capital professionals play a vital role in ensuring fair, progressive and responsible practices for their workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is therefore critical that HR professionals are well-equipped with a strong knowledge of not only Singapore’s employment legislation and regulations, but also the Labour Movement, tripartism and wider tripartite framework, including how to build more progressive workplace practices and workplaces that uphold the values of diversity, equity and inclusion.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is especially critical for MNCs employing foreign HR professionals who operate within and beyond the Singapore context.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Following the rise of Automated Employment Decision Tools (AEDT), which are AI technologies that substantially assist or replace discretionary decision-making in hiring or promotions, I also submit that guidelines or regulations be introduced to ensure companies and HR's responsible use of AI.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Measures, such as requiring companies to conduct a third-party bias audit or to disclose where such tools are used to rank candidates or assess employees for promotion or even dismissal, could be considered.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In an evolving economic, demographic and regulatory landscape, and after what we witnessed during the pandemic, HR professionals are increasingly playing a strategic role in key business decisions and, hopefully, more in the boardroom as well as in addition to operations and compliance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Strengthening our human capital capability and leadership as well as developing the NextGen HR leadership pipeline not only ensures that businesses attract, develop and retain top local talent, but they also foster progressive and inclusive workplaces that support workers at all levels.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is to also reaffirm our commitment to safeguarding Singaporean workers' lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, the nature of work, workplaces and workforce have changed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: That same solidarity must guide us now as we advance our growth frontier in an inclusive way, so that we move onward together for a better tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And just like in previous Budgets, by successive PAP Governments, over the past many decades.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We have come to expect our Budgets to look and smell like this, but really, we should never take it for granted.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because it speaks of a special brand of governance and political leadership that we have been fortunate to have here in Singapore, a special political will to do right by our people and a special compact between the political leadership and citizens.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If elections were really the prime motivation behind this Budget, the Government must be mad to not have spent down more of this surplus on short-term measures, whether cash or vouchers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think, very simply, because it allows this Government to achieve a more or less balanced fiscal position, over its whole term of Government, from 2020 to 2025, if we exclude the amount drawn down from past Reserves in this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The COVID-era Budgets may be quite a distant memory already for some, but back in FY2020, just five years ago, at the start of this Government's term, we incurred an unprecedented deficit of more than $50 billion.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Not $5 billion or $6 billion, but over $50 billion in deficit.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And then, we ended FY2021, FY2022 and FY2023 more or less balanced.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, this surplus in FY2024 and the projected surplus in FY2025 – and importantly, excluding the drawdown from past Reserves – taken together, these will really just allow the Government to finish its five-year term more or less balanced.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And this is also what successive PAP Governments have committed to do.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, rather than seeing these surpluses as potentially fomenting cynicism amongst Singaporeans, that somehow, the Government has been collecting more taxes and monies than the nation needs, I think Singaporeans can, instead, draw confidence that these surpluses represent this PAP Government's consistency and the will to maintain fiscal prudence over its entire term of Government, across many terms of Government past, and well into future terms of Government, if the PAP were to continue receiving the mandate to form the Government of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is how we should be looking at the surpluses for these two FYs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, the amount of resources that the Government is deploying to take care of Singapore and Singaporeans is really not in question.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But what is equally important and perhaps more important as we deploy ever more resources, is to make sure that these resources are allocated effectively.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance himself has emphasised this in his Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The classic pain point arising from our current PCI-based means-testing framework is this: take an elderly couple, retired, with a child who is already an adult, working and single.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If this single, adult child continues to stay with the elderly couple, then all three of them are taken as one household; this child’s income from work is taken into the assessment of the household's per capita income; and based on our current means-testing framework, the elderly couple will be deemed to have more means in this household because of the higher PCI.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be clear, no means-test will be perfect or, in economic parlance, no means-test will be perfectly efficient.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Every means-test will have its inefficiencies and trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And in an earlier era, where our population was much younger and the resources needed to support our seniors were on a much smaller scale, the inefficiencies in our current means-testing framework for seniors might not have mattered as much.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, while there were inefficiencies in the allocation of resources to seniors specifically, there were probably also efficiencies in having a common means-testing framework for the whole population generally; there were efficiencies in having a means-testing framework that also applied to working adults and young children, as it applied to seniors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And, indeed, with a much younger population, the efficiencies could well have more than made up for the inefficiencies.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But, as our population continues to age rapidly, as we have many more seniors and as we spend much more per senior and, as the average household structure around our seniors in our society continues to change, I think the balance has fundamentally shifted.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the inefficiencies in our current framework to allocate resources to seniors matter much more now.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, we should get it right and we should fundamentally rethink to make sure our allocation framework remains fit for purpose.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And also, to anchor this refreshed means-testing framework for our seniors on two key considerations that matter most to our seniors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One, our seniors are at a different life stage.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They are most likely not working at all, or working at a much reduced pace, suitable for their current life stage and drawing much lower pay.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, current assessable income will not be the most accurate nor the fairest way of assessing a senior's overall means.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Instead, I think lifelong income, proxied by lifelong contributions to CPF, is probably the most accurate and the fairest way to assess a senior's means, at his or her current life stage.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Two, our seniors do not want to be a burden to their child, no matter how well the child is doing, or how filial he or she may be.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And therefore, while we place a lot of value on personal responsibility and family support, we also need to recognise this basic desire of most seniors in Singapore, to not want to burden their children and I put it to this House that our public policy should be tilted in favour of this basic wish of our seniors to not burden their children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, our means-testing for seniors should move away from including their children's means, whether the children are staying with them in the same address or not.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In summary, my first suggestion is to rethink and rebase our means-testing framework for seniors specifically.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Specifically, I urge the Government to allocate even more resources to ITE students and to reduce the gap in our allocation of resources between ITE and other post-secondary students.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To be clear, successive PAP Governments have been strongly committed to education, to investing in Singaporeans and developing their potential through education.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, the very first PAP Government invested one-third of its yearly Budgets from 1959 to 1963 in education; more specifically, to provide basic education for a very young and growing population.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And also, to be clear, over the more recent decades, successive Governments have invested strongly in ITE in particular.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, our ITE system has grown by leaps and bounds and produced very, very good outcomes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I now have young residents, who are starting out in ITE as Year 1 students, telling me that choosing to go to ITE has been the best decision of their lives.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, we ought to be very proud of how far our ITE system has come.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And yet, I think we can do more and strike an even better balance in our allocation of resources to ITE relative to other segments of higher, post-secondary education.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Of course, more spending on education does not automatically or always produce better educational outcomes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I think there is something to be said about the principles, the equity and the reconcilability of this structural gap in Government recurrent spending between ITE and other segments of higher education in our system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I do believe there is scope to consider a reallocation of spending to achieve a better balance and a smaller gap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: With extra funding, ITE can do a lot more to develop their students even more effectively, in various areas.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Help its students even more effectively to discover aspirations, passions, diverse interests and individual strengths and talents.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And ultimately, this will help preserve and enhance social mobility in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Specifically, while I applaud the Government’s very bold moves to put resources directly in the hands of our workers and adult learners, and empower them to take charge of their own learning, in other words, very major moves on the demand side, I also urge the Government to invest boldly and allocate appropriately on the supply side, to build deep and broad and enduring capabilities to uplift the entire adult education ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One, let us uplift the overall quality of adult educators and trainers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We can, and we should, do the same for adult education.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Let us aim for a world-class pool of adult educators and trainers in Singapore, a world-class pool of dedicated, full-time practitioners in adult education, on the supply side.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We must raise a unified fraternity of adult educators and trainers in Singapore, with a high level of professional pride and identity.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On a related note, Minister for Education Chan Chun Sing has said in a speech recently and I quote, “It cannot; it must not; and it must never be the case that ‘only good teachers go to good schools’”, and this applies to our formal schooling system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I put it to this House that we should aim for the same in our adult education and training, especially in our IHLs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Xie, you have less than two minutes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the years, we have witnessed a profound shift in the landscape of women’s rights, opportunities and empowerment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Central to this journey, the Labour Movement has been unwavering in its commitment to advocating for policies and programmes that not only uplift women but ensure they thrive through the many undulating seasons of their lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The NTUC Women and Family unit has prioritised engaging with women and gathering feedback through various channels to stay attuned to the ground.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Regular surveys, kopi chitchats, small group discussion hosted by our union leaders and extensive outreach efforts ensure that the voices of our working women are heard and reflected in policy decisions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The insights gathered culminated in the White Paper on Singapore Women’s Development, aligning national priorities with the real experiences of women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The NTUC Women and Family unit works closely and regularly with the PAP Women’s Wing’s research group, where I declare I am the Women's Wing Research Group Team Head, to explore critical issues affecting women in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through quarterly surveys, we reflect the voices of thousands of women, and we research on issues such as flexible work arrangements, challenges related to heavy menstrual bleeding, financial burdens and resources available to caregivers, and concerns about retirement and re-employment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The extensive feedback we have gathered through ground sensing empowered us to influence policies and implement concrete action plans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the NTUC has always taken action to create inclusive workplaces, to better the lives and livelihoods of our caregivers in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Back in 2013, the NTUC Women and Family unit launched Project Liquid Gold to advocate for better support for working mothers who wish to continue breastfeeding after returning to work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The initiative aimed to raise awareness of the importance of breastfeeding and encourage employers to provide dedicated nursing spaces in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While this initiative sparked many good conversations, even today, mothers continue to struggle to find suitable spaces for breastfeeding.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some are forced to express milk in washrooms or meeting rooms, sometimes blocked just by sheets of mahjong table paper.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One breastfeeding mother I spoke with, was so frustrated with her boss who told her to breastfeed in the shared common toilet, that on the occasion of him celebrating the birth of his grandson, she took the opportunity to ask him, nicely but firmly, if he would think twice about having his grandson being fed with milk prepared in the public toilet.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And it is precisely conversations like this that helps to push the boundaries on what is possible and fair in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, Project Liquid Gold has evolved into the Better Workplace Campaign, expanding its focus to support women and promote work-life harmony.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The campaign recognises and highlights progressive employers who implement flexible work arrangements and work-life harmony practices, as well as adopt policies to address workplace harassment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers are rewarded with either a wellness corner or a lactation space in their offices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The campaign not only inspires others to adopt similar practices but also helps close the gender perceptions by creating more inclusive, equitable and supportive work environments for women employees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond advocacy, the NTUC Women and Family unit together with our partners, have launched several initiatives aimed at empowering women and caregivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One such initiative is the Women Supporting Women Mentorship Programme, which was first introduced in 2020.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recognising that not all women are prepared for intense one-on-one mentoring, we introduced with one of our partners, SG Her Empowerment, the SHE Supports Friendship Circles, a many-to-many mentorship model.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, our Friendship Circles have garnered the support of 22 professional female groups from women in construction to women in cybersecurity, from working caregivers to women wanting to return to the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our circles form a network of 30,000 females, and we support each other through issues such as Balancing Work and Caregiving, and breaking into new exciting careers such as NGOs and Digital Entrepreneurship spaces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mentorships are critical in equipping and empowering women to reach their potential at work and in life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For two and a half years, she struggled to find a job and through Yayasan MENDAKI’s Women @ Work programme and the NTUC Women Supporting Women Mentorship Programme (WSW), she met Ms Noorfarahin Bte Ahmad, a Union Leader and an NTUC WSW Mentor.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through shared life experiences, Mdm Nurhani regained her confidence to secure a job with INSEAD Business School as a Development Coordinator.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have many other examples of how mentorships and female support can positively impact lives, and we call on the Government and progressive companies to provide more resources to mentorship programmes, both at community and national levels to empower and embolden women to reach for the stars both at home and in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are prioritising flexible work arrangements, improving access to affordable childcare and healthcare services, and increasing financial assistance and subsidies for families.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement has advocated for flexible work arrangements (FWAs) since the 1990s and caregivers have shared that FWAs are their most preferred form of support in balancing work and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we thank the Government for heeding our calls for Enhanced Paternity and Shared Parental Leave, and indeed, it has started to move the needle in reframing gender stereotypes in parenting, with two-thirds of our survey respondents agreeing that their partners shares parenting responsibilities equally, parental/caregiving leave forms just a part of a broader caregiving ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other initiatives, such as FWAs, and caregiving support such as childcare services, trusted helpers at home, completes this ecosystem of comprehensive support for women and their families; and allows women to return to the workplace with peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our young families have shared that they face financial pressures while raising a family.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I had spoken previously at the PAP Parliamentary Motion on Supporting Singaporeans in Starting and Raising Families that this would need to be taken with the view of providing more employment opportunities for return to work mothers, allowing for more sustainable long term financial independence.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I shared that we would expand our popular C U Back (CUB) at Work Programme which helps caregivers, especially women, return to work with flexible work options to more segments of underserved women workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: FWAs are a sustainable way for caregivers to stay in the workforce, and more needs to be done to make FWAs more inclusive and accessible across different job types.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through CUB, we hope to demonstrate to all employers that they can support our workers to better balance their work and life demands at every stage of their lives, while accessing a larger, and productive pool of Singaporean talent.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With SMEs employing up to 70% of the Singaporean workforce, SME employers with less resourcing often struggle to find temporary replacements when staff go on FWAs or parental leave.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: SME owners may also face financial strain when reimbursing employees for parental leave.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such targeted assistance for SMEs would align with the Government's push for larger families and increased workforce participation for our females.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, in the spirit of promoting inclusive workspaces, FWAs go a long way to providing a means of livelihood for PwDs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ensuring that there is availability of suitable jobs with FWA is critical to securing our Singaporean workplaces as places for our PwDs to be empowered with independence and dignity.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We call on the Government to build up a base of job coaches, so that jobs can be effectively redesigned to win-win outcomes for our employers and their PwD employees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also thank the Government for extending the Enabling Employment Credit to end-2028, which provides wage offsets for companies to hire employees with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, workers with disabilities will also want to reskill and upgrade, so that their skillsets remain relevant.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Depending on circumstances, PwDs may need more support for training, and the Government has an Open Door Programme Training Grant which funds employers up to 95% of course fees by SG Enable's Enabling Academy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, employers and workers may require more industry-specific training that is offered outside Enabling Academy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit be expanded to support the training of differently-abled employees, who may require some forms of training to be tailored to their needs as well as industry requirements?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recognising the importance of fostering strong, harmonious relationships between employers and migrant domestic workers, the NTUC Women and Family unit, in collaboration with the Centre for Domestic Employees, launched monthly advisory clinics in 2021.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These clinics serve as a platform for employers to understand their responsibilities and build positive, respectful relationships with their migrant domestic workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through these clinics, we observed that the majority of employers wanted advice and tips on creating strong, healthy relationships with their helpers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many pointed to shifts in the workforce: migrant domestic workers are increasingly younger, often from the millennial generation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One employer shared that she was unsure of how to navigate her relationship with her young helper who was in her 20s, as her previous helpers were all in their 40s.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She shared very pragmatic concerns, such as how to set boundaries on the use of handphones and the use of social media within the home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unlike the more extreme hateful relationships we see frequently played up in social media, I was very heartened to see that many Singaporean employers genuinely care for their migrant domestic workers, though they are often unaware of the resources available to better support them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This shows the important role that our migrant domestic workers play in the ecosystem of care for Singaporean families, and we call on the Government to provide more support and assistance to our families in regard to greater access and affordability of migrant domestic workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From policy advocacy and flexible work arrangements, to mentorship and returner programmes, the NTUC remains dedicated to ensuring that all women – regardless of their circumstances and where they are in the lives – receive the support they need to reach for the stars, both at home and in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together, we can create a more inclusive society where women are empowered, supported and given the opportunity to reach their fullest potential.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This shows that the measures put in place by the PAP Government, which includes bringing in good investments and creating good jobs, keeping the Singapore dollar strong to combat imported inflation, expanding the Progressive Wage Model to uplift wages of lower-income workers and various other schemes, have borne fruit.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While inflation this year has eased and is expected to average between 1.5% and 2.5%, the price increases of the past will not go away and we will have to adapt to the new reality of higher prices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is why I am glad that the Government has taken decisive moves to help Singaporeans cope with higher prices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my speech today, I wish to highlight how we must improve consumer protection, so that consumers can reap the full intended benefits from the various support measures provided by the Government.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must not allow unscrupulous businesses to profiteer from these support measures, at the expense of our consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will also highlight how we can do more to uplift the wages of our lower-income brothers and sisters, so that they do not get left behind as Singapore progresses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The additional $800 in CDC Vouchers, additional U-Save rebates, increase in ComCare assistance schemes and the new SG60 Vouchers, will certainly help Singaporeans from all walks of life better cope with today's higher prices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Radin Mas, we have rolled out various community initiatives last year to help our own residents cope with cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We launched the "Radin Mas Care For You Vouchers", where each month, a set of local discount vouchers is distributed to 3,000 eligible households residing in Radin Mas.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We opened JamPacked@Radin Mas, a community minimart to allow lower-income residents to redeem $50 worth of groceries monthly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These daily essentials are contributed by our supermarkets and kind donors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But instead of distributing pre-packed bags of groceries, residents come down to the minimart to redeem what they need.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This cuts down on waste, which in turn, encourages more frequent and generous donations by donors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We also set up a community fridge at Telok Blangah Crescent, to allow residents to collect free fruits and vegetables, which have been rescued from the nearby markets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since we launched what we call "the Magic Fridge" in November 2024, we have given away more than 1,000 kilogrammes of free fruits and vegetables.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Radin Mas, we have a strong community spirit where those who have more, chip in to help those who have less.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In his Budget speech, the Prime Minister announced that over $600 million will be set aside by the Government and Tote Board to match donations made to charities and social causes, in an effort to encourage philanthropy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But we should do more to encourage philanthropy in all forms, beyond just monetary donations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Government will encourage a more caring Singapore and encourage more ground-up initiatives, like what we have started in Radin Mas, across our nation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond Government initiatives and community-led programmes, the private sector too must play its part in our whole-of-nation effort to help curb rising cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC and our enterprises are committed to do our part in ensuring that essentials remain accessible and affordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Over the same period, FairPrice has also returned more than $250 million in rebates to NTUC union members and FairPrice members.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But, Sir, we must ensure that Singapore has a robust consumer protection regime and a price transparent market, to ensure that consumers fully reap the benefits of Government and community-driven initiatives to cushion our rising cost-of-living.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These losses were driven primarily by industries with large, lumpy expenses, such as renovation, bridal and the beauty and spa sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond pre-payment losses, e-commerce related complaints also reached an all-time high, surpassing even the peak brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These are deeply troubling trends and we must take decisive actions to foster a more trusted business trading environment and protect consumers from losing their hard-earned monies to unscrupulous businesses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
