text: This was well before the boom in e-commerce, an industry that had its growth supercharged by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We will engage extensively with the business, legal and academia communities to ensure that a right balance is struck between protecting consumers while balancing Singapore's reputation on ease of doing business, when proposing both legislative and non-legislative changes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Over the past few years, I have advocated for the nationwide implementation of unit pricing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I first raised the issue in this House in 2022, speaking about the need to use unit pricing to combat "shrinkflation", a phenomenon where retailers keep the price of a good unchanged, but shrink its volume or shrink its quality.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unit pricing helps consumers see through pricing gimmicks quickly and easily.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Several countries have long implemented unit pricing, such as the UK, Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As a start, we could adopt the same parameters as our Disposable Carrier Bag Charge, where only larger players need to comply with the requirement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The implementation of unit pricing will help consumers combat shrinkflation and allow them to stretch their dollar when shopping for groceries and other essential items.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Lim Swee Say puts it best, when he said that "a job is the best welfare and full employment is the best protection for our workers." While I am heartened that Singapore's Gini coefficient, which measures income inequality, fell to a record low in 2024, we must continue our efforts to uplift our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Last year, we celebrated the 10th anniversary milestone of our Progressive Wage Model (PWM), a unique Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: From the very beginning, NTUC championed the idea of a wage ladder that would correspond to workers' skills, productivity and job responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: More importantly, this has translated into actual wage increases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is higher than the median worker in the same period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond just wage growth, workers are also leveraging PWM as a catalyst to actively advance their career and upgrade their skills, ensuring that they are well-equipped for better job opportunities and higher-paying job roles in the long run.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I call on the Government to continue its strong support for PWM.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us jointly uplift our lower-wage workers by providing them with stable jobs that have a progressive wage ladder and good career prospects.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC will always stand alongside our lower-wage workers, taking action to uplift their wages and work prospects to ensure that no worker is left behind.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Tensions between big global powers are rising and trade wars loom on the horizon.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The use of tit-for-tat tariffs by major economies as a foreign policy tool will impact Singapore's open and trade-dependent economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am heartened that Budget 2025 takes decisive steps in helping Singaporeans navigate through the uncertainty by investing in our workers and in providing a slew of cost-of-living support to all segments of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we spend prudently to support our nation, we must remember the importance of enhancing consumer protection and price transparency.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must help consumers make informed purchasing decisions and not fall prey easily to unscrupulous businesses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC cares for our lower-wage workers and will always strive to improve their lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must continue to review sectors where the introduction of PWM can result in better wages and better work prospects for our lower-income brothers and sisters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will also continue to work with the Government agencies and industry stakeholders to improve our work environments, workplace safety and mental health of all workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Here, I would like to record my thanks to the hon Member Hazel Poa for suggesting in her speech yesterday for a right to disconnect, something that I have been championing since 2020.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am glad that more Members, including the Progress Singapore Party, are now supporting this too.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But we must continue to do all we can to ensure that no one is left behind as our economy progresses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Although this is later in the afternoon now, it is not time to disconnect yet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I stand here as a Labour Member of Parliament to once again speak up for and focus on advancing the interests of our older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First of all, I must observe and say that our older workers have made much progress in terms of their employment, in terms of their wage and employability over the decades.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is due to the enlightened policies of the People's Action Party Government and the hard work of the tripartite partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The percentage of active CPF members who turn age 55 and who have been able to save up to their cohort Basic Retirement Sum has increased from six in 10 in 2016 to about seven in 10 in 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: MOM projects it to reach eight in 10 by 2027.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Labour Movement is certainly heartened that our work advocating for improvements for the sake of our older workers, together with the support and partnership with our tripartite partners, have borne fruit systematically to improve older workers' livelihoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Older workers have even more improvements to look forward to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To boost the retirement adequacy of both current and future cohorts of senior workers, NTUC has advocated for increases in CPF contribution rates for our senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I look forward to the scheduled increases up to 2030 in line with the recommendations of the Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These increases will allow the contribution rates of those aged above 55 up to 60 to match those of younger workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On our part, the NTUC and our enterprises have moved ahead and raised our retirement and re-employment ages from 1 January 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Public Service has also announced that it will raise its retirement and re-employment ages from 1 July 2025, which is a year ahead of the national timeline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Additionally, the new Matched MediSave Scheme will help eligible older workers increase their MediSave balances and better cater for their healthcare needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The extension of the Senior Employment Credit till end-2026 is also welcome.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will help businesses defray part of their hiring costs for older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That should make older workers more attractive to hire.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Just in January this year, Parliament passed the Workplace Fairness Bill into law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This Act is an important step in our fight against ageism and all forms of discrimination in the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Unions will work proactively and sensibly with companies to foster age neutrality and fairness in the treatment of older workers in our workplaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But how do we ensure that we can hold on to our gains and build positively on them as we move into the future?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is not a trivial remark, because we must not underestimate the immensity of the challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As many colleagues have already said in their speeches, the world is entering into a very difficult and turbulent geopolitical and geo-economic era.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: What we are seeing now is a world where win-win mindsets wane.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And instead, we see law-of-the-jungle and beggar-thy-neighbour instincts rise and be on the ascendant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In such a climate, safeguarding our gains and achieving further good progress is not going to be easy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It requires sustained, strong mutual understanding of joint interests and ever closer collaboration on the part of the tripartite partners to look for bold and innovative pathways forward.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I cannot over-emphasise this, because if you look back, progress has not been easy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But compared to the path ahead, I think the path that we have trodden so far is still relatively more stable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The road ahead is not going to be like that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I expect it to be a lot more bumpy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While the employment and labour force participation rates for our older workers have reached new highs in recent years and even bucked the trend in the rest of the world, it is not without its challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Through NTUC's extensive engagements with PMEs through the work of our PME task force, many older PMEs have shared that they had faced significant hurdles in getting back into work after mid-life job loss.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Many also indicated that new jobs often entail substantial downward adjustment of the pay and job nature.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This points to the need for more concerted efforts to help middle-aged jobseekers adjust and transit so as to benefit from their continued contributions while managing the negativities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NTUC understands these challenges that our older PMEs are facing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Initiatives, such as the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme, stem from our work with our tripartite partners to innovate practical help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We thank the Government for introducing the scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Examples of this close collaboration, looking forward, analysing what the real challenges are based on our older workers and finding win-win ways, practical pathways, practical arrangements that are sustainable and implementing them in good time is our hallmark.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This must continue to describe our joint approach going forward.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Earlier, I said that I expect the road ahead to be more bumpy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is firstly because the lower-hanging fruits that policy levers can achieve have been well harvested over the past years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: More importantly, we must expect the international business environment, likely one where there will be a pronounced increase in nativist and protectionist behaviour by countries big and small, to put pressure on our businesses' cost and market access.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As a result, there will be knock-on effects for both enterprises and their workforces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The inherent vulnerability of older workers is, therefore, likely to be put under more pressure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this regard, our tripartite partners must carefully monitor the external environment and its impact on our economy and labour market and, at the same time, plan ahead together to move swiftly to seize opportunities and be able to protect our joint gains and not let them slip away.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We have to come together, look at the picture together and find the way forward together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Next, I want to speak about the importance of training in the face of such uncertainty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Against this backdrop of heightened uncertainty and economic challenge, it is important that we keep our focus on strengthening our fundamentals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This remains our best bet to tackle all scenarios.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For older workers and their companies, one such fundamental must be the workforce competency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This relates directly to a company's competitiveness and resilience and an older worker's employability and work prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Sixty-six percent of younger workers, defined as those below 35 years old, said that there would be sufficient good jobs in the market for them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Earlier findings from NTUC's #EveryWorkerMatters Conversations also found that a significant proportion of older workers are worried that they would not be given equitable consideration and access to skills upgrading and training opportunities compared to younger peers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If you are talking about these concerns in a stable environment, it is one thing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But if you are talking about these concerns in such a time of volatility, then I think we have to be even bolder, and I believe that it is a great opportunity, in fact, for Singapore Inc to once again rise to the occasion and upskill our workforce, older workers included, to uplift our competitiveness, enhance our enterprise resilience, improve our career adaptability and forge ahead of other economies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Every time we had a crisis, we upturned the downturn.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We turned; we not only made lemonade out of lemons, but we turned challenges into opportunities, and we must do so because, if we do not and others do, then both our companies and workers will pay dearly for it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NTUC stands ready to work hard and work hand in hand with businesses and the Government to move in these areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On company-level business road mapping and workforce training, NTUC’s CTCs continue to scale, broaden and deepen their effectiveness within the companies and the sectors to benefit workers of all levels and wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NTUC is also reimagining our Job Security Council to achieve faster, wider and better outcomes in industry manpower, skills, job design and match outcomes, in close liaison with the Government and industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Beyond safeguarding the interests of older workers currently in the workforce, the tripartite partners must also press on with innovative thinking on how to further activate, mobilise and enable more Singaporeans to rejoin and participate in our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Getting more Singaporeans to participate in our economy is important to businesses, certainly very important to our returning workers and very important to our overall national resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In a speech I made at the Budget debate back in 2019, I specifically pointed to the potential benefit of enabling a considerable number of middle-aged caregivers to remain in work or to return to work for the purposes of increasing the participation of Singaporeans within our workforce and economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At that time, I had pointed out that for that to happen, it certainly takes a host of adjustments in companies, workers and Government policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And this ranged from flexible work arrangements to job redesign to self-employment on the part of the labour market and what employers and businesses can do because when you make your jobs more flexible, then it is not a zero one, either a full-time job or there is not a job.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There are different combinations in which a person can continue to have the opportunity to stay at work while catering to care responsibilities, for example.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But for those who have already left because of whatever the reason, including where the companies do not yet offer those flexible arrangements, to come back is a different proposition because they have to care for someone at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, for them, it is not only whether there are potential employers with flexible work arrangements ready to receive them back.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is also that they need a system that creates affordable, accessible and sustainable senior care of various types so that they, as caregivers, have truly viable alternatives to provide that care to their loved ones and then they can come back.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I think we are more ready than before.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The environment we must deal with will be increasingly challenging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must come together even more to seize opportunities, overcome constraints and to forge ahead for the sake of our older workers, for the sake of Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As I have engaged with residents, many have expressed how the disbursements projected for this year come at a timely moment as families plan their budgets for the year ahead.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Today, I wish to focus on an urgent and critical issue: strengthening mental health support for seniors in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Earlier this month in Parliament, I spoke about the importance of mental health support for children and youths.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In this Budget Debate, I call for immediate action to address the growing mental health challenges faced by our seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The correlation between mental health struggles and suicide is well-documented and, for seniors, this issue is particularly alarming.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many of them face profound grief, loss and significant societal changes as they age.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Yet, they are the least likely to seek help, either from healthcare professionals or informal networks, compared to younger cohorts.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This highlights the urgent need for targeted intervention to support their mental well-being.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While our existing mental health strategies have made strides, more can be done to support our seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore is not just ageing; we will soon become a super-aged society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is time we recognise and address the unique mental health challenges faced by our seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our seniors face a series of irreversible losses; spouse, friends, physical health, employment and independence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many, particularly men, are unprepared for widowhood or retirement and struggle with isolation as they try to build new support systems.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The stigma surrounding mental health worsens the issue.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many seniors fear being labelled "siao", or “crazy” in English, and the term 精神问题, “mental health problem”, carries strong negative connotations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Unlike younger generations, who benefit from awareness campaigns, seniors often suffer in silence, avoiding help due to societal perceptions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The rise in scams targeting seniors adds another layer of distress.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many who lose their life savings in financial and love scams feel too ashamed or afraid to confide in their families, intensifying their emotional turmoil.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This sense of shame, rooted in our Asian "face-saving" culture, can spiral into severe depression or even suicide.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Additionally, digital isolation has become a growing concern.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As society becomes more digital, many seniors struggle to keep up, leaving them unable to access important services or stay connected with loved ones.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The shift to online banking, tele-health and digital Government services has made it harder for those without digital literacy to reach essential resources, thus increasing frustration and feelings of helplessness.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A senior from Depot Road shared with me just two nights ago, “我英语不好，电脑不会” or “I’m not good in English, nor do I have computer skills".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This dear resident earnestly appealed for more patience and understanding from the community at large.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, the increasing reliance on digital communication by younger generations means fewer face-to-face interactions with seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some observe that children or extended family often choose video calls over in-person visits, deepening their sense of isolation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Here are the proposed interventions to support the mental health of our seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: First, may I acknowledge the excellent work already done by our Government and agencies for the welfare of our seniors, including the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC), Age Well SG, Healthier SG, SG Digital Office, as well as Active Ageing Centres I have the joy of working with across Dover, Depot and Telok Blangah; Active Global, FaithActs, Montfort Care, NTUC Health, St Andrew’s Senior Care, St Andrew's Hospital and Sunlove.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Building on these efforts, we must make mental wellness the next frontier in ensuring Singapore is a safe place to age well.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Before outlining specific interventions, it is important to recognise the diversity among seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They go through distinct life stages; young seniors in their 60s-70s, seniors in their 70s-80s, and seniors 80 and above, each facing unique challenges that require tailored mental health strategies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The first proposed intervention: Pre-Retirement Mental Health Preparation and Workplace Support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Just as we encourage financial planning for retirement, we must also advocate for mental health preparation before seniors enter their later years.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Missing this window to equip them with coping strategies could mean missing the opportunity altogether.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The transition out of active employment is a critical mental health juncture.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is tied to identity, purpose and social connections, especially for men.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This planning should help them adjust to new routines, social networks and purpose-driven activities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Second, strengthening Community-Based Support Networks and Senior-Led Initiatives.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Once seniors leave the workforce, staying engaged in meaningful activities becomes essential for their mental well-being.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Community engagement and support groups must, therefore, form the core of our strategy, providing spaces where seniors feel a sense of belonging and purpose.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: First, we need targeted support groups for new retirees, widowers and those struggling with depression.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is especially crucial to ensure support for seniors in their 80s, who often experience the loss of close friends and spouses, leading to a shrinking social circle.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Intergenerational interactions also offer a meaningful form of community engagement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At Telok Blangah, NTUC Health partners Blangah Rise Primary School every third Monday of the month to run sports activities, where our seniors and students connect.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Feedback has shown that these precious seniors look forward to the innocence and unreserved nature of our youths, while our children enjoy spending time with our seniors, especially those who miss their grandparents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I hope to replicate such initiatives across more neighbourhoods.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Let us also rethink volunteering opportunities for seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many are eager to contribute but find traditional models rigid.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Recently, I met a resident in her early 70s who wanted to pass on her tui-na techniques, a vocation she has practised for decades, as a way of giving back upon her retirement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: By offering skills-based initiatives beyond hobby-centric programmes, we can engage seniors who are willing and able to share their skills and expertise.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For example, at our Telok Blangah Legal Clinic, a retired lawyer continues to contribute his knowledge to both the volunteer team and residents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Beyond structured programmes, we should empower seniors to take ownership of their community spaces.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The "Ibasho" model from Japan offers a compelling example.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: What began as a simple café run by seniors in Ofunato has evolved into a thriving hub with a garden, ramen shop, farmer’s market and daycare.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Closer to home, we see a similar concept in the Health District @ Queenstown’s FaithActs Active Ageing Centre, which includes upcycling workshops, digital clinics and cooking classes.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Such endeavors give seniors a sense of purpose and foster inter-generational bonds.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Imagine retired hawkers mentoring younger residents to prepare meals for vulnerable families or seniors who love gardening teaching students to build gardens in schools.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At Telok Blangah, Chef Benny Se Teo shared his cooking skills with our community, with sessions so popular that we are planning another one in March.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As a growing number of our seniors of tomorrow will be different from the seniors of today, we will need to evolve our approach to meet their changing needs and aspirations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With the right support, their experience and wisdom can drive meaningful projects that strengthen communities and address local challenges.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Addressing mental health among seniors requires understanding the unique challenges they face.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Unlike younger generations, who increasingly embrace the idea that "it is okay not to be okay", many seniors still harbour deep-seated fears and misconceptions about mental illness.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To bridge this gap, we must use media platforms familiar to them, such as Channel 8, Suria and Vasantham, to openly discuss mental health issues through dramas and talk shows.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This will spark conversations in coffee shops and hawker centres, often where our seniors gather.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Radio, too, remains a trusted source for information and entertainment, making it an ideal medium for airing mental health segments in various dialects.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This Saturday, the Telok Blangah Community Club will host a “Mental Health Wellness Carnival” designed for Chinese-speaking seniors, with hopes to extend this to other languages.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our Government’s success in using targeted communication during the COVID-19 pandemic shows the power of reaching seniors where they are at, achieving remarkable uptake rates and safeguarding this vulnerable demographic.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Similarly, by positioning mental health as an essential part of overall well-being, we can break the stigma and promote proactive measures.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To shift the narrative, we need culturally sensitive, language-specific and community- driven initiatives.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must meet seniors where they are, physically and emotionally, creating an environment where seeking help is seen as a strength and not a weakness.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The question is, who should lead this change and what should the model be?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This also calls for a community partnership model, one that involves religious organisations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Temples, mosques and churches are trusted spaces for many of our seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This emotional toll of scams is often underestimated, leaving many seniors ashamed to seek help or confide in their families, resulting in isolation and distress.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Additionally, Police and community centers should partner with mental health professionals to provide trauma-informed counselling, helping victims regain confidence and dignity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Most importantly, we must educate families to respond with empathy, not blame, through public campaigns that emphasise support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Seniors often feel "stupid" for falling victim to scams, compounding the emotional pain of losing their life savings.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To address the mental health and caregiving challenges facing seniors and their caregivers, we must take a holistic approach.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: First, training counsellors to effectively address grief and loss issues in the elderly is essential, recognising the unique emotional toll of ageing and the varied ways seniors process these emotions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Equally important is equipping caregivers with the skills to identify and manage mental health symptoms in seniors, especially those with high dependency needs, such as dementia.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Caregivers often bear immense emotional and financial burdens, and we must provide more support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Encouraging families to provide care over hiring foreign domestic workers should be supported through policy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Recent reports of elder abuse remind us that our workers need mental health support and training to care for vulnerable seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: By investing in the well-being of both seniors and their caregivers, we foster a community where dignity, compassion and mutual care are at the heart of our shared future.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our approach must be comprehensive and empathetic, starting with prevention through workplace support for those nearing retirement and continue with the community initiatives like the “Ibasho” model, empowering seniors to remain active and engaged members of society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For those in immediate need, we will strengthen our efforts through destigmatising, trauma-informed counselling and greater professional support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: And just as importantly, we must prioritise and support the caregivers who are essential to the well-being of our seniors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our seniors have built this nation with decades of hard work and sacrifice.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Now, it is our turn to care for them, ensuring they deserve the mental health support they need.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Let us build a Singapore where our seniors are not only respected but cherished, and where we provide them with the care, dignity and support that reflect the immense value they have brought to our society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The time to care for them is now, let us honour their legacy by ensuring they can age with the security and compassion they deserve.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With this, Mr Speaker, I fully support Budget 2025, “Onward Together for a Better Tomorrow”.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Second Minister for Finance, would you like to move to adjourn the debate?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is one that is inclusive and diverse and I support it fully.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My speech today will cover two key topics.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, the Culture Pass and second, a proposal to support Singapore's visual arts sector.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This proposal takes inspiration from the strong financial backing that we have seen in this Budget for businesses that are seeking a listing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX).

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In this speech, I would like to suggest similar financial mechanisms to strengthen our local visual arts scene.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is a very commendable initiative that makes arts and cultural experiences more accessible to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, I filed a Parliamentary Question after hearing from arts businesses about their challenges.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I heard that even if they were located in the heartlands, not all arts businesses were eligible for the Community Development Council (CDC) Voucher redemption scheme.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They would have to be considered on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This raised concerns that the arts were not being recognised as an essential part of everyday life.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This money could have been spent in many different ways, but it has come to the arts and this is a very important and powerful message.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Since the initiative was announced, some questions have emerged from the arts community and I would like to take this opportunity to highlight them here.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Can credits be shared among family members and friends?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If not, what provisions exist for those who are unable to use the Culture Pass due to severe health or mobility issues?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While the push for inclusivity in the arts has been very strong, some individuals, for example, those who are bedridden or who are in advanced stages of dementia and, therefore, they are unable to control their moods and behaviour, people in these groups may find it nearly impossible to attend events in person.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Caregivers may then struggle to find suitable options.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I recognise that there is a risk of profiteering if credits are made transferable and I also see how transferability could dilute the scheme's intent, which is, actually, to encourage personal cultural participation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But it would, however, be good to know if there is any plan at the moment for what will happen to unused or unusable credits.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If this happens, it could have the effect of reducing the impact of Culture Pass credits which, really, have been issued to make arts and heritage events more affordable to the general public and not less affordable.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Some artists have also expressed concerns about whether the Culture Pass funds will directly benefit them.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Particularly, there is a question as to the proportion of ticket sales that will be allocated as artist fees, as opposed to being retained by arts intermediaries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is not an easy question to address because it is very much an issue of commercial practice and relative bargaining power between artists and event organisers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In a perfectly ideal scenario, the Government could set guidelines to ensure fair distribution of ticketing funds across all players in an arts or heritage event.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But this could also take away the autonomy of arts groups to plan their own affairs.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It might create additional administrative burdens and reporting obligations for the groups involved.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope, therefore, that the Government will continue, as part of its larger mission through the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY), to educate artists about their legal rights.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This way, artists will be empowered to negotiate for fair remuneration and to reject unethical practices, should they take place, in Culture Pass-funded events.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Another potential issue that has come up is that of ticket wastage.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If credits are used to book tickets, but attendees fail to show up, valuable resources may be lost.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Government put in place a refundable deposit system, or will penalties be imposed for repeated no-shows, such that Culture Pass holders will be encouraged to use their credits responsibly?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I also hope the Government ensures that the benefits of the Culture Pass scheme are equitably distributed across diverse arts groups and not just dominated by the larger, more established institutions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has announced that independent practitioners can also qualify for the Culture Pass scheme and I hope that they will be well-represented in the final selection of chosen entities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Smaller, independent arts organisations must have fair access to the scheme to promote a more vibrant and inclusive arts ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Lest it sound like the arts community is less than supportive of this programme, with all the various questions that have emerged, let me be clear that everyone whom I have spoken to in the community is enthusiastic about this initiative.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The excitement is palpable, such that additional questions I have come across include whether the scheme can be expanded, before it has even formally kicked off.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, will there eventually be an expansion as well to local art?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There are also questions about whether the scheme will be reviewed before 2029 or 2030 and whether there is scope for it to be enlarged or topped up with more even credits before its expiry.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Culture Pass is a very clever initiative, because it goes towards creating demand for arts and heritage performances and events.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In a similar vein, I would like to take the opportunity now to float some ideas for demand-side initiatives that could also boost the visual arts sector.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here, we can draw inspiration from the suite of tax and financial incentives that were announced in this Budget to support and encourage corporate listings in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: From speaking to collectors, business owners, artists and other stakeholders several ideas emerged.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, would the Government consider the creation of a Government-backed art investment fund, with local artworks as underlying assets?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Art is a valuable alternative asset class, has a low correlation to traditional markets and can act as a hedge against volatility.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A 2021 Nomura report suggests that contemporary art as an asset achieved an annualised return of 14% between 1995 and 2020.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's own artists are seeing extraordinary sales results.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore Art Week this year, the works of Singapore women artists Kim Lim and Melissa Tan saw promising record-breaking sales.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Our local artists are also making a splash internationally, with a record number of them being represented at the recent 60th Venice Biennale.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Our local gallerists have also shown remarkable business acumen and the members of the Art Galleries Association Singapore and many other galleries and dealers have done plenty to raise the commercial profile of local artists both in Singapore and overseas.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Public endorsement of local art investment has the potential to strengthen the secondary market.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, art acquisition is costly, with added expenses for storage, framing and preservation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting found that Singapore collectors are highly financially motivated.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: From the report, while the highest-ranking motivation for buying art was that of "self-focus and pleasure" in almost all markets surveyed, Singapore was the only market where financial motivations ranked even higher.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, we even beat Hong Kong in this regard.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They point to clear opportunities: the local art market is showing signs of growth, new collectors are entering, and buyers are financially driven.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While art education and awareness remain crucial for long-term demand, we must also meet consumers where they are.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: And we could perhaps do this by recognising and leveraging their investment mindset to further develop Singapore's art market.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The lack of a vibrant resale market limits participation by buyers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The owners of the Teng Collection, a private art collection and authors of art investment guide Godalisation, as well as other collectors and business owners, have highlighted to me that the absence of a structured secondary market in Singapore is one reason why demand for local art has not yet reached its full potential.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, they would like to advocate for the establishment of a Government-backed art fund to support the sector.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There have been very interesting and dynamic recent entrants to the secondary art market, such as the startup Art Again, an online marketplace for pre-owned art, and We Are Art Collectors – the fractional art ownership platform of Artualize Gallery.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Some galleries as well do engage in secondary sales.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, without greater liquidity, buyers hesitate to enter the market.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: After all, would we not be more motivated to buy art if we knew that it could be resold and that our capital could be recycled?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A useful analogy here is perhaps that of the second-hand designer handbag market.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: One reason why people do not hesitate to buy Louis Vuitton handbags is because they know that they can resell them easily.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A strong secondary market would give buyers the confidence to invest more freely.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If local art is seen as a good investment, buyers will be encouraged to acquire it and not just blue-chip pieces.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There could be interest in spotting "the next big thing" as well, in terms of emerging artists.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As more buyers see investment value in collecting Singapore art, resale activity would increase, making it easier for collectors to trade works.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This cycle benefits not just artists and galleries, but also auction houses, dealers and visual art-related businesses, such as framing, conservation and art logistics entities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The third point I would like to make is that sovereign wealth funds are already recognising art's value.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In a similar but not fully identical point, Abu Dhabi's ADQ recently acquired a stake in Sotheby's, signalling institutional confidence in art-related assets.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If other nations see strategic merit in high value art-related investment, why not Singapore?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If good returns are achievable, perhaps the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (GIC) or Temasek could consider creating a dedicated local art investment portfolio, perhaps parked in a fund structure and focusing on blue-chip works alongside some experimental pieces.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Investment returns could then be derived from things like capital appreciation, leasing and financing models.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Such a Government-backed art investment fund could catalyse institutional and private participation and send a strong market signal.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It could be advised by expert advisory panels, comprising investment professionals, financial institutions, art and culture leaders and economists, to ensure that financial sustainability is coupled with proper corporate governance.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It could position local art as a credible alternative asset class while ensuring that artists, collectors and galleries benefit from greater financial participation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If the art investments are successful, a percentage of profits can also then be channelled back into arts charities, adding a useful social mission as well to the investment concerned.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond liquidity, MAS' focus on tax incentives, regulatory streamlining and research development grants to encourage local listings, mirrors the structural support that Singapore's art market could also stand to benefit from.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We should take a closer look at our artwork appraisal and valuation capabilities as well as the incentives and reliefs that we can offer in terms of direct and indirect taxes.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I have cited examples of what other countries have done in both of these areas in previous speeches, and there is no shortage of reference points to start a comprehensive review of the various financial possibilities for our visual art market.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There are, of course, existing measures that are and continue to be useful.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This ensures that investors' capital will directly benefit the local economy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think that many arts businesses are even aware of this option for fundraising.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As I have previously raised in an Adjournment Motion, the Government could look to Creative UK as a case study.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This network supports the United Kingdom's (UK's) creative industries by providing scale-up financing, connecting investors with arts entities and educating arts groups on securing funding through equity, debt and grants.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A similar centralised networking portal in Singapore would help local arts entities to access investment opportunities and financial support more effectively.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government will, at the very least, consider engaging with financial and arts institutions, gallerists, dealers, collectors, arts business owners and artists.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Together, they could create a working group or a task force to embark on a more comprehensive study on how structured financial mechanisms can be put in place to better support Singapore's visual arts creative economy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I will not deny that there are different views on this point, the idea of mixing art with commerce can always be a little bit controversial.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But if viable, these measures can ensure that Singapore's art ecosystem is not just vibrant but economically robust.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If it succeeds, it can provide arts workers with stability, opportunities and a strong foundation for long-term careers, one that is driven by genuine consumer interest and demand.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I want to thank Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and his team for a generous, inclusive and empathetic Budget this year.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It reaffirms that we have a leadership and Government that is committed to enable Singaporeans and to ease our burdens whenever required to do so, at the extent that is prudent and fair for all.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I rise today to address two pressing concerns that lie at the heart of our nation's future, which cannot really be solved by money: (a) the opportunity cost of our academic-centric education system on personal fulfilment; and (b) the concerning trend of declining fertility rates in our hyper-competitive society.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These two issues, although seemingly distinct, are deeply interconnected, requiring not just fiscally generous grants but a fundamental shift in our policy mindset.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Yes, Singapore has long prided itself on being a global leader in education.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Our students consistently rank at the top of international assessments, which is a testament to our system's rigour and discipline.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, we must ask ourselves: is this really still the best way forward?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These are signs of a generation that feel a lack of meaning in their lives, are high-strung and easily triggered.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Parenthood is daunting for most young couples, especially financially daunting.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Imagine having to join that $1.8 billion rat race just to feel like you are being a decent parent, and you are not causing your child to lose out or letting them down.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And this pressure flows downwards onto the children as well, because when parents are sacrificing so much of their own resources, time, money and effort, in the hope that they can at least catch up academically with their peers.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: All children want to live up to their parents' expectations and the more parents invest, the more pressure the child feels, regardless of whether they know to articulate it or not.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Our unwavering emphasis on academic excellence has created an opportunity cost, one that diminishes our youths' ability to discover, nurture and pursue personal passions beyond the prescribed curriculum.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, in my Budget speech, I spoke about shifting from a performance-based culture to an appreciation-based culture, so that Singaporeans can feel the intrinsic rewards from what they do and derive motivation and satisfaction from contributing to something beyond delivering key performance indicators (KPIs).

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This year, I stress the importance of having a purpose-based culture.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: History has repeatedly shown that excellence is derived through purpose rather than pressure.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Walt Disney's creative empire was built on a purpose to create places where families could have fun together.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Oprah Winfrey built a media empire from the purpose of empowering women and promoting positive self-image through her talk shows.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Steve Job's passion and purpose was to build an enduring company where people were motivated to make great products.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These examples highlight how intrinsically driven individuals pursuing their passion leads to long-term success.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Today, a child's schedule is filled with school, tuition and enrichment classes, leaving little room for unstructured exploration, creative thinking or simply being a child.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The consequence is a workforce that is well-trained but often disengaged, with morale easily impacted by negative experiences that are bound to be encountered in the day to day.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Without a strong anchor powered by personal purpose and intrinsic passion for what one does, this day-to-day unhappiness easily chips away at one's well-being and motivation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Studies suggest that when children are constantly evaluated based on external validation, they struggle with low self-esteem, burnout and difficulty making independent life choices.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Research in the International Education and Research Journal indicates that while extrinsic motivation, such as recognition from teachers and parents, can offer short-term incentives, intrinsic motivation is what fosters lifelong passion and excellence.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is important that children and youths are given time and opportunity to explore life, in order that they may discover their passion or purpose.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Right now, too much of their mental and emotional bandwidth is spent on ensuring or worrying about whether they can perform up to par in standardised settings.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I acknowledge the Government's commendable efforts in recent years to introduce student-led learning in secondary schools, the shift away from mid-year examinations and the expansion of applied learning programmes.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These are important steps in the right direction and I ask that we take another bold step forward.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: A paradigm shift is needed, one that balances academic proficiency with opportunities for passion-based exploration.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore's success has always been built on adaptability.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: So, let us adapt again to foster a generation that thrives not only academically but also holistically, where passion and pleasure fuel purpose and performance, not pressure.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With these shifts away from exam-based assessments, we can minimise the role and effect of "money" in children's educational outcomes, taking the pressure off young parents to avail their bandwidth and energy towards other personally meaningful pursuits that also make them positive role models for their children towards a purpose-driven life.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I have been in some conversations with older Singaporeans about the dismal birth rate and I often hear young people being judged as selfish for, I quote, "wanting to enjoy their own life instead of sacrificing for children." I want to speak up for all millennial and younger Singaporeans, that wanting to have more joy and enjoyment in life is not selfish.It is human.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In the 1970s and 1980s, when we were still trying to develop our economy, there were not many options for entertainment, recreation or opportunities for activities to derive enjoyment from.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Between work and home, ekeing out a living, home and kids afforded more joys.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Having kids, nurturing kids and having the joyful companionship of growing kids were enjoyable.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There was less entertainment, less distraction, fewer options and less comparison.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Today, family life no longer conjures up the notion of joy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Having a family brings with it notions of obligations, duty, pressure and sacrifice.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: All of these do not seem pleasurable at all to the current generation who have different and higher aspirations for their lives.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, a whole other host of pleasurable activities are now accessible.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is unnatural to ask people to choose pain over pleasure.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: While financial assistance is crucial, we must redefine the experience of parenthood to align with the aspirations of young Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Alongside financial support, we must reframe the narrative around parenthood.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Rather than merely compensating for the costs, let us shift attention and resources towards promoting the joys of parenthood and helping people see the intrinsic rewards of raising a family.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to amplify positive parenthood stories that resonate with the aspirations of the current generation, for example, how lifestyle and travel experiences are more meaningful and fun when shared with a spouse and children than alone.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can help the public realise that the same skills honed through parenthood, such as socioemotional awareness and regulation, communication and negotiation skills, strategic decision-making for use of resources and fostering healthy teamwork with one's spouse, are all life and leadership skills that apply professionally, too, to help one thrive in their career.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Let us engage employers as allies to reshape workplace culture for better employee satisfaction and retention.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Encouraging businesses to promote work-life reconciliation, such as family-friendly workplace cultures, "right to disconnect" policies or more "Bring Your Kid to Work Days", can make parenthood a compatible aspiration rather than a burden.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, we may need to slay the sacred cow of "self-sufficiency".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This is a social compact narrative we have held onto the past decades as a cornerstone of our social support policies, when in reality, all the social transfers that the Government has been rolling out is actually speaking to the opposite.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If we adjust that mindset towards "collective sufficiency", Singaporeans can feel less like they need to go it alone.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to invest in support networks for parents, where families feel connected, supported and less isolated in their parenting journeys.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Having community spaces and informal childminding networks that parents feel safe to park their kids with – in the neighbourhoods – while they run errands or go on a short date with each other, can go a long way to create a sense of psychological security around raising children.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The role of parenthood in providing emotional fulfilment is not talked about nor shared enough as yet.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We are living in a time of geopolitical turmoil.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Governments and businesses with global footprints are rushing to understand the impact of the new United States (US) tariffs and the responses of targeted countries, while watching for the next wave of actions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Headline-grabbing as they are, the US tariffs are but part of a broader America-first agenda.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, we see China pivoting from the West to strengthen its trade, military and diplomatic positions with the rest of the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A global South gaining in confidence, forming and expanding alliances, like BRICS, and crafting their own paths in search of growth amid geopolitical fractures.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We are also grappling with shocks from evolving conflicts, increasingly frequent and increasingly devastating impacts of climate change and polarised populations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A small, open trade-dependent economy, we have been committed to a rules-based trading system and a neutral and pragmatic principles-based foreign policy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And this instability, this increasing tendency of great powers to break rules, norms and long-standing alliances is disquieting.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is at stake is not just whether we can grow the economy 1% or 3% this year or next year.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is whether we can sustain our hard-earned position in this world: a global trading and business hub, a financial powerhouse, a technology and innovation hub, a shining little red dot on the global economic and geopolitical stage.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we do not measure success by these numbers alone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We measure success based on the success of our people, on the degree to which our people are fulfilling their potential, on our ability to provide not just jobs, but better jobs, better opportunities, better lives for all Singaporeans, including seniors, ex-offenders, persons with disabilities or special needs and their caregivers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And this is why our new social compact matters.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Budget advances Forward Singapore (Forward SG), with short-term measures to help all Singaporeans and investments for the future to keep our economy growing and our people thriving.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet I believe a deeper treatment of the shifting landscape and what it means for Singapore is helpful.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singaporeans deserve a fuller understanding of what is going on, the potential impact on Singapore and what other countries are doing and what we might do in response to plan their own lives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some say that in spite of geopolitical headwinds, Singapore's value proposition would not suddenly become unattractive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some say we need not worry, since we have a trade deficit with the US; and some say Singapore might even benefit, for example, from China Plus One.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Did you ever imagine a day when the US would vote with Russia on a United Nations (UN) resolution backed by Europe?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As former British Prime Minister Lord Palmerston once said, nations have no permanent friends or allies, they only have permanent interest.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The fact is, these trends are changing fast and the outlook is uncertain.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Within each of these trends, there are challenges but also opportunities for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What uncertainty does do is compel us to reframe our strategies and build a new vision for the future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must articulate how we will thrive in the shifting landscape and I say we must build a future founded on resilience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our financial strength, far-sighted leadership, good governance and stability and the successive generations of the People's Action Party (PAP) Governments have helped us weather and emerge stronger out of many storms.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: From the struggles of the early years of Independence to COVID-19, we must protect and not squander these.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, there are facets of resilience that we need to develop or strengthen further as we confront a future of heightened uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Three, I will focus on in my speech: a supply chain resilience, climate resilience and above all, a resilient people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Resilience is not just about being strong and stoic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Resilience is about our ability and willingness to adapt, to innovate, to overcome, to turn adversity into advantage, recognising that our greatest strength is our unity, holding dear our foundational values of openness, multiculturalism and self-determination.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: COVID-19 and the Russia-Ukraine and Middle East conflicts laid bare the impact of supply chain disruptions and the importance of resilient supply chains.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Trade disputes, sanctions, unexpected crisis and conflicts can ripple through economies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Geopolitics is not the only thing affecting global supply chains.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Climate change, digitisation and AI talent shortages are also reshaping supply chain.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: All this affects Singapore on three levels: one, our own needs; two, as a global foreign direct investment (FDI) and business hub; and three, as a logistics and trading hub.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It could have a profound impacts on cost supply and price volatility and inflation, on FDI and jobs, especially in key sectors, like manufacturing and the digital economy, and on trade, our lifeblood.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If the price of steel is very volatile, what happens to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and their Singaporean workers in industries, like construction, that have traditionally kept very little wiggle room in their contracts?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Or if tariffs, export controls or data sovereignty requirements are placed on data centres and AI infrastructure, what happens to our digital and AI hub ambitions?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For countries and companies, the strong and stoic approaches to building supply chain resilience are stockpiling and onshoring or reshoring.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And as geopolitical headwinds grow stronger, companies must diversify sources, rethink their logistics and supply chain strategies, refine their go-to-market, invest in new partnerships and try and shape policy and negotiation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To help them reconfigure their supply chains, companies will need a deeper level of insight into their supply chain.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, insight into the landed cost of components that go into the products they buy that will help them figure out optimal so sourcing strategies for each component and not just the finished product.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They can also break up their manufacturing processes and move different processes to different sites to improve trade compliance and reduce cost.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government can also champion new partnerships and contracting models, focusing on collaboration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: An ecosystem approach will benefit many sectors as supply chains around us reconfigure.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I think whether China Plus One will directly benefit Singapore is arguable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A lot of what is moving out is of lower value-add, too low for our relatively high-cost base.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But there are indirect benefits in managing this new supply chain as a connector, as an orchestrator, enhancing our position as a trading hub.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And so, we should build up supply chain and procurement centres of excellence here.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We know climate change is existential for us.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We know that whether 40 degree-days become the norm or flooding in Woodlands or Bukit Timah will become more frequent or whether parts of Marine Parade will sink under rising sea levels, will depend more on what other companies do than what we do.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we still need to be build climate resilience, even if it is the strong and stoic kind.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am glad Budget 2025 puts more in climate adaptation and resilience by topping-up funds for coastal protection, for example, alongside climate mitigation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In my Budget 2021 speech, I called for Singapore to act boldly on the green economy with President Trump's executive order to pull the US out of the Paris Agreement, US firms are awaiting clarity on the new administration's climate actions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But climate change is not waiting and refuses to be ignored with extreme weather becoming more common.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Europe remains steadfast in its commitment to its Green Deal while adapting for economic realities; while Asian companies are primed to seize opportunities with many doubling down on investments in green business build builds, electric vehicles (EVs), batteries, solar, green hydrogen, low carbon, agriculture technology – setting the stage for another revolution, clean energy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's geographic constraints lead to a limited ability to deploy large-scale renewable energy sources and high cost.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Importing energy and green and green hydrogen have their own high challenges.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While critics say that SMRs are costlier than renewables and slow to deploy, the high cost of renewables in Singapore make us uniquely positioned to make the business case work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It must be complemented with strong regulatory support, capability build and very importantly, stringent safety regulations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To gain the political support needed to make nuclear energy a key pillar of our green economy, we need to assess and develop these conditions carefully.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At milestones like this, we often recognise the struggles and sacrifices made by our pioneer generations in building Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Sustaining the miracle of Singapore is not about resting on our laurels.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to invest in education and lifelong learning healthcare, including mental health and social well-being.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In my maiden speech in this House, I called for the Government, businesses and citizens to make us the nation that learns the fastest, to invest in our people and double-down on skilling and lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am heartened by how SkillsFuture has evolved since then.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must make sure that these programmes are properly curated to improve the chances of participants landing a better job.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With SkillsFuture in full flight, the next area to focus on is economic empowerment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to continue to create job opportunities and push for fair wages to give Singaporeans financial stability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need a national programme for career guidance and development that helps individuals navigate their career progression.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And we need to do much more to encourage entrepreneurship and innovation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They must want to work on moonshot projects: in AI, green energy and other critical areas.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
