text: But I think we have found an approach in Singapore that works for us.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not perfect, but we continue to make it better.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The lower and middle-income will receive more support, while the higher-income and wealthier segments of the population will contribute more.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is a fair and progressive tax and redistribution system, anchored on our values of a fair and just society.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And the strength of our fiscal system is internationally recognised.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is hard-earned credibility that we have built up over many, many decades.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not something we should take for granted, because that same credibility can be quickly destroyed in the wrong hands.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And so, at the end of the day, on something as fundamental as this, Singaporeans will decide.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Will they prefer a government that underestimates our needs, spends more from our hard-earned reserves, and leaves us weaker?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Or will Singaporeans prefer a government that steadfastly upholds fiscal responsibility and discipline, and ensures we have enough resources for current and future generations to handle unexpected challenges?

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We take our duty as stewards of the country seriously.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We remain true to our mission and manage our finances carefully for the benefit of all Singaporeans, now and in the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to do our best to convince Singaporeans that ours is the right approach.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Thriving amidst adversity is never easy but that is what the Singapore story is all about from the very beginning, and we have strong foundations today that give us confidence to move forward.

speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, let us write the next chapter of our Singapore story and move onward together for a better tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I assure him that my clarifications will not be with an eye on election rallies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, on the question of Climate Vouchers for individuals who are living in private household residences, the irony here is that the cost of living affects people across the board, including those in private dwellings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And giving them assistance also makes the point that the issue cuts across all segments of society, which was the metapoint that I made when I addressed the subject before I made that point in my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second issue, the Prime Minister asked about "Where is the turbocharging?" on the matter of inflation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I took reference from the reply that was given by the Government in early 2024.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think it was referred to by Member Saktiandi as well, where the MAS set out a projected number.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, if you take that figure with the lower end of the estimate at 2.5%, that is 40%, and that is the contribution of the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MOF was making assessments and detailed projections and would come back with detailed revenue updates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So far, we have not received these updates, and I hope the Prime Minister can share with us what these numbers are.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2023, the Prime Minister also spoke, towards the end of his speech, about the occasional papers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MOF released an occasional paper in 2023, covering the medium-term fiscal outlook up to FY2030.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But that paper did not include corporate income tax revenues that would accrue arising from BEPS.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And, finally, Sir, in the course of our last Budget debate as well, I remember a senior PAP backbencher saying that he was pleasantly surprised about what he had said only two three weeks earlier in the context of the Motion that we had in Parliament on the reserves, he had hoped that our corporate tax collections would overtake NIRC within a 10-year time frame.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And merely two weeks later, during the 2024 Budget debate, that that overtaking had occurred: NIRC became the second top revenue source and corporate income tax overtook it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister said that it was not so clear cut whether that trajectory would continue and that it was too early to tell whether it can be sustained, so we will continue to monitor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask the Prime Minister whether there is some clarity now, on that point?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is meant to encourage everyone to go for energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Members have asked for this, residents themselves have asked for this and we think that, in the broader scheme of things, it is a move we can make.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean, the WP is free to object to it if they feel like it is not worth doing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if they feel that they do not want to support this, please say so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we think it is a worthwhile move to make to encourage energy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And the explanation he gave that the impact of GST on inflation, the once-off effect or the transitory effect, is high as a proportion of the base inflation, actually does not make sense.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because if I take that view, then I really should be raising GST at the time of very high inflation, then the proportionate impact would be quite small, because the 1% on a very high inflation base means that there is very little impact.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if that is the case and that is what the WP feels, then really there should not be any concern about the timing of the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The third set of questions around corporate tax, they are related.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Go back to the beginning of the decade when we started looking at tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Actually, at that time, there was no certainty at all that corporate income tax would go up, even with BEPS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because, remember, a stated objective of BEPS, the explicit-stated objective, one of it, is to transfer and re-allocate profits to market jurisdictions – large economies, markets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are going to be impacted by that very move.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We would have profits re-allocated from us and we would be suffering.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It has not worked out or it still has not been implemented, this part of BEPS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But that was the beginning, what they wanted to do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we were concerned and that is why we did not think that we would be able to get more revenues from corporate income tax.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Later on, BEPS evolved and people started talking about having a minimum corporate tax of 15% applied across all countries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, but that did not mean that competition would disappear and everyone would just operate with a 15% corporate income tax.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have explained, even with a consensus earlier struck on a minimum corporate income tax, countries were already carving out manoeuvring space for themselves to introduce all sorts of different kinds of incentives in order to attract investments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was the reality that we were faced with.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, even if the domestic top-up tax yields more revenue, we are very likely to have to also spend more to maintain our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Thirdly, the situation today has gotten a lot fuzzier because the US has pulled out of the OECD consensus and we have no clue at all how this will emerge in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why it is so difficult to say, let us give an updated projection.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not even know what the global tax arrangement will be like in the next one, two years, given the unpredictabilities we face now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What is the next move going to be?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in the meantime, we are fortunate that even before the domestic top-up tax, the minimum corporate income tax, has kicked in, companies have started to do more substantial activities out of Singapore and our corporate income tax collections have gone up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But as I have explained, it is too early to tell whether this is a lasting trend.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But whatever it is, it is good that we are in such a position and we will make good use of the revenues to ensure that Singaporeans benefit, to ensure that we continue to advance our goals.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, on the occasional papers, I mentioned that we will be committed to publishing and updating them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are no significant updates that we have been able to make in recent times given the very complex global situation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we have not given an update to the occasional paper recently.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But as I have said just now, when we get better clarity around our revenue position, in particular, we will certainly be committed to providing an update to the occasional paper.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Prime Minister mentioned this is because of the bond that we issued to fund the infrastructure and then it comes in as part of the fiscal position.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether we should remind Singaporeans that this is actually a sum of money that we need to pay over a period of time through depreciation of the assets?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Because it comes in as cash now and if we were to use it for our current expenditure, we have to remind ourselves that this is an amount of money that needs to be paid over a period of time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And therefore, we should not see it as surplus, as in, like revenue surpluses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Prime Minister, for this financial year, what is the estimated amount that is attributable to the second instalment of the Forward SG policy moves, whether he anticipates this subsequent instalment to be an even higher amount and whether the $40 billion that was mentioned earlier, is it still the amount that we envisage will be spent?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because as I said, there is no free lunch.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The capitalisation of these large projects is the right thing to do for inter-generational equity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not just to generate near-term fiscal space for us, so we will do more to explain to Singaporeans the treatment of SINGA and why we should not assume that because we are doing this capitalisation accounting treatment, that there is somehow some additional freebie in the near term that allows us to spend more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But overall, if you look at the social initiatives that we are putting together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And a lot of the Forward SG agenda will be on the social spending and the chart I showed just now clearly showed that social spending is rising.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we fully expect more to be spent on this front – on Forward SG and on social development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But as I said in my speech, where I think the squeeze is felt most acutely is by those in the middle, those who are sandwiched by commitments to their parents and children, but who do not happen to work in one of the eight sectors that the PWM currently covers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, the first question I have is what is what is being done to help these workers realise wage increments that are commensurate, both with their contributions to greater productivity and the high cost of living?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Related to this, the Prime Minister emphasise that skills upgrading and re-training is key to elevating nominal wages and I do not disagree with this in principle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But as I explained in my speech, real wage gains over the past five years have not kept up with increases in productivity and the cost of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, the question that begs to be asked is, how can the Government assure Singaporeans who do choose to re-train and reskill and upskill, that those efforts will ultimately be rewarded by actual wage increments when the unfettered labour market does not seem to already be doing so?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are pushing their wages through progressive wages, Workfare and many other initiatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we are also focused on the middle-income and on the broad middle to ensure that Singaporeans do enjoy continued real wage increases.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Generally speaking, we have been able to achieve positive outcomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I know Assoc Prof Jamus Lim talked about the last five years of data where wages seem to lag behind productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But you can slice data over any shorter-term period and look at the lags or when sometimes wages will be lagging behind, sometimes wages will be ahead of productivity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Certainly, in the last five years, wages have not caught up with productivity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if you look at the longer-term time frame, we want to ensure wages do match productivity increases and it has been so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will continue to ensure this remains.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The best way to do that is to ensure a strong, vibrant economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But not just leaving it to market forces alone, but to support workers with all the investments we are putting into SkillsFuture, which is not only benefiting the lower-wage workers, but supporting the broad middle of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we are redoubling efforts, investing more in every worker through a whole range of incentives and schemes and programmes through working with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), our brothers and sisters in the Labour Movement through the Company Training Committee (CTC) grants, working with enterprises who are prepared to do work workforce transformation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are putting in place all the building blocks that are necessary to strengthen our SkillsFuture system and to make sure that Singaporeans continue to enjoy sustained real income increases.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The first question is, with the generous support measures, including the SG60 vouchers, I would like to ask the Prime Minister what impact these measures will have inflation on inflation?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The second question is, I think what the Prime Minister spoke about the uncertain environment globally that is actually unfolding; actually, that is really real.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As far as the Cost-of-Living Support Package is concerned, this is not new.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have been providing it in previous Budgets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But this year, because of SG60, we have a special package to share the fruits of a nation's progress with all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not going to be year after year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And within the parameters and the amounts that we are giving out through SG60, overall, there should be a manageable impact on inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second question on worst case scenarios, I mean, there is a whole range of them that we will have to prepare for.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have said, it can go from something as extreme as conflict in Asia, which we have not seen for the most part in decades, but we have to be prepared now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The risk is not insignificant; it has certainly gone up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You have hotspots in our part of the world where accidents, miscalculations can happen and it will certainly have a knock-on impact on sentiment, confidence and the whole economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But you could also have other kinds of emergencies and threats, cybersecurity, pandemics, supply chain disruptions, a whole range of things can happen, and even if they do not happen nearby, within Asia itself, something that happens far away can have knock-on impacts here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But at the same time, draw confidence from the fact that our fiscal strength allows us to respond swiftly to any emergency.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, let me clarify that PSP is not displeased with the vouchers, because we believe that they will help Singaporeans in the short term, but not over the long term.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Prime Minister has said that he has concrete plans for the future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, can I ask if his plans include plans to lower our high cost of living with measures that have longer-term effects rather than vouchers?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Prime Minister not agree that this problem can be managed if we have differentiated rules based on age, for example, giving younger CPF members greater leeway in investing in higher risk, higher return instruments, and for older workers to limit their exposure to such investments?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, there are Lifecycle Funds, Target Date Funds, which provide that kind of glide path that Ms Poa talked about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you are young, you take higher risk, and then as you get older it, the portfolio becomes a sort of a safer portfolio in order to minimise the risk.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Actually, these funds are already available in the market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They tend not to be very popular with Singaporeans for some reason, but they are available and we hope that we can make them more accessible to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But anyway, as I have highlighted the considerations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are studying the matter and we will look further into it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the earlier question on whether we are doing more in terms of structural programmes and schemes to help Singaporeans cope with the cost of living, yes, of course, we are.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have mentioned just now, and all that I have said in the round-up speech, the bulk of our Government spending is in this, it is directed towards these structural longer-term programmes: in education, SkillsFuture, job training, upgrading Singaporeans, in ensuring that our economy is strong, so that Singaporeans earn higher incomes on a consistent basis, but at the same time, providing a social support system to provide greater assurances on the basics in life and to make sure that if anyone suffers a setback, we are there to catch them and help them recover stronger.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us try not to put a wedge between the Government and the people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no point in saying the Government is rich and has strong fiscal position and then painting this as being detrimental to the well-being of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, it benefits Singaporeans in so many ways because we are able to invest more in Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are able to provide them with more support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are able to help them with so many different areas of life and ensure that everyone benefits from a higher standard of living.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is easy to talk about spending more, sailing closer to the wind.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You know, we have so much money, let us just be a bit more cavalier and relaxed about our fiscal rules; do not have to be so tight.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But at the end of the day, who bears the price?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If something were to go wrong, if a crisis were to hit, if we end up physically weaker as a country, who pays the price?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us not gamble with Singaporeans' lives and future.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: I also raised a number of questions about how the Culture Pass is going to be administered.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: Could I ask if the Prime Minister has a response to those questions?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I mentioned, not in the context of earnings management of companies, but how if you look at it in the context of transparency and the matching principle, in the sense that if you look at these top-ups to the funds, they are to meet our spending needs in the future, similar to how if you look at our SINGA expenditure, our development expenditures, these are also spendings that are meant for longer-term needs and purposes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But in the sense that if you have the spending made from the endowment and trust funds, we get a lot less granularity versus the regular expenditures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I mean, those who go to the Budget website can see the whole full Heads of Expenditure under the different Ministries, under different spending categories.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, in that context, under the whole premise of greater transparency and the matching of the expenses against the periods in which they are incurred.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would the Prime Minister be able to share the rationale behind this?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We highlight what they are and if there is a need for more information on the spending and expenditure associated with each of these funds, we will take a look at how we can put out more information.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any more clarifications for the Prime Minister?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At your instruction that I should ask all the questions in one go, and I have a lot of questions, so I have actually waited until the last one.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If any other Members want to raise questions, I would encourage them to raise them before me.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Okay, I have questions in three categories: one, on the Budget structure, I have two questions; two, on the NIRC, I have three questions; and on public housing, I have four questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the Budget structure, first, I want to highlight or emphasise that PSP is all for fiscal prudence.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I think the Prime Minister and Finance Minister and the Government have always been taking the attitude that for the surpluses, the "more the merrier".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what I want to say is that surpluses are not always the "more the merrier".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would like to ask the Prime Minister: is the Government aiming to run a balanced Budget over its term, or as much surpluses as possible, because we are of the view that surpluses coming from over taxation and overcharging are the drivers of structural inflation in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And some of this has been transferred to GIC already.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, these are the two questions for the Budget structure.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You can move on to your next three questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, my next three questions are on the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government has repeatedly highlighted that NIRC contributes 20% of the Budget resources, implying that this money was spent on the current generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: To determine whether this is actually the case, I would like to ask the following questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think it is about $70 billion or $80 billion, but I would like the Prime Minister to confirm.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In other words, these are the NIRCs that have been allocated to the Budgets over the last few years, not spent and still remaining in the endowment and trust funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Third question, we already have the SINGA framework which can be used to fund important infrastructure like Changi Airport and coastal protection at a much lower cost to the people than raising revenue from GST hike or COEs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My last category, Speaker, is on public housing and I have four questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: PSP has presented the Affordable Homes Scheme and Millennial Apartment Scheme as viable solutions to our current housing problems.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government has been criticising our ideas without much basis because it does not seem to have done research on them, and at the same time, the Government is not offering enough explanation as to how it is going to solve the ongoing problems that we are already experiencing today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First question, what is the latest update on the solution for the lease decay problem?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second question, can I ask the Prime Minister whether the Government has a better solution than the Affordable Homes Scheme to the lease decay problem, which threatens Singaporeans' retirement security because their retirement funds are tied to the value of their flats which may soon decay for those living in older flats?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Four, what safeguards does the Government have in place if the resale market price collapses in the near future because of the increase in supply from the ramping up of the BTO supply in recent years?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And, sorry, Speaker, since you said I should ask all my questions, there is one more question I want to ask.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I would also like to chip in on the point raised by the Leader of the Opposition on turbocharging inflation due to the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think the information provided by the Prime Minister is not enough to describe the situation because: one, the ground inflation is actually much more than what is reflected in the statistic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have lived in Singapore for more than 60 years and in my personal experience, even including the experience in the 1970s when I accompanied by mother to go to the community centre to buy cheap rice from NTUC, the recent few years, really I can feel it, the prices are just leapfrogging, especially for cooked food.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think the word "turbocharging" is not too far from the truth.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But he is an economist, I am an economist.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We know that there is such a thing as anticipatory behaviour.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: A lot of the merchants were already raising prices in 2022.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the 6% is a more of, a better reflection that people are anticipating that GST is coming.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Anyway, so, combining all three years, we have more than double-digit increases in inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, on the Budget structure, I think Mr Leong has mischaracterised the Government's position.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not the bigger the surplus, the merrier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not just look at it from that point of view.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We adopt a responsible and prudent fiscal approach in budgeting.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are prepared to spend more if they are good ideas.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I said, the issue is not about spending more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The issue is about getting the policies right and making the right decisions to support Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if this entails more spending, we will.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As you have seen in our social development spending, it is rising.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I fully expect it to rise further.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The issue at hand is really about the approach towards thinking about budgeting.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our approach is one where we recognise that there are fiscal rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if there are fiscal rules, let us respect the rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us not just keep thinking about changing the rules the first time we run into trouble and need more money.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us stay disciplined, operate within these fiscal rules and, if we need more money, we raise the revenues to support and cover the additional spending needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the fundamental approach that we adopt.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think PSP may have a different approach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And they are fine to have a different approach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But as I say, have a care about what you want and how you want to manage our country's finances.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You may think it is not a big deal, just spend more, disregard the rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But step by step, these are sure ways to weaken Singapore fiscally.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And when that happens, it is Singaporeans who suffer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We expect to run balanced Budgets over the medium term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Okay, that answers the first part on the Budget structure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All the NIRC revenue goes into the Consolidated Fund and then we spend from the Consolidated Fund.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong's objection appears to be some of the spending goes into these funds, the endowment and trust funds, and that these are not real spending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But that is not the case, as I have tried to explain just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In some instances, like the Changi Airport Fund, we are going to expend, spend the money quite soon when we build Terminal 5.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In some cases a bit longer, but certainly within this generation, we will be spending a lot of that money.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And there are good reasons why we set them aside now in order to spend and make sure that we have the resources we need for these near-term and longer-term expenditures, which will be spent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong says better to fund these projects through SINGA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are, I think he said, lower cost.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Actually, SINGA is not lower cost at all.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is just that SINGA is a different way of financing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For very large, long asset life projects, we think from an inter-generational equity point of view, it is better to spread it out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are going to have real spending needs which will be covered through these funds and we will have projects that are funded by SINGA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And overall, if you look at the revenue moves that we have made – GST, as well as the other revenue changes, tax changes we made in this term of Government – as I have explained, we are now in a good fiscal position.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it gives us the ability to move quickly and to do things for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Having this strong fiscal position does not come at the expense of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you look at the tax burden, if you look at what we impose as taxes relative to many other advanced economies, our tax burden is in fact quite low.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is objective data; you just have to compare.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we intend to keep our overall tax burden low.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we will maximise effectiveness from every amount that we spend in order to make sure we maximise the benefits and outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Thirdly, on public housing and lease decay, what is our solution?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have explained the broad outlines of VERS already and we will provide more details in due course.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the pricing will have to look at Singaporeans' incomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And as I had illustrated with a concrete example, the BTO price for that particular example has been updated in line with median incomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that will be the way we ensure that BTO and HDB will continue to be affordable.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Are we worried that we are over building?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I thought Mr Leong and PSP are worried about not enough flats.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we had this debate with the WP a few years ago about are we over building and therefore we are going to have a property market crash.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If we are concerned about high prices, then we need to build more, particularly because we have to catch up with the disruption in supply that happened during the COVID years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And it is because of that disruption in supply that has created that imbalance in the market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is exactly why we have to build more now to restore that balance, and as I said just now, we can be assured that we will be able to restore balance because HDB flats are only purchased by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will be able to build enough HDB flats for every Singaporean household.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The Prime Minister mentioned earlier on that had there not been a GST increase, we would have run a deficit over the past two years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I recall, during our debate on the GST that the fiscal hole that would have been met by the GST increase would have been something in the order of $3.7 billion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I understand that last year, we ran a very small surplus, but this year we appear to have run a significant surplus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, were GST receipts substantially larger than we expected this year?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is both factors, not just GST alone.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I find it strange that we have spent all this time trying to defend a surplus, while most developed economies in the world are begging for a surplus.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: So, I had to stand up and say this.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, we have benefited a lot through the reserves that we have had, not just the NIRC, but the fact that we have been able to maintain such high quality credit ratings, which make people want to lend to us, which make people want to invest in our country and which make global companies want to come here and pay corporate income tax to us.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think we should be thankful of where we are.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We should be thankful to our preceding generations for putting us where we are and we should make sure that we keep up the good work that has been done by our preceding generations for us and keep on adding to that.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to add a question for the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: They are here one year, they are gone the next year, largely because of profitability, largely because of the fluidity of capital today.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: What strategies do we have in place to keep Singapore attractive as we deal with a very complex world where many people are competing for investment dollars and consequently, new projects, which can be a source of significant corporate income tax on the revenue side?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: On the employment side, we are investing a lot in SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: But many of the skills that will be needed in a few years, especially because through the advent and the expansion of AI, we do not know as yet.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: So, how do we plan for the unknown?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: If I may say, it is very hard to do.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: But what plans do we have in place other than what we are good at it already, which is being nimble?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the point about how we make our investments sticky, which is really what Mr Parekh talked about, how do we anchor these investments, recognising that they have many options and the MNEs do have leverage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The simple answer and the only answer is that we have to up our game.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This adds value to me and I want to do more out of Singapore." That is something we will continue to do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Having good local companies help too, something that Mr Parekh talked about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because when they have good local companies based here, they supply to the MNEs, they form partnerships with the MNEs, it strengthens the ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is what we are committed to doing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is what all the initiatives in the Budget seek to do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On SkillsFuture and training for future skills, it is inherently a very difficult topic.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: No one can tell what the new requirements of the future are.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I think there are some basics which we can already train for, there are some fundamentals we can train for, and we are doing that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And in designing many of our programmes and courses, the course providers, our IHLs, the partners we work with, do not just design these courses in a vacuum.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They often engage industry partners and understand what the latest business trends are, what are the latest requirements, and then customise skills programmes accordingly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is a fundamental approach we take which hopefully will enable us to be quick, nimble and to be able to adjust to new and shifting trends.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I wish to make another pitch to the Prime Minister to consider measures to lower cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Does he not agree that if we lower cost of living, it will benefit all Singaporeans, whereas if we take the approach of investing in education and training, to raise wages, then, not everybody can benefit from that, especially older Singaporeans and retirees?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Second clarification, since the Prime Minister mentioned that our CPI data is collected correctly, can I ask how our CPI calculations take into account shrinkflation – that means the price may remain the same, but the portion is smaller?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean, if we have talk about some of the big items of cost of living, what are they?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our approach is, let us get the pricing right.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because if you do not get the pricing right, basically, you are giving a subsidy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We get the pricing right, then, we will subsidise where there is a need to, and we have, on housing, for example.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We can debate how much subsidy is correct, but we are, and we are doing more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so, all of the measures that we are doing, it is not just about equipping, training, empowering Singaporeans with skills to get better incomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is also to strengthen our safety nets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is also to strengthen our safety nets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is to make sure Singaporeans are able to afford the basics, be it healthcare, retirement, housing or education, and it is to make sure that we are able to help those who suffer setbacks and enable them to recover and bounce back stronger.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On CPI, the Department of Statistics has its methodology.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think there are different ways in which we can address that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Melvin Yong mentioned some of that, through Price Kaki and also through maybe getting retailers to put out unit prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are some measures we can think about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it is a constant battle to make sure that we ensure Singaporeans have the ability to cope with cost pressures which we know exist.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Setting aside the headline statistics, setting aside the fact that CPI inflation is easing, we do recognise that there are real concerns because Singaporeans have to adjust to new price realities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we are doing more to help them through cost of living support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we are doing more to make sure that Singaporeans will have enough in this Budget to address their concerns on cost of living.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have a few more clarifications arising from what he has replied just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, the difference between PSP and PAP is that PSP prefers to put more money into the pocket of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can VERS be a solution anymore, because the lease decay itself has already set in, as demonstrated in the Ang Mo Kio Selective En Bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS) case.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The economics of SERS has totally changed as a result of the lease decay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And so, we would have expected that the same economics will be applied to VERS.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Given the economics have changed, will VERS continue to be a viable solution?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Anyway, the Government owes Singaporeans a clear answer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Since my housing Motion, when the Government promised to update us on VERS, it is more than two years already.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And the lease decay problem has surfaced for more than seven years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Till today, there is no clear answer about lease decay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Government is using the Prime and the Plus schemes to slow down the increase to $1 million, but on the other hand, increasing the HDB deficit, which, in turn increases the burden on the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Last question, on whether the ramp-up of this BTO supply now will eventually lead to an adjustment of the resale market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Actually, PSP's stance has always been, we are not in favour of just ramping up the supply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We have said in our Housing Motion that we should also increase the supply of quality rental flats so that this does not become a supply in the hands of owners but is a rental flat supply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because if we increase the number of owners owning flats, then, there will be a point where all the Singaporeans have owned flats already, and the next thing will be a downward adjustment in our HDB prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not about the Government holding back something.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is about making sure that all that we collect goes back to Singaporeans in different ways.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some, of course, are direct transfers, but not all of it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: After all, the PSP itself says that you should not do so much because this will create entitlement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, yes, some part of it goes into direct transfers, short-term measures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But a lot of it goes into a whole range of different programmes which benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are putting back the funds to benefit all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the size of the endowment trust funds, I do not have the figures off-hand.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We can deal with that separately in the COS or in a separate Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because the first flat for VERS is not due anytime soon.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But eventually, the time will come when we have to do VERS and as we approach that date, we will certainly provide more details.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The issue around Plus and Prime flats, let us be very clear.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Why did we have to do Plus and Prime flats?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because for Standard flats, we know that the resale market moves up and down in the near term, but we will price the BTO flats not based on resale market alone, but we look at incomes and price for affordability.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if we apply that same subsidy to localise popular areas, the flats will be more unaffordable, and can we make the subsidy more?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Well, we can, but then, you have a problem where there will be a lottery effect.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: People will immediately know the subsidy is greater in these popular areas, "Let us go for that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that is a fair and equitable way and that is why we have the Plus and Prime framework.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On rental flats, do we want to have home ownerships for all Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is what Singaporeans want and I think that gives every Singaporean a stake in our nation's success.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It has been the foundation of Singapore society, the foundation of Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I hope it is not an old clarification, a repeated clarification.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I just want to clarify one last point with the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: He did not really quite answer my question.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Without the Prime and Plus scheme, do you agree that our BTO price, in certain areas, would have gone above the $1 million?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When my parents bought their Marine Parade flat in the 1970s, it was $30,000 or $30,000 plus.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At that time, will they ever, ever imagine that they could sell the flat for $500,000 in the 1990s?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is because our standards of living have gone up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That progress, that success has benefited every homeowner in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A concrete stake in our nation's progress and not just that, but eventually, a home and a nest egg which you can tap on for retirement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a sound and a key pillar of our social compact, which we will continue to improve, enhance and build upon.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: When will the Government be able to let us know the details of VERS?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not have the answer now, but you can ask the Minister for National Development at the COS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am sure he will give you a response.
